# Vercel

Run Endtest automated tests automatically when Vercel deployments are created.

Part of the Endtest documentation (Integrations). Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/docs/integrations/vercel

---
## Overview

The Endtest Vercel integration lets you run Endtest automated tests automatically when a Vercel deployment is created.

When a deployment is triggered in Vercel, Endtest can start a test execution and report the result back to Vercel as a deployment check.

This is useful when you want every Preview or Production deployment to be validated by an Endtest test suite before your team treats the deployment as ready.

## What the integration does

The integration can:

- Detect new Vercel deployments.
- Run an Endtest API request for the selected Vercel project.
- Pass the Vercel deployment URL into your Endtest API request.
- Show an **Endtest** deployment check inside Vercel.
- Mark the check as passed or failed based on the Endtest result.

## Requirements

Before configuring the integration, make sure you have:

- An Endtest account.
- A Vercel account.
- A Vercel project connected to the integration.
- An Endtest test suite or test case that can be executed through the Endtest API.

## Step 1: Create the Endtest API request

In Endtest, open the test suite or test case that you want to run from Vercel.

Generate or copy the Endtest API request for that execution.

The API request should be the same request you would normally use to start an Endtest execution from a CI/CD system.

For example, it may look similar to this:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://app.endtest.io/api.php" \
  -d "appId=YOUR_APP_ID" \
  -d "appCode=YOUR_APP_CODE" \
  -d "action=startTestSuite" \
  -d "testSuite=YOUR_TEST_SUITE_ID"
```

Use the API request generated by your own Endtest account. Do not use the placeholder values above.

## Step 2: Use the Vercel deployment URL in your test

If your Endtest test should run against the newly deployed Vercel URL, use one of these placeholders inside the API request:

| Placeholder | Description |
|---|---|
| `{{VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URL}}` | Full deployment URL, including `https://` |
| `{{VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_HOST}}` | Deployment host only, without `https://` |
| `{{VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URL_ENCODED}}` | URL-encoded deployment URL, useful inside query parameters |

For example:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://app.endtest.io/api.php" \
  -d "appId=YOUR_APP_ID" \
  -d "appCode=YOUR_APP_CODE" \
  -d "action=startTestSuite" \
  -d "testSuite=YOUR_TEST_SUITE_ID" \
  -d "baseUrl={{VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URL}}"
```

The exact parameter name depends on how your Endtest API request is configured.

## Step 3: Install the Endtest integration in Vercel

In Vercel, open the Endtest integration page and click **Connect Account** or **Add Integration**.

During the installation flow, Vercel will ask you to authorize Endtest.

After authorization, Vercel will open the Endtest configuration page.

If you are not already signed in to Endtest, sign in first and then open the configuration page again.

## Step 4: Configure the Vercel project

On the Endtest Vercel configuration page:

1. Select the Vercel project.
2. Paste the Endtest API request.
3. Choose which deployment types should trigger Endtest.
4. Save the configuration.

The available options are:

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| **Preview deployments** | Run Endtest for Vercel Preview deployments. |
| **Production deployments** | Run Endtest for Vercel Production deployments. |
| **Blocking check** | Make the Endtest deployment check blocking in Vercel. |
| **Enabled** | Enable or disable this project configuration. |

For most teams, enabling both **Preview deployments** and **Production deployments** is a good starting point.

Use **Blocking check** only if you want Vercel to treat the Endtest check as required before the deployment is considered fully valid.

## Step 5: Trigger a Vercel deployment

After saving the configuration, trigger a deployment in Vercel.

You can do this by:

- Pushing a commit to the connected Git repository.
- Creating a Preview deployment.
- Redeploying an existing deployment.

When Vercel creates the deployment, the Endtest integration will create an **Endtest** deployment check.

When the deployment becomes ready, Endtest will start the configured test execution.

## Step 6: Review the result

After the Endtest execution finishes, the Vercel deployment check is updated.

Possible outcomes:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Passed | The Endtest execution finished successfully. |
| Failed | The Endtest execution failed, had errors, or could not be completed. |
| Running | Endtest is still executing the test. |

You can open the Endtest results page from the execution result to review screenshots, logs, videos, and step-level details.

## Recommended setup

A common setup is:

- Run tests on every Preview deployment.
- Run a smaller smoke suite on every Production deployment.
- Use the Vercel deployment URL placeholder so the test runs against the exact deployment.
- Enable blocking checks only for stable smoke tests.
- Keep longer regression suites non-blocking or trigger them separately.

## Example API request with a deployment URL

This example shows how a Vercel deployment URL can be passed into an Endtest execution:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://app.endtest.io/api.php" \
  -d "appId=YOUR_APP_ID" \
  -d "appCode=YOUR_APP_CODE" \
  -d "action=startTestSuite" \
  -d "testSuite=YOUR_TEST_SUITE_ID" \
  -d "variables[baseUrl]={{VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URL}}"
```

Your actual request may use a different action, test suite identifier, or variable format.

## Troubleshooting

### The Endtest check does not appear in Vercel

Make sure:

- The Vercel project is selected in the Endtest configuration page.
- The configuration is enabled.
- The deployment type is enabled. For example, Preview deployments require **Preview deployments** to be checked.
- The Endtest integration is installed for the correct Vercel account or team.
- A new deployment was created after the integration was configured.

### The check appears but stays running

The Endtest execution may still be running.

Open Endtest and check the execution results for that test suite or test case.

If the execution does not start, verify that the API request is valid.

### The check fails

Open the Endtest result page and review:

- Failed steps.
- Screenshots.
- Browser logs.
- Network logs, if enabled.
- The deployment URL used by the test.

A failed check usually means either the deployed app has an issue, or the automated test needs to be updated for that deployment.

### The wrong environment is tested

Make sure your API request uses:

```text
{{VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URL}}
```

instead of a fixed staging or production URL.

If the API request contains a hardcoded URL, Endtest will run against that URL instead of the newly created Vercel deployment.

### Preview deployments are not triggering Endtest

Open the Endtest Vercel configuration page and make sure **Preview deployments** is checked for that project.

### Production deployments are not triggering Endtest

Open the Endtest Vercel configuration page and make sure **Production deployments** is checked for that project.

## Security notes

The integration uses Vercel OAuth to connect your Vercel account to Endtest.

Your Endtest API credentials should be kept inside the Endtest configuration page and should not be committed to your source code repository.

The Vercel deployment URL placeholders do not contain secrets. They are replaced at runtime with the deployment URL for the current Vercel deployment.

## Removing the integration

To remove the integration:

1. Open Vercel.
2. Go to the Endtest integration installation.
3. Remove or disconnect the integration.
4. The related Endtest Vercel configuration will stop being used for future deployments.

You can also disable a specific project from the Endtest Vercel configuration page by unchecking **Enabled** and saving the project settings.

## Summary

The Endtest Vercel integration connects Vercel deployments with Endtest automated testing.

Once configured, each selected Vercel deployment can automatically trigger an Endtest execution and display the result directly in Vercel as a deployment check.

---

# Argo

Integrate Endtest with Argo Rollouts and Argo CD as deployment gates and post-deployment validation checks.

Part of the Endtest documentation (Integrations). Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/docs/integrations/argo

---
## Overview

Integrate Endtest with Argo Rollouts and Argo CD to run automated end-to-end tests as deployment gates and post-deployment validation checks.

The official integration can start one Endtest test suite or multiple test suites in a single API request. It waits for every returned execution to finish and exposes the combined result as a Kubernetes Job exit code:

- exit code `0` when every Endtest execution finishes with no failed assertions and no execution errors
- a non-zero exit code when any execution reports failed assertions, execution errors, an invalid response, or a timeout

With Argo Rollouts, that result determines whether a canary or blue-green deployment continues. With Argo CD, the same integration can run as a `PostSync` hook after an application is deployed.

The integration source code and Kubernetes manifests are available in the [Endtest Argo repository](https://github.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo).

## Prerequisites

Before configuring the integration, make sure you have:

- an Endtest account
- an Endtest App ID and App Code
- an Endtest API request that starts the test execution or executions you want to use
- a Kubernetes cluster
- Argo Rollouts, Argo CD, or both

For more information about API requests, see the [Endtest API documentation](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/how-to-use-the-endtest-api).

## Run one or multiple Endtest test suites

To start one test suite, use an API request containing `suite`:

```text
https://app.endtest.io/api.php?action=runWeb&appId=APP_ID&appCode=APP_CODE&suite=SUITE_ID&platform=windows&os=windows11&browser=chrome&browserVersion=latest&resolution=1280x1024&geolocation=sanfrancisco&cases=all&notes=
```

To start multiple test suites, assign the same label to those suites and use `label` instead of `suite`:

```text
https://app.endtest.io/api.php?action=runWeb&appId=APP_ID&appCode=APP_CODE&label=Critical&platform=windows&os=windows11&browser=chrome&browserVersion=latest&resolution=1280x1024&geolocation=sanfrancisco&cases=all&notes=
```

A request that starts multiple suites returns a comma-separated list of execution hashes:

```text
HASH_ONE,HASH_TWO
```

The integration sends all returned hashes to the Endtest `getResults` API in one request:

```text
https://app.endtest.io/api.php?action=getResults&appId=APP_ID&appCode=APP_CODE&hash=HASH_ONE,HASH_TWO&format=json-light
```

For one completed execution, Endtest returns one JSON object. For multiple completed executions, Endtest returns a JSON array containing one result object per execution.

While multiple executions are still running, the JSON array can temporarily contain status strings such as `Test is still running.`, `Processing video recording.`, or `Stopping.`. The integration treats those entries as pending executions and continues polling until every execution has produced a final result object.

The Argo gate passes only when every final result object contains:

```text
failed = 0
errors = 0
```

If any suite has failed assertions or execution errors, the complete deployment gate fails.

## How the integration works

1. Argo creates a Kubernetes Job from the Endtest analysis template or Argo CD hook.
2. The Job reads the Endtest App ID, App Code, and API request from a Kubernetes Secret.
3. The runner sends the API request and receives one hash or a comma-separated list of hashes.
4. The runner polls Endtest with all returned hashes.
5. The runner accepts a single result object, a completed array of result objects, or a temporary array containing pending status strings.
6. When any execution is still pending, the runner waits and polls again.
7. The Job succeeds only when every execution contains zero failed assertions and zero execution errors.
8. Argo continues or blocks the deployment based on the Job result.

## Create the Endtest Secret

Create a Kubernetes Secret in the same namespace where the Rollout, AnalysisRun, or Argo CD application runs:

```bash
kubectl create secret generic endtest-credentials \
  --from-literal=ENDTEST_APP_ID='your-app-id' \
  --from-literal=ENDTEST_APP_CODE='your-app-code' \
  --from-literal=ENDTEST_API_REQUEST='your-complete-endtest-api-request'
```

The Secret must contain these keys:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: endtest-credentials
type: Opaque
stringData:
  ENDTEST_APP_ID: "your-app-id"
  ENDTEST_APP_CODE: "your-app-code"
  ENDTEST_API_REQUEST: "your-complete-endtest-api-request"
```

Do not commit a populated Secret to source control. In production, use your existing secret-management solution, such as External Secrets, Sealed Secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, or another Kubernetes-compatible secret provider.

## Install the Argo Rollouts analysis template

The recommended option is the cluster-scoped template, which can be reused by Rollouts in multiple namespaces:

```bash
kubectl apply \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo/v0.2.1/manifests/cluster-analysis-template.yaml
```

Verify the template:

```bash
kubectl get clusteranalysistemplate endtest
```

A namespace-scoped version is also available:

```bash
kubectl apply \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo/v0.2.1/manifests/analysis-template.yaml
```

Use the namespace-scoped version when you want the template to be available only inside one namespace.

## Use Endtest in a canary rollout

Add an Endtest analysis step after exposing the candidate version to a percentage of traffic:

```yaml
strategy:
  canary:
    steps:
      - setWeight: 20
      - pause:
          duration: 2m
      - analysis:
          templates:
            - templateName: endtest
              clusterScope: true
          args:
            - name: secret-name
              value: endtest-credentials
            - name: number-of-loops
              value: "20"
            - name: poll-interval-seconds
              value: "30"
      - setWeight: 50
      - pause:
          duration: 5m
      - setWeight: 100
```

When every Endtest execution passes, Argo proceeds to the next rollout step.

When any Endtest execution reports failed assertions or execution errors, the analysis fails and the rollout does not continue to the next traffic weight.

A complete canary example is available in the repository:

```bash
kubectl apply \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo/v0.2.1/examples/canary-rollout.yaml
```

You can monitor the rollout with:

```bash
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout example-app --watch
```

## Use Endtest in a blue-green rollout

For blue-green deployments, run Endtest against the preview environment before Argo promotes it to the active Service:

```yaml
strategy:
  blueGreen:
    activeService: example-app-active
    previewService: example-app-preview
    prePromotionAnalysis:
      templates:
        - templateName: endtest
          clusterScope: true
      args:
        - name: secret-name
          value: endtest-credentials
        - name: number-of-loops
          value: "20"
```

Configure the Endtest API request so the test suite or label targets the preview URL.

When every execution passes, Argo can promote the preview version. When any execution fails, the active Service remains on the previous version.

A complete blue-green example is available in the repository:

```bash
kubectl apply \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo/v0.2.1/examples/blue-green-rollout.yaml
```

## Test the integration with a standalone AnalysisRun

Before adding the integration to a production Rollout, test it independently:

```bash
kubectl argo rollouts create analysisrun \
  --global \
  --from endtest \
  --name endtest-smoke-test \
  --argument secret-name=endtest-credentials
```

Print its final phase:

```bash
kubectl get analysisrun endtest-smoke-test \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"\n"}'
```

A successful Endtest execution should produce:

```text
Successful
```

Find the Kubernetes Job created by the AnalysisRun:

```bash
kubectl get jobs \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/name=endtest
```

Inspect its logs:

```bash
kubectl logs job/<job-name> -c endtest
```

For multiple executions, the logs first show pending progress when necessary, then every completed suite separately, followed by a combined result:

```text
Endtest executions are still running: 2 pending (1/20).
Endtest executions completed: 2.
Execution 1 of 2
Test Suite: Checkout
Failed: 0
Errors: 0

Execution 2 of 2
Test Suite: Login
Failed: 0
Errors: 0

Combined result
Executions: 2
Failed: 0
Errors: 0
Endtest release gate passed.
```

## Use Endtest as an Argo CD PostSync hook

For Argo CD applications that do not use Argo Rollouts, run Endtest after the application has been synchronized and becomes healthy.

Add the official hook manifest to the same Git repository that Argo CD synchronizes:

```bash
curl -o endtest-post-sync-job.yaml \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo/v0.2.1/manifests/argocd-post-sync-job.yaml
```

The Job contains these annotations:

```yaml
annotations:
  argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PostSync
  argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation,HookSucceeded
```

Argo CD runs the Job after the application resources have been synchronized.

When every Endtest execution passes, the hook succeeds. When any execution reports failures or errors, the hook fails and the Argo CD sync operation is marked as failed.

The default hook reads the `endtest-credentials` Secret:

```yaml
envFrom:
  - secretRef:
      name: endtest-credentials
```

The Secret must exist in the namespace where the hook Job runs.

## Template parameters

The Endtest analysis template supports these parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `secret-name` | `endtest-credentials` | Kubernetes Secret containing the Endtest App ID, App Code, and API request. |
| `image` | `ghcr.io/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo:0.2.1` | Endtest Argo runner container image. |
| `results-format` | `json-light` | Endtest result format. Supported values are `json-light` and `json`. |
| `number-of-loops` | `20` | Maximum number of result checks. |
| `poll-interval-seconds` | `30` | Delay between result checks. |
| `request-timeout-seconds` | `30` | Timeout for each Endtest API request. |

The integration uses `json-light` by default because the deployment gate only needs summary fields. Use `json` when you also want the full logs and media URLs returned by the API.

You can override the format or image version in a Rollout:

```yaml
args:
  - name: image
    value: ghcr.io/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo:0.2.1
  - name: results-format
    value: json
```

Pinning a specific image version is recommended for production deployments.

## Result behavior

The release gate passes only when every Endtest result object contains:

```text
failed = 0
errors = 0
```

A test execution with no assertions is considered successful when it completes with no execution errors.

The release gate fails when:

- any Endtest execution reports one or more failed assertions
- any Endtest execution reports one or more execution errors
- the start request returns an invalid hash or comma-separated hash list
- the number of returned result objects does not match the number of execution hashes
- the result API returns malformed or unexpected data
- an execution returns the terminal `Erred.` status
- the executions do not complete before the polling limit
- a required Secret value is missing
- the runner cannot reach the Endtest API

## Troubleshooting

### The AnalysisRun remains Running

Check the Job and Pod:

```bash
kubectl get analysisruns
kubectl get jobs
kubectl get pods
```

Inspect the Job logs:

```bash
kubectl logs job/<job-name> -c endtest
```

Check recent Kubernetes events:

```bash
kubectl get events \
  --sort-by=.lastTimestamp \
  | tail -30
```

### The container is waiting in ContainerCreating

The cluster may still be downloading the Endtest image.

Inspect the Pod:

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>
```

The official image is public:

```text
ghcr.io/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo:0.2.1
```

### The AnalysisRun is Failed or Error

Inspect the Job logs:

```bash
kubectl logs job/<job-name> -c endtest
```

Common causes include:

- incorrect App ID or App Code
- an invalid or incomplete API request
- one or more executions containing failures
- one or more executions containing errors
- a mismatch between execution hashes and result objects
- a polling timeout
- a missing Kubernetes Secret

### The Secret cannot be found

Make sure the Secret exists in the same namespace as the AnalysisRun or Rollout:

```bash
kubectl get secret endtest-credentials
```

When using a `ClusterAnalysisTemplate`, the template is cluster-scoped, but the generated Job still reads the Secret from the namespace where the AnalysisRun executes.

## Security

The official integration includes the following security defaults:

- Endtest credentials are read at runtime from a Kubernetes Secret
- credentials and the API request are not printed in Job logs
- the container runs as a non-root user
- the Kubernetes manifests disable service-account token mounting
- the container uses a read-only root filesystem
- Linux capabilities are dropped
- the official container image is published through GitHub Container Registry

For production environments, restrict access to the Secret and use your standard Kubernetes secret-management and RBAC policies.

## Source code

The integration is open source:

[github.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo](https://github.com/endtest-technologies/endtest-argo)

# Bamboo Server

Integrate Endtest with Atlassian Bamboo Server to trigger automated test plans from your build pipeline and surface results inside Bamboo dashboards.

Part of the Endtest documentation (Integrations). Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/docs/integrations/bamboo-server

---
## Instructions

You can use our `Endtest API` in order to integrate Endtest with Bamboo Server.

This can be done by creating a `test.sh` file and executing it from a Bamboo Server task.

**test.sh**
```sh
#!/bin/bash
hash=$(curl -X GET --header "Accept: */*" "${3}")
for run in {1.."${4}"}
do
  sleep 30
  result=$(curl -X GET --header "Accept: */*" "https://app.endtest.io/api.php?action=getResults&appId=${1}&appCode=${2}&hash=${hash}&format=json")
  if [ "$result" == "Test is still running." ]
  then
    status=$result
    # Don't print anything
  elif [ "$result" == "Processing video recording." ]
  then
    status=$result
    # Don't print anything
  elif [ "$result" == "Stopping." ]
  then
    status=$result
  elif [ "$result" == "Erred." ]
  then
    status=$result
    echo $status
  elif [ "$result" == "" ]
  then
    status=$result
    # Don't print anything
  else
     echo "$result" | jq
     exit 0
  fi
done
exit
```

This sample script would require the following arguments:
1. The `App ID` for your account.
2. The `App Code` for your account.
3. The API Request for starting the test execution.
4. The number of times the API request for fetching the results will be sent once every 30 seconds.

For example, if you know that your test execution usually takes 3 minutes, you should use the value 7.

`7 x 30 seconds = 210 seconds > 3 minutes`

Don't forget to make your Shell script executable by running the following command:

```console
sudo chmod +x test.sh
```

And you would also need to install the `jq` package:

```sh
sudo apt-get install jq
```

The command for running the sample Shell script would have the following format:

```sh
./test.sh app-id app-code api-request-to-start-test-execution number-of-loops
```

Let's pretend we have the following values:

```
App ID = 44233559

App Code = 22381137

Endtest API Request to start test execution = "https://app.endtest.io/api.php?action=runWeb&appId=44233559&appCode=22381137&suite=380667&platform=windows&os=windows10&browser=chrome&browserVersion=latest&resolution=1280x1024&geolocation=sanfrancisco&cases=all&notes="

Number of loops = 10
```

The command for running the sample Shell script would look like this:

```sh
./test.sh 44233559 22381137 "https://app.endtest.io/api.php?action=runWeb&appId=44233559&appCode=22381137&suite=380667&platform=windows&os=windows10&browser=chrome&browserVersion=latest&resolution=1280x1024&geolocation=sanfrancisco&cases=all&notes=" 10
```

The JSON with the results contains the following keys:

* `test_suite_name` `{string}` - The name of the test suite.
* `configuration` `{string}` - The configuration of the machine or mobile device on which the test was executed.
* `test_cases` `{int32}` - The number of test cases.
* `passed` `{int32}` - The number of assertions that have passed.
* `failed` `{int32}` - The number of assertions that have failed.
* `errors` `{int32}` - The number of errors that have been encountered.
* `start_time` `{timestamp}` - The timestamp for the start of the test execution.
* `end_time` `{timestamp}` - The timestamp for the end of the test execution.
* `detailed_logs` `{string}` - The detailed logs for the test execution.
* `screenshots_and_video` `{string}` - The URLs for the screenshots and the video recording of the test execution.
* `test_case_management` `{string}` - The name, status and external IDs for each test case. 

You can also use the value of the `hash` variable to generate the link to the Results page for that test execution:

```sh
results=https://app.endtest.io/results?hash="$hash"
```

>You can find more details about our API in the [Endtest API](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/how-to-use-the-endtest-api/) chapter.

---

# Test Case Management

Integrate Endtest with Zephyr, TestRail, Xray, and qTest. Sync automated test results back to your test case management tool of choice automatically.

Part of the Endtest documentation (Integrations). Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/docs/integrations/test-case-management

---
## Introduction

You can associate your existing Endtest Test Cases with the corresponding Test Cases in your Test Case Management (TCM) tool.

Endtest does not yet integrate directly with these tools, but there are multiple ways to fetch the results and update the entries in your TCM tool.

## Add External IDs

1. Go to your TCM tool (TestRail, Zephyr, XRay, etc)
2. Copy the ID of the Test Case from the TCM tool.
3. Go to your Test Case in Endtest.
4. Click on the `Info` button from that Test Case.
5. Add the copied ID in the `External IDs` input.
6. Click on the `Save` button.

The Test Case from Endtest is now associated with the Test Case from your TCM tool.

And the test executions results will now include the External IDs.

 Multiple External IDs can be added in the `External IDs` input, separated by commas. 

## Fetching the results

The test execution results contain the following details about each Test Case:

| Item           | Description                               |
|----------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Test Case Name | The name of the test case from Endtest    |
| Test Case ID   | The ID of the test case from Endtest      |
| External IDs   | The External IDs copied from the TCM Tool |
| Status         | Passed / Failed                           |

 The `Status` depends on the number of `Failed Assertions` and `Errors` from that Test Case. If either of them is greater than 0, the status will be `Failed`. 

Those items are included in the `Test Case Management` component of the results.

The `Test Case Management` component can be obtained in the following ways:

* Fetch the results with the [Endtest API](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/how-to-use-the-endtest-api)
* [Email Notifications](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/email-notifications/)
* [Webhook Notifications](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/webhook-notifications/)
* Export the Results in XLSX format from the [Results](https://app.endtest.io/results) page

## Updating the Test Cases in your TCM tool

Since Endtest is not directly integrated with your TCM tool, it cannot automatically update the entries in your TCM tool.

Those entries can be updated manually or programatically, by using the information from the `Test Case Management` component of the test execution results from Endtest.

To update them programatically, you would need to use a script or orchestration tool that fetches the results from Endtest and connects to the API of your TCM tool.

> **Note:** We are currently developing direct integrations with multiple TCM tools. Once those integrations are launched, the script or orchestration tool will no longer be needed to programatically update the Test Cases in your TCM tool.

# SSO

Enable SSO on Endtest with Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, JumpCloud, or any SAML 2.0 provider to centralize access management for your team.

Part of the Endtest documentation (Integrations). Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/docs/integrations/sso

---
## Introduction

Endtest supports Single Sign-On (SSO) with SAML and OpenID Connect protocols.

That means your users can login using your corporate identity provider.

![endtest sso](https://app.endtest.io/images/sso.jpg)

## Auth for all SSO providers

Our platform offers SSO support for most SAML or OIDC identity providers (Okta, Entra ID, OneLogin, etc).

This functionality is only available for teams who are on the Enterprise Plan.

To enable SSO for your team, reach out to our Customer Support on the online chat or send an email to `contact@endtest.io`.

Each SSO Identity Provider requires specific information to create and configure a new Connection.

Often, the information required to create a Connection will differ by Identity Provider.

## SSO Domain Lock

SSO integrations can be configured with `Domain Lock`. When enabled, your users will be able to login only with SSO.

If `Domain Lock` is not enabled, your users can login with both password and SSO.

You can see if `Domain Lock` is enabled in the `Team` section from the [Settings](https://app.endtest.io/settings) page.

![endtest sso settings](https://app.endtest.io/images/sso_status.jpg)

## Adding new users

The flow for adding new users in Endtest does not change after SSO has been enabled for your team.

You can still add new or existing users to your team, and the SSO settings will be automatically applied to their account.

## Directory Sync

Endtest does not perform any sync operations with your SSO provider.

So, if you remove a user from your SSO provider, that doesn't mean the user will be removed automatically from Endtest.

However, they won't be able to login via SSO anymore.

If you add a new user in your SSO provider, that does not automatically add the user to your team in Endtest.

You still have to add the user in your team in Endtest.

# The 10 Best AI-Powered Test Automation Tools in 2026

A hands-on comparison of 10 AI-powered test automation tools, tested across real-world scenarios including email verification, iframes, multiple tabs, SMS, PDFs, API workflows, AI test creation and more.

Published October 1, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/10-best-ai-powered-test-automation-tools

---
I know, I know, you probably rolled your eyes when you saw the title.

But hear me out, there are hundreds or thousands of "best test automation tools" articles that are low-effort AI-generated pieces for SEO purposes.

And it frustrates me that no one ACTUALLY tries to do a fair and in-depth comparison of those tools.

But that changes today. I'm writing a detailed and transparent article about this topic, based on the intensive research I did in the last few days.

I've been working in web development for almost 15 years, and my main focus was always on test automation.

I feel like most software tools nowadays are like cars: there is no "the best one", but there is "the best one for your team, budget, situation, etc."

Most of the "reviews" we see today are superficial, just listing some features and making some shallow comparisons and drawing some obvious conclusions. We don't see any actual proof that the author tried those tools. And we don't see any insights beyond what we can find out from the marketing pages of those tools.

But it's not as easy as you may think to try out a tool, because some tools don't give away free trials, because they want to be in control of the first impression.

They want to show you how their tool works in a predictable situation in a demo call, before anyone in your team gets a chance to try it out.

And yes, I don't like dealing with sales reps.

Believe me, I pulled a few strings to get access to some of these tools, mostly by asking friends to sign up with their company emails and book demos.

Other tools have an even sneakier approach, mimicking a "developer-friendly" attitude, making you think it's just some cool open-source tool, getting you to put it in your stack and then casually trying to upsell it to your management, without you even knowing about it.

Even if such things leave a bad taste, I'm going to ignore them for the purpose of this review, because we'll be focusing only on the technical capabilities.

## What tools are we going to review?
There are TOO MANY test automation tools, so I picked out 10 by looking at G2 and Capterra reviews, Reddit mentions and appearances in job listings.

## What scenarios are we testing?

We'll try the exact same functional scenarios across all 10 tools. These are some difficult scenarios where testing tools might hit a wall:

1. Sign up using email verification.
2. Interact with elements inside an iframe.
3. Interact with elements that have dynamic or unreliable attributes.
4. Complete a flow spanning multiple browser tabs.
5. Assert that a page is displayed in a specific language.
6. Reuse values and groups of steps.
7. Extract a verification code from a real SMS message.
8. Download a PDF and extract information from it.
9. Send an API request and use its response in a browser step.

Testing 9 different scenarios across all 10 tools seems like a healthy way to review them.

Beyond those 9 scenarios, I'm also evaluating the tools on these aspects:
1. Creating Tests with AI
2. Autonomous Test Generation
3. Creating Tests Without AI
4. Execution Performance
5. Test Transparency & Readability
6. Cross-Browser Testing
7. Maintenance & Debugging
8. Documentation & Customer Support
9. Enterprise Readiness
10. Portability & Vendor Lock-In
11. Pricing & Value
12. Overall Usability

## Methodology

Since I wanted to make this comparison as consistent as possible, I followed the same process for each tool.

For the functional flows, I used the exact same websites and the exact same approaches.

For AI-generated tests, I tried to use the same instructions in the prompts (whenever possible).

No tool received more patience than the others.

When something was failing, I just checked the docs to see if there was some obvious setting or recommended approach that I missed.

I didn't label a scenario as successful just because the vendor's documentation said it's supported. I actually tried it myself.

And just to clarify:

✅ Passed means the tool handled the scenario without unusual intervention.

⚠️ Passed with workaround means the scenario worked, but required custom code, extra config, a third party service or some workaround.

❌ Failed means I couldn't get the scenario to work in a reasonable way.

I also don't consider using an external service equivalent to a built-in functionality.

For example, if a tool can get an SMS message only by integrating with another SMS provider, that's not really the same as the platform providing an actual real phone number and receiving the SMS itself.

The same logic applies to email verification, PDF files and other things.

For execution speed, I calculated the average number of executed steps per second for the same tests.

Execution speed also depends on the website, browser, network, etc.

For subjective criteria such as usability, readability and maintenance, I used these ratings:

Excellent: Among the strongest tools tested in this area, with no major shortcomings.

Good: Strong overall, but with some noticeable limitations.

Average: Gets the job done, but has meaningful trade-offs.

Poor: Significant limitations or friction compared with the other tools.

Great. Now that we got that out of the way, let me show you what those exact scenarios looked like.

## 1. Sign up using email verification.

I gave the instruction to create an account on some website and to verify the email.

While all the tools were able to enter the details and submit the form, very few were able to handle the entire scenario.

Endtest entered a random endtest-mail.io address, which it was able to access via the [Endtest Mailbox](https://endtest.io/docs/web-tests/how-to-test-emails).

![Endtest signup flow with email validation](https://app.endtest.io/images/endtest_sign_up_with_email_validation.png)

*The full signup flow with email validation in Endtest.*

![Endtest Mailbox used to validate an email during a signup flow](https://app.endtest.io/images/validate_email_with_endtest_mailbox.png)

*Validating the email using the [Endtest Mailbox](https://endtest.io/docs/web-tests/how-to-test-emails).*

[mabl](https://www.mabl.com/) and [Testim](https://www.testim.io/) also handled it well.

But the rest got stuck or gave a message that this isn't supported.

## 2. Interact with elements inside an iframe.

I tried it on this page:
https://www.w3schools.com/tags/tryit.asp?filename=tryhtml_select

Just click on the Run button, then interact with the elements from the iframe on the right side.
And then click on the Run button again.
And ideally, you should see that the test switched to the iframe, and then switched out.

Endtest and [mabl](https://www.mabl.com/) handled it perfectly, but the rest had some issues.

![mabl handling interactions inside an iframe](https://app.endtest.io/images/mabl_iframe.png)

*[mabl](https://www.mabl.com/) correctly handling the iframe scenario.*

Some didn't capture any events inside the iframe. And some captured the events, but registered them as being on the main DOM, instead of the iframe.

[Testim](https://www.testim.io/) didn't work for this scenario. I also tried using a Custom Step as a workaround, but that didn't work either.

![Testim failing the iframe scenario](https://app.endtest.io/images/testim_iframe.png)

*The iframe scenario in [Testim](https://www.testim.io/).*

## 3. Interact with elements that have dynamic or unreliable attributes.

Recording steps is easy, but getting those steps to be reliable is not.

Bad locator:
//*[@id="input-89437291"]

Better locator:
//input[@name="email"]

Endtest, [ACCELQ](https://www.accelq.com/) and [Testim](https://www.testim.io/) handled this beautifully.

![ACCELQ login scenario showing generated test steps](https://app.endtest.io/images/accelq_login_scenario.png)

*An [ACCELQ](https://www.accelq.com/) scenario from the locator and dynamic-element testing.*

Those tools detected that certain attributes were dynamically generated, and didn't use them in the selectors generated for those steps.

As for the rest of the tools, they had no shame in using those obviously dynamic attribute values.

Hint: Dynamic attribute values usually have numbers or random characters; it's not that hard to detect them.

Worth mentioning here that [mabl](https://www.mabl.com/) was able to pass this one after changing the settings to make it ignore those specific attributes.

## 4. Complete a flow spanning multiple browser tabs.

There are many situations where a test might need to switch across different tabs.

My typical approach involves:

- switch to a tab that was opened by clicking a button
- open a new empty tab and switch to it
- switch back and forth across multiple tabs (5-6)
- close the current tab

Most tools were able to handle this easily, since the browsers also make it easy.

[Testim](https://www.testim.io/) was an exception here. I couldn't get the multiple-tab flow to work, and I also tried using a Custom Step as a workaround, but that didn't work either.

![Testim failing a test that spans multiple browser tabs](https://app.endtest.io/images/testim_failed_multiple_tabs.png)

*The failed multiple-tab scenario in [Testim](https://www.testim.io/).*

## 5. Assert that a page is displayed in a specific language.

This is what I would call a "fuzzy" assertion, something that you wouldn't be able to verify so easily with tools from 5 years ago.

For example, let's say a website has a button to switch the language to French. We then want to go to a certain page and verify if the entire content is actually displayed in French.

This isn't something that can be handled by a classic "Element Contains Value" assertion.

And seeing "lang=fr" in the current URL doesn't actually prove that the content is displayed in French.

The only solution is for the tool to use an "AI Assertion" to verify the situation.

And since all the tools have AI Assertions, all of them did well.

![Endtest AI Assertion checking the language of a page](https://app.endtest.io/images/endtest_ai_assertion_to_check_language.png)

*Using an [Endtest AI Assertion](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-assertions) to check the language of the page.*

![ACCELQ assertion used during the language assertion scenario](https://app.endtest.io/images/accelq_assertion.png)

*An assertion in [ACCELQ](https://www.accelq.com/).*

## 6. Reuse values and groups of steps.

I'd expect modern test automation tools to allow you to use the same best practices as scripting languages.

And that includes the ability to reuse values (variables) and groups of steps (components, test cases, etc.).

For example, if you have a login flow, you'd want to define the username and password and the steps in only one place, and then be able to reuse that login across other tests.

The obvious advantage is that if something changes in your login flow, you would only need to update it in one place.

From what I tested, all the tools seem to have this functionality, in one way or another.

![mabl variables used to reuse values across tests](https://app.endtest.io/images/mabl_variables.png)

*Using variables in [mabl](https://www.mabl.com/).*

![Testim shared steps used to reuse groups of steps](https://app.endtest.io/images/testim_shared_steps.png)

*Using Shared Steps in [Testim](https://www.testim.io/).*

## 7. Extract a verification code from a real SMS message.

The best example here is a login flow with 2FA enabled, where you get an SMS with the authentication code.

Ideally, this should be achieved natively in the tool, without using third-party integrations and complicated workarounds.

That means the tool would need to assign a real phone number to your team, because we want to see if the SMS was actually delivered, and not just extract the authentication code from a database or an endpoint.

Surprisingly, only [Endtest](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/read-sms) and [Functionize](https://www.functionize.com/) support this SMS flow.

![Functionize SMS verification flow](https://app.endtest.io/images/functionize_sms_verification.png)

*SMS verification in [Functionize](https://www.functionize.com/).*

All the other tools required you to call some external provider to achieve that.

## 8. Download a PDF and extract information from it.

This is trickier than it sounds, because any tool can open a PDF and take a screenshot.

But extracting actual information from the PDF isn't so easy, since most of these tools use WebDriver or Playwright under the hood, and those do not have the functionality to extract information from a PDF file.

And again, a user would expect to be able to do that directly, without involving other third party tools.

And ideally, we'd expect more than a visual validation for the contents.

This functionality should work for PDFs opened in a new tab or downloaded (even downloaded via API steps).

Autify doesn't support PDF testing at all. It only allows you to see the URL of the PDF, but you can't inspect, extract or validate the contents of the PDF itself.

## 9. Send an API request and use its response in a browser step.

In advanced E2E flows, you often have situations where you need to send an API request and then reuse the returned value in a UI step, or vice versa.

That's why it's important for UI steps and API steps to be in the same interface.

Most tools handled this well, since they have a "Send API request" type of action.

![Katalon API request used in an end-to-end test](https://app.endtest.io/images/katalon_api_request.png)

*An API request in [Katalon](https://www.katalon.com/).*

## As for these evaluation criteria:

### 1. Creating Tests with AI

This refers to providing granular or high-level instructions to create a test.

That means the tool has to understand each instruction, inspect the elements, find the best locator, verify that the step works and save the step.

It doesn't mean just blindly converting user instructions into a test.

Both speed and reliability matter here, but reliability is more important. Because I'm OK with the test creation process taking a bit longer, as long as I can actually rely on that test later.

### 2. Autonomous Test Generation

This involves giving a URL and some directions to the tool and expecting the tool to explore the web application and come up with scenarios and completed tests.

We don't want the tool to just look at the website and print some scenarios. We expect it to actually navigate all the flows and generate executable tests.

Ideally, this shouldn't be divided into separate features. I don't want a feature that "comes up with test cases" by looking at specs, and then another feature that attempts to automate those test cases.

And I don't want something that comes up with questions for me related to each scenario.

I want something like an autonomous QA colleague, where I provide some direction and then they go and do their work and keep me updated.

The [Endtest Bot](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/endtest-bot) is the best example here, because it's like hiring a test automation expert that works independently.

### 3. Creating Tests Without AI

Some users don't want AI in their workflows. This should not shock you.

They have their reasons, either because they're working in sensitive domains (healthcare, defense, etc) or because they want to be in full control of the process.

A modern test automation tool should not force a user on the AI path.

[Endtest](https://endtest.io/docs/web-tests/how-to-create-web-tests) allows users to create tests in 3 different ways without using AI:

- [Endtest Web Recorder](https://endtest.io/docs/web-tests/how-to-create-web-tests)
- Manual test creation
- Import tests from files

### 4. Execution Performance

We're talking about the actual test execution speed here. And we want to have realistic expectations, because that speed also depends on the web application and it also depends on the browser.

For this comparison, I'm referring to cloud executions, not tests executed locally on your own machine.

Making calls to some AI endpoint during the test execution for each step is not a good approach, because that adds a delay.

So, you shouldn't have steps stored as "Click on Login button", because that means it will call the AI each time it executes that step, in order to figure out which one is the Login button.

The only time when it's acceptable for the tool to call an AI endpoint during the test execution is for situations that can't be resolved without AI, such as AI Assertions or self-healing.

For my benchmark, I think it's fine if a test automation tool has a speed of around 1 step/second. If the speed is slower than that, it's possible that the tool is doing things it doesn't need to.

From what I could figure out, some tools have lower speeds either because their cloud infrastructure is more complicated than it needs to be or because they're collecting too many artifacts.

Ideally, you should allow the user to configure what artifacts need to be collected. And the tool should fetch the DOM only when there is a failure, and not for every step.

### 5. Test Transparency & Readability

The last thing we want is a black box.

We don't want a test that shows us high-level instructions like "Perform the login" or even granular instructions like "Click on the Login button".

Storing tests as instructions for an AI invites ambiguity. You're not sure what that test will do, and you're not sure if it's the right thing.

The steps should be stored as human-readable instructions, but with clear selectors and parameters. So a test executed 1000 times will run the exact same instructions each time.

The other thing we don't want is for the output to be code. Using no-code tools to generate code tends to turn into a messy process.

### 6. Cross-Browser Testing

Whatever you might hear on LinkedIn or X, cross-browser testing is still important in most large organizations.

A large online retailer that spends tons of resources to optimize every detail doesn't want to miss out on purchases because the checkout flow is broken in Firefox or Safari.

And no, not everyone is using Chrome.

For those who are old enough to remember the Selenium days, you had to put in some effort to make the same test work on all major browsers, because options and capabilities had to be configured differently for each one. And even some things like tab switching or JS execution worked differently across different browsers.

The less obvious aspect is that Chrome on Windows is different from Chrome on Mac or Chrome on Linux, even if they look and work in the same way.

I've seen plenty of situations where a bug was present on Chrome on Windows, but not on Chrome on Linux.

It's somehow similar to games; a game might have a bug on PlayStation 5, but it might not have that bug on the PC version.

And don't even get me started on Headless Chrome.

Ideally, you want the option to run a test on browsers on Windows and macOS machines.

If a tool doesn't mention the operating system, there is a possibility that they're using headless browsers on Linux containers, which is cheaper for them, but not ideal for the user.

If someone says "A customer said they can't finish the purchase flow, they're on Safari on macOS", you don't want your answer to be "I don't know, our tests are running on headless Chrome on Linux. Tell them to try on Chrome."

### 7. Maintenance & Debugging

In test automation, most of the time and resources are consumed with maintaining and debugging tests, not with creating tests.

So, if someone brags that they just created 500 tests in 5 minutes, you can assume they don't have much experience in test automation.

The challenge is that having more and more tests means we have a lot more logs and errors to understand.

And this is a fantastic use case for AI.

Self-healing has been around since 2017, way before the GenAI boom. Back then, it was done by storing backup selectors during successful test executions and relying on those backup selectors when something went wrong (if the ID changed, maybe the other attributes stayed the same).

But now self-healing is powered by AI, which can analyze the step, the screenshot and the DOM and fix the test for you.

And most tools have some sort of "Analyze Failure with AI" functionality, to help you understand why an error happened.

And some even have "AI Summary" buttons for the logs, so you get an "executive summary" without having to read the entire logs.

### 8. Documentation & Customer Support

You'd expect everyone to have detailed, up-to-date docs nowadays, but it's not always the case.

I did find plenty of inconsistencies and outdated information.

Given the high price of most of these tools, I expected outstanding 24/7 technical customer support, but that's far from the truth.

I'd expect businesses to understand that not having real human technical support saves some money, but it also adds friction to the success journey of a user.

### 9. Enterprise Readiness

In general, these tools are more popular in the enterprise space than in the SMB space.

And thus, I'd expect enterprise features such as integrations, SSO, role-based access, API access, and security certifications (such as ISO 27001).

Most of the tools did really well here, with the exception of Katalon. I think the reason for that is that Katalon was initially a desktop app and they're still trying to navigate through the transition to being a cloud platform.

### 10. Portability & Vendor Lock-In

It's common sense to expect a modern platform to offer the option to take your data wherever you want.

That doesn't mean they should build a "Migrate to Competitor" feature, but it simply means offering the option of exporting your data in a useful format.

Some vendors used to provide an export output that was almost "intentionally" obfuscated and difficult to understand. But now AI makes it easy to insert exported data from one tool into another tool.

Having a simple option to export a JSON or a CSV is more than enough.

### 11. Pricing & Value

This one is a big differentiator.

The price tag can really change someone's impression of a tool. And I'm going to go on a rant here.

No one likes companies that hide their prices. Do they imagine that their pricing would scare potential users from trying their product?

In an ideal situation for such vendors, they'd expect a user to sign up for a free trial and then recommend the tool to their company and that user would never even find out what their company actually ended up paying for that tool.

Users know what cloud infrastructure and tokens typically cost; you can't overcharge them without causing resentment.

Having a very limited free plan or a very limited cheap starter plan as a "hook" is also a strategy that leaves a bad impression.

My view has always been that we should set prices based on "costs + margins" instead of "how much would they be willing to pay?"

For example, [mabl](https://www.mabl.com/) and [Functionize](https://www.functionize.com/) are good tools, but their prices are significantly higher than similar competitors, and it's difficult to justify such high prices.

### 12. Overall Usability

All the tools have decent usability. These are tools that have been on the market for a number of years, so they've had plenty of time to refine their UX.

That means the small things can really make a difference. And that's where you can almost tell when a company is actually using their own tool.

I honestly think Endtest really has the most intuitive UI. And there's so much attention put into all the details.

For example, in the [Endtest Web Recorder](https://endtest.io/docs/web-tests/how-to-create-web-tests), there's a toggle to start with a clean session.

When viewing the steps of a test case, you can also view them as a flowchart or as an AI summary.

On the opposite end, I found [TestMu](https://www.testmuai.com/kane-ai/)'s UI to be a bit confusing and couldn't understand what was happening at some moments.

[mabl](https://www.mabl.com/) has also improved its usability. A few years ago, it used unconventional names for certain items ("journeys" instead of "test cases"). I'm glad they gave up on that and started using the industry-standard terms.

## Individual Tool Summaries

### Endtest

**What I liked**

- Very intuitive UI
- Transparent pricing, with unlimited AI
- Really comprehensive E2E testing features

**What I didn't like**

- Not enough videos in the docs
- The Endtest MCP doesn't allow me to create tests with my own AI models

**Biggest surprise**

- The number of [integrations](https://endtest.io/integrations). There are a lot more than I expected.

**Real-world scenarios:** 9/9  
**Execution speed:** 1.21 steps/sec

**Best suited for:** Enterprises and SMBs. And any team that needs a reliable AI-powered test automation tool that is also affordable.

- Great toolkit for E2E testing flows
- The API testing functionality is better than I expected

**What I didn't like**

- Execution speed was quite low compared with most of the other tools
- Some of the more advanced scenarios needed workarounds

**Biggest surprise**

- The API testing features. I wasn't expecting them to be this good.

**Real-world scenarios:** 6/9 + 3 workarounds  
**Execution speed:** 0.38 steps/sec

**Best suited for:** Enterprises

---

### [Functionize](https://www.functionize.com/)

**What I liked**

- Good enterprise functionality
- Native SMS testing, which almost nobody else has

**What I didn't like**

- Some browser scenarios that I expected to be easy didn't work that well
- The tests don't feel as transparent and readable as I'd like

**Biggest surprise**

- The native SMS testing. They actually give you a phone number and let you test the real SMS flow, which is surprisingly rare.

**Real-world scenarios:** 6/9 + 2 workarounds

**Best suited for:** Enterprises

- Some advanced E2E scenarios still need workarounds
- Portability isn't as good as with tools that let you work directly with standard code formats

**Biggest surprise**

- How much [BrowserStack](https://www.browserstack.com/low-code-automation) has expanded beyond just browsers and devices. This is basically a full testing platform now.

**Real-world scenarios:** 5/9 + 2 workarounds  
**Execution speed:** 0.83 steps/sec

**Best suited for:** Enterprises, especially teams that already use [BrowserStack](https://www.browserstack.com/low-code-automation)

### [Autify Nexus](https://autify.com/products/autify-nexus)

**What I didn't like**

**Biggest surprise**

**Real-world scenarios:** 3/9 + 4 workarounds

**Real-world scenarios:** 3/9 + 4 workarounds

**Best suited for:** Teams that want AI-powered test creation and access to a large browser/device cloud

### [ACCELQ](https://www.accelq.com/)

- Strong enterprise features

**What I didn't like**

- Portability isn't as good as with tools that focus more on code export
- Pricing isn't very transparent

**Real-world scenarios:** 5/9 + 1 workaround  
**Execution speed:** 0.71 steps/sec

**Best suited for:** Enterprises that want a codeless automation platform with strong governance features

### [Tricentis Testim](https://www.testim.io/)

- Excellent maintenance and debugging features

**What I didn't like**

- Autonomous test generation is still pretty limited
- I couldn't get iframe or multiple-tab scenarios to work, even with a Custom Step workaround
- SMS and PDF scenarios needed workarounds
- Portability could be better

**Biggest surprise**

**Real-world scenarios:** 5/9 + 2 workarounds

**Best suited for:** Teams that have flows that do not involve multiple tabs or iframes. And teams that need to automate testing for Salesforce flows.

### [UiPath Test Cloud](https://www.uipath.com/product/test-cloud)

- Integrates really well with the rest of the [UiPath](https://www.uipath.com/product/test-cloud) ecosystem

**What I didn't like**

- The whole platform can feel more complicated than a dedicated web testing tool

- Some things feel designed more around the wider [UiPath](https://www.uipath.com/product/test-cloud) automation ecosystem than web testing specifically

**Biggest surprise**

**Real-world scenarios:** 5/9 + 3 workarounds  
**Execution speed:** 0.62 steps/sec

**Best suited for:** Large enterprises, especially companies that already use [UiPath](https://www.uipath.com/product/test-cloud)
