# Do You Really Need Dedicated QA Engineers?

A practical framework for deciding when dedicated QA engineers improve product quality, when developers can cover testing, and where AI fits.

Published September 9, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/do-you-really-need-dedicated-qa-engineers

---
I've been working in the QA industry for almost 15 years.

During that time, I've had conversations about testing processes with people from thousands of companies. Tiny startups. Large enterprises. Companies with dedicated QA departments. Companies where developers test everything. Companies with sophisticated automation infrastructure. Companies where someone remembers to click around the application five minutes before a release.

I've seen a lot of different approaches work.

And I've seen a lot of them fail.

So when someone asks me, **"Do we really need dedicated QA engineers?"**, my answer is probably less satisfying than the confident takes you'll find on LinkedIn:

It depends.

That's not a way of avoiding the question. It's the actual answer.

## Don't copy another company's QA strategy

A common way to make engineering decisions is to find a successful company and copy what they do.

"Google does this."

"Amazon does that."

"Company X doesn't have QA."

Therefore, we should do the same thing.

The problem is that your company is not Google.

Even the premise is often wrong. Google is frequently mentioned as an example of engineering organizations where developers own quality, yet Google has also employed dedicated Test Engineers focused on finding failure modes, improving test infrastructure and increasing product quality.

Amazon currently hires dedicated Quality Assurance Engineers. Airbnb has a Quality Engineering organization with engineers responsible for test cases, automation coverage, test infrastructure and release quality.

These companies are also enormous. Practices differ between teams, products and points in time.

There is no universal Big Tech consensus that somebody forgot to tell the rest of us about.

And even if there were, copying Google's organizational structure without copying Google's engineering talent, infrastructure and budget would be a strange experiment.

A company might have 30 highly qualified engineers working on something another business would assign to five people.

Context matters.

## Agile does not mean "developers do all the testing"

This is another idea that gets distorted.

Testing in Agile should not be a separate phase that begins after development is "finished." Quality work should happen throughout the sprint, with developers, testers, product owners and other stakeholders collaborating continuously.

That's very different from saying:

> Developers should build the feature and then test the feature themselves.

Those two ideas somehow became interchangeable in some organizations.

They aren't.

The whole-team approach to quality means that everyone contributes to quality. It doesn't mean every specialization suddenly stops existing.

Your designer cares about quality too. That doesn't mean your backend engineer should redesign the checkout screen between two pull requests.

Your Product Owner cares about quality. That doesn't mean they should start debugging race conditions in JavaScript.

And your developers absolutely should test their code. That doesn't mean they should be the **only** people testing it.

ISTQB's guidance on test independence is much more nuanced than the usual internet debate. Developers can find defects in their own code, but independent testers can identify different failures because they approach the product with different assumptions, backgrounds and cognitive biases.

That distinction matters.

## The person who built it shouldn't be the only tester

Suppose I misunderstand a requirement.

I implement the feature according to my misunderstanding.

Then I test the feature according to that same misunderstanding.

There's a decent chance it passes.

This is one of the simplest arguments for independent testing.

The developer knows how the feature was built. That's useful.

The tester doesn't necessarily think about the feature the same way the developer does. That's also useful.

You want both perspectives.

It's the same reason cross-checking appears in high-reliability environments. A second person isn't valuable because the first person is incompetent. They're valuable because two people are less likely to have exactly the same blind spot.

That doesn't require a separate QA department with 40 people.

On a small team, another developer might test the feature. The Product Owner might validate important flows. A founder might do exploratory testing.

The important thing is that "the person who wrote it tested it" shouldn't be your entire quality strategy once failures actually matter.

## Testing is a skill

There's a subtle assumption behind the "developers can just do the testing" argument:

Testing is something anyone can do after they're done with their real work.

I don't think that's true.

Writing reliable software is a skill.

Understanding a product deeply is a skill.

Understanding how real users behave is a skill.

Knowing how to systematically find defects is also a skill.

Good testers don't just take the requirements and verify that each sentence is technically true.

They ask annoying questions.

What happens if I do this twice?

What happens if the network disappears here?

What if I'm already logged in?

What if I'm not logged in?

What if I came here from a different page?

What happens on Safari?

What happens with a very long customer name?

Can I go backward in this flow?

What happens if the API takes six seconds instead of 200 milliseconds?

Does this technically work but feel terrible to use?

That mindset takes time to develop.

And if your software engineers already feel overwhelmed by the amount of code they're expected to produce, adding another major responsibility doesn't magically create more hours in the week.

Sometimes it just means less development gets done.

Sometimes it means less testing gets done.

Sometimes both get done badly.

And sometimes people burn out while management congratulates itself for creating a "high-ownership engineering culture."

## Your industry changes the answer

A two-person startup building an experimental social app has a very different risk profile from a two-person startup building software used in a hospital.

The phrase "move fast and break things" sounds very different when the thing you're breaking is connected to healthcare, aviation, banking, financial infrastructure, automotive systems, defense, energy or utilities.

In those environments, quality problems can go far beyond an annoyed customer refreshing a page.

There can be financial consequences, regulatory consequences, contractual consequences and, in some cases, safety consequences.

But you shouldn't limit this thinking to traditionally regulated industries.

A product can become mission-critical without belonging to a mission-critical industry.

Endtest is a good example.

Our software is often deeply integrated into customers' CI/CD pipelines. If we break the wrong functionality, we aren't simply making a dashboard slightly inconvenient. We can interrupt the processes customers use to validate and release their own software.

The relevant question isn't:

**Is this an internal application or a customer-facing application?**

It's:

**What happens when this application doesn't work?**

Some internal applications are far more critical than many public websites.

## Budget matters too

Now let's go in the opposite direction.

Imagine you have three developers, six customers and $4,000 in monthly recurring revenue.

Should your next hire automatically be a dedicated QA engineer?

Probably not.

Your scarce resources may generate significantly more return somewhere else: another engineer, sales, customer support, product development or simply extending your runway.

At that stage, a reasonable quality strategy might involve developers testing each other's work, founders testing important flows, good unit and integration coverage, a focused automated end-to-end suite, and careful testing before releases.

You accept some risk because eliminating that risk would cost more than the business can reasonably justify.

That's not negligence.

That's prioritization.

But the equation changes as the company grows.

If you have thousands of paying customers, healthy revenue and enough engineering work to keep ten developers busy, the cost of adding a strong QA engineer may be tiny compared with the value of preventing defects, reducing developer interruptions and improving release confidence.

Quality has a cost.

Poor quality has a cost too.

The second number is just harder to put into a spreadsheet.

## The consequences can take years to appear

This is why I'm skeptical of organizational decisions justified entirely by immediate cost savings.

"Let's eliminate QA and have developers test everything."

"Let's replace customer support with chatbots."

"Let's remove this review step."

On a spreadsheet, the benefit appears immediately.

Three salaries disappeared.

Great quarter.

The downside is delayed.

Maybe defects gradually increase.

Maybe releases become more stressful.

Maybe developers spend more time reproducing customer issues.

Maybe customers stop trusting new releases.

Maybe the product develops dozens of small usability problems that aren't individually severe enough to trigger an incident but collectively make the experience worse.

Maybe customers eventually leave.

By then, the person who made the original decision may be in a different role or at a different company.

Complex systems are inconvenient that way.

The effects don't always arrive in time for the quarterly review.

## Be suspicious of simple answers to complicated questions

This principle extends far beyond QA.

Ask a good doctor what you need to do to live a long and healthy life.

You'll probably hear about exercise, nutrition, sleep, genetics, stress, alcohol, smoking, preventative care, existing conditions and a dozen other factors.

There will be a lot of "it depends."

Then ask a health influencer.

You may discover that the answer was cold plunges all along.

Preferably combined with the supplement they're selling.

Software management has its own version of this.

Every few months, someone discovers a revolutionary new rule.

Everyone should write JavaScript.

Everyone should be full-stack.

Nobody needs QA.

Nobody needs Product Managers.

AI will replace developers.

AI will replace testers.

Everyone should do everything.

You can usually identify questionable advice by how few conditions are attached to it.

The more complicated the system, the more suspicious I become when someone claims to have found one universal organizational rule.

## AI doesn't remove the need for testing judgment

AI makes this discussion more interesting.

It can write code.

It can generate unit tests.

It can create Playwright tests.

It can inspect a page and suggest test scenarios.

Those are useful capabilities.

But "Claude ran some Playwright tests" and "we have a reliable quality process" are not the same statement.

For a prototype with zero users, having an AI agent build a feature and run a few browser tests may be exactly the right tradeoff.

I wouldn't apply the same standard to a mature product that people depend on every day.

Real users are using your web application in Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge. They're on Windows and macOS. They have different screen resolutions, network conditions, browser extensions, permissions, account histories, data and geolocations.

They're also doing things you didn't expect them to do.

This is why [cross-browser testing](https://endtest.io/product/validate/cross-browser-testing) and end-to-end testing against realistic environments still matter.

A collection of AI-generated Playwright scenarios running headlessly in a Linux container can be useful.

It isn't reality.

## Automation is leverage, not a substitute for thinking

I'm obviously a believer in test automation. I've spent a large part of my career working on it.

Done well, automation is enormous leverage.

A test that would require a person to repeat the same 15-minute workflow every day can run hundreds of times across different environments without that person touching it.

That's valuable.

Done badly, test automation can become a second buggy software product that your engineering team has to maintain.

You end up with flaky tests, false positives, false negatives and people rerunning failed pipelines until they turn green.

Eventually, nobody trusts the suite.

The goal isn't maximum automation.

The goal is maximum useful confidence for the resources you're spending.

And despite what some AI demos imply, not every useful quality check should be automated.

Some flows are expensive to automate relative to their value.

Some change too frequently.

And some aspects of quality are fuzzy.

Does this onboarding flow make sense?

Does this interface feel confusing?

Does something about this interaction feel wrong?

Would a non-technical customer understand what to do next?

AI is getting better at these questions.

Humans are still remarkably good at noticing the little things that make software pleasant or unpleasant to use.

## Unit tests don't replace end-to-end testing

These layers solve different problems.

A unit test can prove that a function behaves exactly as expected while the product remains completely unusable.

The backend can work.

The frontend can work.

The API can work.

The authentication provider can work.

The payment integration can work.

And the complete checkout flow can still be broken.

That's why [end-to-end web testing](https://endtest.io/product/test-types/web-testing) exists.

You're testing the system the way a user encounters it, not merely proving that individual pieces behave correctly in isolation.

Good engineering organizations use multiple layers of testing.

They don't spend their time arguing about which single layer should replace all the others.

## AI-generated test scenarios are a starting point

Another trap in the AI era is confusing a long list with a comprehensive list.

Ask an LLM for test scenarios and it can generate 50 of them in seconds.

The output looks impressive.

Happy path.

Invalid input.

Empty input.

Long input.

Special characters.

Network errors.

Permissions.

Mobile.

Accessibility.

Great.

But the scenarios that matter most are often buried in knowledge that isn't contained in the ticket.

A particular enterprise customer has an unusual workflow.

Users regularly open three tabs.

Customers from one country use a specific payment method.

An old account type behaves differently.

A workflow depends on an email arriving before another request completes.

Users don't understand what a particular button means and repeatedly click it twice.

AI doesn't magically know those things.

Analytics and session recordings can reveal some of them.

Customer support can reveal others.

The rest comes from actually talking to users and understanding the product.

That's why I prefer using AI to **expand** a test strategy rather than define it.

Come up with the important scenarios yourself.

Then ask AI what you may have missed.

The order matters.

## A good QA engineer is more than someone who executes tests

This is another reason the discussion gets confused.

If your definition of a QA engineer is someone who receives a finished feature, manually follows five written steps, marks it "passed" and sends it back, then yes, you may question the value of the role.

That's a very narrow version of QA.

A strong QA engineer learns how the product works and why customers use it.

They talk to Product Owners before implementation.

They challenge ambiguous acceptance criteria.

They talk to developers about testability.

They identify risky areas before code is written.

They build and maintain useful automation.

They perform exploratory testing.

They understand which browsers, devices and environments your customers actually use.

They investigate production defects and use what they learn to prevent similar failures.

They become a bridge between the business side of the product and its technical implementation.

That's a valuable person to have around.

But the word **strong** matters.

Hiring inexperienced, disengaged QA engineers and throwing tickets over the wall to them isn't going to magically produce a great product.

A small number of skilled and motivated QA engineers who have enough time to understand the product can be far more valuable than a large QA team measured by how many test cases it executes.

## So, do you need dedicated QA engineers?

Here's the framework I would use:

1. **How expensive is a defect?** A typo on an experimental landing page and an incorrect financial transaction deserve different quality strategies.
2. **How many real users depend on the product?** More users usually means more environments, more workflows, more edge cases and a larger blast radius.
3. **How stretched is the engineering team?** If developers are already overloaded, assigning them an entire second discipline doesn't make the work disappear.
4. **How complex is the product?** Multiple integrations, browsers, devices, roles, permissions and workflows all increase the value of specialized testing.
5. **How much can you afford?** A pre-revenue startup shouldn't copy the staffing model of an enterprise company, but a profitable company shouldn't use startup scarcity as an excuse forever.
6. **How critical is the software?** Regulation matters, but so does practical dependency. Ask what happens to customers when the product fails.
7. **Who provides the independent perspective?** Even without a dedicated QA employee, somebody other than the author of the feature should critically evaluate important changes.
8. **Who understands your users?** Effective testing requires knowledge of what customers actually do, what they care about and what environments they use.

If you're building an early product with little revenue, few users and low consequences when something breaks, I probably wouldn't rush to hire dedicated QA engineers.

Use the resources elsewhere and build a sensible lightweight testing process.

If you have the budget, a growing user base, significant product complexity and customers who depend on your software, dedicated QA engineers become much easier to justify.

And if failures can cause serious financial, regulatory, operational or safety consequences, I would be extremely careful about designing your quality strategy around saving one salary.

## Quality is everyone's responsibility. Testing doesn't have to be.

There's a sentence I agree with:

**Quality is everyone's responsibility.**

Developers should care about quality.

Product Managers should care about quality.

Designers should care about quality.

Executives should care about quality.

QA engineers should care about quality.

But "everyone is responsible for quality" does not logically lead to "therefore nobody needs to specialize in testing."

Security is everyone's responsibility too.

Most serious companies still hire security specialists.

The AI era is actually making this distinction clearer.

We're discovering very quickly that producing code wasn't the entire job of building good software.

Code is becoming cheaper to generate.

Judgment isn't.

Understanding users isn't.

Knowing which compromises are safe isn't.

Recognizing that something technically works but shouldn't ship isn't.

Knowing where to look for the failure nobody else considered isn't.

Those are human inputs.

And as our ability to produce software gets faster, I suspect they'll become more valuable, not less.

So don't hire QA engineers because some testing handbook says every team needs them.

And don't fire them because somebody posted that developers should own everything.

Look at your product.

Look at your users.

Look at the consequences of failure.

Look at your team.

Look at your budget.

Then make the decision that fits the company you actually have.

---

# CI/CD Test Automation: The Real Maturity Check

A practical guide to making automated tests reliable in CI/CD, from rate limits and flaky browsers to real Windows and macOS execution.

Published August 25, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/ci-cd-test-automation-real-maturity-check

---
There is a point where an automated test suite stops being a collection of scripts and starts becoming part of your engineering process.

That point is usually when you put it in the CI/CD pipeline.

Before that, things can look surprisingly good.

Someone creates a few Selenium or Playwright tests. They run them on their laptop. Everything passes. They show the team. Maybe they even run the entire suite a few times without a failure.

Great.

But a laptop is a very forgiving place to run automated tests.

You control the browser version. You control the screen resolution. You're probably already authenticated. Your IP address already has access to the staging environment. Your machine isn't competing with five other builds for CPU. And if something fails, you can just run it again.

CI/CD removes most of those conveniences.

That's why I think putting automated tests into the pipeline is one of the best maturity checks you can give a test suite.

## The pipeline is where tests get audited

A test that works on one person's computer proves something.

A test that runs automatically after every build, on infrastructure nobody is babysitting, proves a lot more.

The pipeline asks questions your local environment doesn't:

Can this test start from a clean state?

Can it authenticate without a person helping it?

Can it find the right test data?

Can it survive a slower environment?

Can it upload and download files?

Can it run at the same time as other tests?

Can it produce enough evidence for somebody else to understand a failure?

And, perhaps most importantly:

**Can the team trust it enough to let it influence a release?**

That's a much higher bar.

I've seen plenty of automated test projects that looked healthy until they were connected to CI. Suddenly the pass rate dropped, execution times became unpredictable, and failures appeared that nobody had seen locally.

That's not CI breaking the tests.

That's CI exposing the tests.

## Your CI runner should orchestrate tests, not become a browser lab

One pattern I don't love is putting the entire browser-testing infrastructure directly inside the CI runner.

A GitHub Actions job starts.

It installs Node or Python.

It installs Playwright or Selenium dependencies.

It downloads browsers.

It starts a headless browser inside a Linux container.

Then it runs the complete end-to-end suite there.

Technically, this works.

For some tests, it's perfectly reasonable.

But I wouldn't make that the only environment responsible for deciding whether a web application is ready for real users.

A better architecture is to let CI/CD orchestrate the tests while dedicated testing infrastructure executes them.

Something like this:

```text
New build
    ↓
Deploy test environment
    ↓
CI/CD pipeline sends test command
    ↓
Dedicated Windows / macOS test machines
    ↓
Real browsers execute the tests
    ↓
Results, screenshots, logs and artifacts
    ↓
Pipeline decides whether to continue
```

Your GitHub, GitLab, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, or other runner doesn't need to become the browser infrastructure itself.

It can simply call an API or execute a lightweight command that says:

> Run regression suite 42 against this environment.

That separation turns out to be useful.

Your build infrastructure can change without changing your browser infrastructure. Your test machines can be upgraded independently. You can control browser versions, resolutions, concurrency and operating systems in one place.

And your pipeline remains relatively boring.

Boring pipelines are good.

## Run important tests where your users actually run the app

Headless Chrome on Linux is fast and useful.

I wouldn't get rid of it.

It's excellent for fast checks where you want feedback in a few minutes.

But there is a dangerous leap between:

> Our application works in headless Chromium inside a Linux container.

and:

> Our application works for our customers.

Those aren't always the same thing.

If your customers use Chrome and Edge on Windows, you should test meaningful flows there.

If they use Safari, at least part of your release process should involve real Safari on macOS.

This matters for things such as fonts, rendering, scrolling, browser APIs, file downloads, native behavior, viewport handling and browser-specific JavaScript behavior.

The goal of automated testing isn't to make the pipeline green.

The goal is to catch situations that would otherwise make users unhappy.

A test suite that passes beautifully in an environment none of your customers use can create a dangerous sense of confidence.

That's why, for release-critical end-to-end tests, I prefer [real browser testing on Windows and macOS](https://endtest.io/product/test-types/web-testing) rather than relying exclusively on headless Linux containers.

You can still keep fast containerized tests earlier in the pipeline.

Think of them as different layers, not competing philosophies.

## What usually breaks when tests move into CI/CD

This is where the maturity check gets interesting.

There are a few problems that show up over and over.

### 1. Rate limiting

Your application may happily accept a person clicking through checkout once.

Then your pipeline runs 40 tests in parallel.

Suddenly the authentication service, API, payment sandbox or third-party provider starts returning `429 Too Many Requests`.

The test didn't necessarily discover a product bug.

It discovered that your automated testing architecture behaves differently from a human.

The fix might involve controlling concurrency, creating dedicated test accounts, coordinating test data, or working with the service's rate limits instead of blindly adding retries.

### 2. Access denied to test environments

The developer's laptop can reach staging.

The CI runner cannot.

Maybe staging is behind a VPN. Maybe there is an IP allowlist. Maybe a firewall rule only permits corporate addresses.

This is another reason remote execution architecture matters.

You want stable, known testing machines whose IP addresses and permissions can be managed intentionally.

Environment access shouldn't be rediscovered during every build.

### 3. File uploads and downloads

File testing has a habit of working perfectly until the tests leave somebody's laptop.

A local test might reference:

```text
/Users/alex/Desktop/invoice.pdf
```

That file obviously won't exist inside a random CI container.

Downloads introduce another set of problems: temporary directories, browser permissions, generated filenames, cleanup and retrieving the downloaded artifact after the run.

If uploading and downloading files are meaningful parts of your product, they need to be treated as first-class parts of the testing infrastructure.

Not clever workarounds inside individual tests.

### 4. Flakiness

This is the big one.

The pipeline is often slower than the computer where the test was written.

Animations take slightly longer.

An API responds in 1.8 seconds instead of 700 milliseconds.

A JavaScript component renders in a different order.

The screen resolution changes.

A button moves below the fold.

Five browsers are running simultaneously.

Suddenly that innocent-looking two-second sleep isn't enough anymore.

And this is where teams often make the situation worse by adding more sleeps and more retries.

A mature test suite waits for conditions, not arbitrary amounts of time.

It understands when an element is actually ready.

And when it fails, the failure is treated as information rather than immediately being hidden behind three retries.

### 5. Test data collisions

Two pipeline jobs create a user with the same email address.

One deletes an account while another test is still using it.

A test assumes the database starts empty.

Another assumes last night's test data is still there.

Tests that depend on shared mutable state tend to become much more fragile as soon as parallel execution arrives.

Unique data, reliable setup and reliable cleanup matter much more in CI than they do on a laptop.

### 6. Secrets and authentication

Passwords, API keys and authentication tokens shouldn't live in test code.

In CI/CD, credentials need to come from a proper secrets system.

Authentication flows also need to survive clean sessions.

If a test only passes because the person who created it still has a valid browser cookie from Tuesday, it isn't really automated yet.

### 7. Resource contention

There is a strange class of flaky tests that aren't really flaky at all.

The machine is flaky.

CPU gets saturated.

Memory gets tight.

Four browsers compete for resources.

The page takes twice as long to render.

Then someone spends two days rewriting selectors.

Dedicated execution capacity can eliminate a surprising amount of this noise.

## Retries are useful. Invisible retries are dangerous.

There is nothing inherently wrong with retrying an infrastructure failure.

Networks fail.

Browsers occasionally crash.

Services occasionally return something strange.

But retries should not turn a failing test into a passing test without leaving evidence behind.

If a test fails the first time and passes the second time, that is still useful information.

A team should be able to see:

- the original failure;
- whether a retry happened;
- screenshots or video from the failed attempt;
- the page state;
- logs;
- how frequently the same test needs retries.

Otherwise, your CI dashboard says everything is green while reliability quietly gets worse every month.

Eventually developers learn that "green" doesn't mean much.

And once engineers stop trusting automated tests, rebuilding that trust is much harder than building the tests in the first place.

## Not every test needs to block every pull request

Putting automated tests in CI/CD doesn't mean running 900 browser tests before somebody can merge a typo.

The test strategy should match the stage of the pipeline.

A practical setup might look like this:

**Pull request:** fast smoke tests covering the most important functionality.

**After deployment to staging:** critical end-to-end user journeys.

**Main branch or release candidate:** broader regression coverage across your important browsers and operating systems.

**Scheduled runs:** longer combinations, edge cases and less critical regression scenarios.

You want feedback early without making developers wait unnecessarily.

But you also want a point before production where the application is tested like the application your customers will actually use.

This is where [cross-browser testing](https://endtest.io/product/validate/cross-browser-testing) becomes much more valuable than simply running the same headless browser 50 times.

## CI/CD also tests whether your automation is keeping up

There is another reason I like using CI/CD integration as a maturity check.

It exposes whether the automated tests are actually keeping up with development.

A company can say:

> We have 700 automated tests.

That sounds impressive.

But if those tests validate the application from three sprints ago, the number doesn't mean very much.

When the tests are part of the pipeline, there is pressure to keep them current.

A developer changes onboarding.

The onboarding tests need to change.

The checkout flow changes.

The checkout tests need to change.

A new feature ships.

Someone needs to decide what automated coverage it requires.

That is healthier than having one automation engineer maintaining a separate backlog that is permanently one release behind the product.

The pipeline makes outdated automation visible.

## A failing test becomes harder to ignore

There is also an organizational effect that doesn't get discussed enough.

A local test can fail quietly.

Someone runs it.

It fails.

They run it again.

Maybe they fix it next week.

Maybe nobody ever knows.

A pipeline failure has a history.

Build 381 passed.

Build 382 failed.

Here is the test.

Here is when it started failing.

Here is the screenshot.

Here is the log.

Here is the commit associated with it.

Suddenly the test has accountability.

That's a good thing.

Putting automated tests in the pipeline puts both the tests and the people maintaining them in the spotlight.

Weak tests become obvious.

Outdated tests become obvious.

Flaky tests become annoying enough that somebody eventually has to fix them.

And strong tests become something the engineering team genuinely depends on.

## Make failures cheap to investigate

If automated tests are going to stop releases, they need to explain themselves.

A message that says:

```text
ElementNotFoundException
```

isn't enough.

A useful failure should give the team enough context to make a decision quickly.

Ideally that includes the failed step, browser and operating system, screenshot, video, logs, page source, timestamps and environment information.

You shouldn't need the original test author sitting next to you to understand what happened.

This is one of the reasons we've built Endtest so a CI/CD system can simply [trigger executions through the API](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/how-to-use-the-endtest-api), while the actual browser execution and evidence collection happen on dedicated testing infrastructure.

The build system asks for the test.

The testing system handles the test.

That separation becomes increasingly valuable as suites grow.

## What mature CI/CD test automation looks like

You probably have a reasonably mature setup when:

- tests can start from clean, repeatable conditions;
- important end-to-end flows run on the browsers and operating systems your customers use;
- your CI runner triggers tests instead of carrying the entire browser infrastructure itself;
- test data can survive parallel execution;
- uploads, downloads, authentication and external services are handled deliberately;
- flaky tests are investigated instead of endlessly retried;
- failures contain enough evidence for someone else to diagnose them;
- automated coverage changes during the same sprint as the product;
- the team trusts a red test enough to investigate it;
- and the team trusts a green build enough to ship it.

That last part is the entire point.

## The pipeline is a test of the tests

The first milestone in test automation is creating a test.

The second is making it pass.

But neither one tells you whether you have a mature test automation system.

Put it in the pipeline.

Run it repeatedly.

Run it without the person who created it.

Run it on clean machines.

Run it after every meaningful product change.

Run important flows on the actual browsers and operating systems your customers use.

Then see what happens.

CI/CD has a habit of exposing every shortcut hiding inside a test suite.

That's useful.

Because the best automated tests aren't the ones that look impressive during a demo.

They're the ones your team forgets to worry about because they run every day, catch real regressions, leave useful evidence when something breaks, and quietly give everyone more confidence to ship.

---

# How to Reduce Defects in Production

Reduce production defects by keeping end-to-end tests current, making quality a team responsibility, and helping developers understand users and business risk.

Published August 12, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/how-to-reduce-defects-in-production

---
Production has a strange reputation in software.

A defect shows up there and everyone talks about it as if production somehow created it.

"It happened in production."

"We had an issue in production."

"An edge case appeared."

Then comes the technical explanation. A race condition. An unexpected state. A browser-specific problem. A service returned something we didn't expect.

But in many cases, the defect didn't suddenly appear in production. Production was simply the first place where someone found it.

The bug was probably sitting there in development. Then it moved to the test environment. Then staging.

Nobody encountered the exact combination of data, permissions, browser, timing, actions, or previous state required to trigger it.

Then the release went live.

A real user happened to take that path.

And now it's a production defect.

There are obviously genuine production-only problems. Traffic, infrastructure, configuration, third-party systems, and scale can create conditions that don't exist elsewhere.

But a surprising number of production defects aren't like that.

They're functional defects that made it through several environments without anyone finding them.

So if you want fewer defects in production, don't start with "how do we fix production defects faster?"

Start with:

**Why didn't we find them earlier?**

## 1. Get automated tests into the sprint

Here's a development process I've seen variations of many times.

Developers work on features until the final days of the sprint.

Meanwhile, the one or two people responsible for automation have their own backlog of test scenarios to automate.

Development moves faster than that backlog.

So the automated tests are always one release behind.

The framework is perpetually "almost ready."

The test suite is going to cover the new functionality soon.

Probably next sprint.

Then the end of the current sprint arrives and everyone realizes the new functionality hasn't really been tested.

So the entire team spends a few frantic hours manually clicking around before the release.

That's manual testing with an automation side project, not a test automation strategy.

And when a defect later reaches production, the team is surprised.

The most useful automated test is generally one that exists while the feature is still being developed.

That's the window where it can catch a regression before release, run repeatedly while the code changes, and give the team confidence about what they're shipping.

Creating a beautiful automated regression test three weeks after the feature has already gone to production is still useful.

But you've missed its most valuable moment.

This is also why I don't think unit tests alone are a reasonable answer to functional quality.

Unit tests are excellent for validating small pieces of behavior. They're fast, deterministic, and extremely valuable.

But they don't magically prove that a real user can log in, change a subscription, upload a document, complete checkout, receive the right confirmation, and see the correct result afterward.

We've known this for decades.

Different tests catch different categories of problems.

If production defects are happening in real user flows, you need tests that actually exercise those flows.

## AI doesn't fix a bad testing process

AI makes automated testing faster.

It does not remove the need to think.

There's an increasingly common workflow that looks like this:

"Here is my application. AI, generate some tests."

That's easy.

It's also lazy.

AI will usually produce reasonable scenarios. It will cover the obvious paths. It may even find cases you didn't immediately think about.

But the creative part of testing still matters.

A good tester doesn't only ask:

> What should happen when the user does the correct thing?

They ask:

What happens when the user has two tabs open?

What if this account was created three years ago?

What if the payment succeeds but the next request fails?

What if the user navigates backward?

What if this field contains something unexpected?

What if the session expires halfway through?

What if the same action is performed twice?

And there's another problem with outsourcing the thinking to AI. People get less creative when they stop exercising that part of the process.

A better workflow is the opposite.

First, have a human think about the functionality and write down the important scenarios.

Then ask AI:

**What did I miss?**

Now you're combining human understanding of the product with the breadth and speed of AI.

That's much more powerful than starting with an empty prompt and accepting whatever test cases a model generates.

## Don't let the developer test their own assumptions

There's another rule I strongly believe in.

The person who implements a feature shouldn't be the only person designing the functional tests for it.

Ideally, someone else creates or reviews those tests after the developer explains how the feature works.

The reason is simple.

The developer has assumptions.

Some of those assumptions are embedded in the implementation.

If that same person creates all the tests, those assumptions can easily become embedded in the tests too.

Now you have code and tests sharing the same blind spot.

Independent verification is an important principle in high-assurance and mission-critical software for exactly this reason.

You want another brain looking at the problem.

And this doesn't need to become some giant bureaucratic QA process.

A developer can explain a feature to a colleague in ten minutes.

That colleague can ask three questions the original developer never considered.

Those three questions might be more valuable than another hundred lines of test code.

## The ideal test automation team is the whole team

If only one person knows how to maintain the automated tests, you don't really have a test automation system.

You have a test automation person.

That's fragile.

And it creates a throughput problem.

Five developers can produce new functionality much faster than one automation engineer can reproduce everything in a separate automation framework.

The obvious solution is getting more people involved.

Developers. Testers. Product-minded engineers. Anyone who understands the functionality.

But there's a problem.

Most people don't want to learn another framework, maintain another repository, debug another dependency tree, and spend half a day figuring out why some selector generated nine months ago no longer works.

You might think AI solves this.

Just ask Claude to generate Playwright tests and now everyone can contribute.

I don't think that's the answer either.

You can very quickly create a black box containing thousands of lines of AI-generated test code that nobody really understands.

The tests pass.

Great.

But does everyone know what they're actually checking?

And when they fail six months later, who understands why?

This becomes even more dangerous if your team is already using AI heavily to build the product itself.

AI writes the implementation.

Then AI writes tests for the implementation.

You can end up with a double blind spot where neither side received enough independent human reasoning.

The better approach is to make the tests themselves understandable.

This is one of the reasons we built [Endtest](https://endtest.io/).

Tests in Endtest are represented as readable steps that people across the team can inspect, modify, run, and maintain without living inside a test framework repository.

AI can help create tests, generate assertions and variables, repair broken elements with Self-Healing Tests, and even [analyze failed test steps](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/analyze-failures-with-ai).

But the test doesn't disappear behind the AI.

The human-readable steps remain there for the team to review and control.

That's an important distinction.

**AI should make it easier for humans to maintain good tests. It shouldn't make humans irrelevant to testing.**

And when contributing to tests doesn't require everyone to become an expert in a separate testing framework, you have a much better chance of getting the whole team involved.

That's how you get tests written during the sprint instead of three weeks later.

## 2. Bring accountability back to software quality

Here's the second way to reduce production defects.

Accountability.

Nobody likes that word.

Software teams have become extremely careful about avoiding anything that could sound like blame.

And there's a good reason for that. A culture where people are afraid to make mistakes produces terrible software organizations.

But we've sometimes overcorrected.

A major defect reaches production and the language immediately becomes strangely passive.

"An issue occurred."

"The system allowed an invalid state."

"The validation wasn't triggered."

Then there's a technical postmortem, everyone agrees that software is complicated, and life continues.

That's not enough.

When a notable defect reaches production, the people involved in developing and testing that functionality should discuss it.

Not so someone can be punished, and not so a manager can point at a developer and say, "You caused this."

The goal should be to understand:

**What did we miss, and why did we miss it?**

Was there no automated test?

Was the scenario never considered?

Did the test exist but run too late?

Did nobody understand how customers actually used the feature?

Was one person's assumption accepted by everyone else?

Was Safari excluded from testing even though 18% of customers use it?

Was there a test backlog that everyone already knew was two sprints behind?

Those are process problems you can fix.

Accountability actually helps here.

When people know that important mistakes will be discussed, they pay more attention.

That's not necessarily negative pressure.

It can work almost like gamification.

Professional football teams don't pretend individual mistakes never happen.

If a player repeatedly loses possession in a certain situation, they review it.

They watch the footage.

They understand what went wrong.

The player learns from it. The coach learns from it. The rest of the team learns from it.

Nobody says:

"Don't worry about it. The ball was lost. These things happen."

The final score is still what matters most.

But football teams measure an absurd number of individual statistics because individual performance affects the final result.

Software teams can learn something from that.

You can have a blameless culture without having an accountability-less culture.

Those are not the same thing.

## 3. Make developers understand the business

There's one more thing that has an enormous effect on software quality, and it's rarely listed under "testing."

Your developers need to understand the business.

The whole business, beyond the Jira ticket.

The product.

The customers.

That means talking to product owners.

Business analysts.

Marketing.

Sales.

Customer support.

And yes, that means spending engineering time in meetings instead of writing code.

I think that's one of the highest-return investments a software company can make.

I've seen situations where technically excellent developers knew surprisingly little about the product they were building.

This becomes especially common in large products where teams own narrow areas.

Imagine you're working on warehouse software for an online retailer.

Your system receives an order, finds the inventory, creates a picking task, and eventually marks the parcel as dispatched.

You could understand that component perfectly.

But you'd make better decisions if you also understood what happened before and after it.

How was the order created?

When is the customer charged?

When is the invoice generated?

What information gets sent to the courier?

How does the customer track the package?

What happens if an item becomes unavailable?

What happens when the customer requests a cancellation while the warehouse is already processing the order?

Suddenly, an edge case inside "your" small area stops being a weird state in a database.

It's a customer who was charged for an order they can't receive.

Understanding users matters just as much.

Suppose you discover a blocking defect that only affects Safari.

"Can't they just use Chrome?"

Technically, maybe.

Commercially, maybe not.

As I wrote in [What Browsers Should You Test Your Website On?](https://endtest.io/blog/what-browsers-should-you-test-your-website-on), browser coverage should be driven by your actual users and the risk associated with those users, not by the browser your development team happens to prefer.

And the same principle applies everywhere.

A checkout defect is not equivalent to a typo on a settings page.

If users encounter a cosmetic problem, many of them will keep going.

If they encounter an error when they're about to pay you, they probably aren't going to contact Support, clear their cache, switch browsers, and try again.

They're going to buy from somebody else.

A developer who understands that will make different testing decisions.

## Production quality starts long before production

Reducing production defects is mostly about moving discovery earlier, not about building a better incident-response process.

You want relevant functional tests running while the feature is being built.

You want someone other than the developer challenging the assumptions behind the feature.

You want the entire team capable of contributing to tests instead of maintaining a permanent automation backlog.

You want AI helping people think and execute faster, not replacing the thinking.

You want production defects reviewed with accountability but without finger-pointing.

And you want engineers who understand what their software actually means to the business and the people using it.

None of these ideas are particularly exotic.

That's part of the problem.

Most teams already know some version of them.

The hard part is organizing development so they actually happen.

Because the objective isn't an impressive automation framework, or 10,000 automated tests, or proudly announcing that 94% of your unit tests pass.

The objective is much simpler:

**Find defects before your customers do.**

Everything else is implementation detail.

If your current automation setup makes it difficult for the whole team to create, understand, and maintain tests during the sprint, you can explore how [Endtest works](https://endtest.io/docs).

# Software Quality Metrics CTOs Should Track in 2026

Track the software quality metrics that matter: release risk, test coverage, automation maintenance, team adoption, and the true cost of testing.

Published August 7, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/software-quality-metrics-ctos-2026

---
CTOs don't need another dashboard with 37 QA metrics.

They need to know something much simpler:

**Can we ship quickly without breaking things?**

That's really the job of a quality strategy.

And yet, a lot of engineering organizations still measure QA using numbers that are easy to collect but don't tell you very much.

Number of test cases. Lines of automation code. Percentage of tests automated. Number of bugs found.

Those numbers can all go up while your ability to ship reliable software gets worse.

In 2026, especially as AI accelerates how quickly teams can build software, I think CTOs need a different scorecard.

Here are the metrics I'd pay attention to.

## 1. Escaped defects

The obvious one.

How many meaningful bugs make it to production?

Not every bug deserves equal weight, of course. A spacing issue in an admin page isn't the same as customers being unable to complete checkout.

So rather than obsessing over the raw number, categorize production defects by severity and affected functionality.

The interesting trend is whether important regressions are becoming less common over time.

If your automated test suite grows from 2,000 tests to 8,000 tests while the number of serious production regressions stays the same, something isn't working.

Test count is an input. Escaped defects are an outcome. CTOs should care much more about the latter.

## 2. Critical functionality coverage

Code coverage is useful to engineers.

It's much less useful as an executive quality metric.

You can have 90% code coverage while having no automated test that verifies whether a customer can actually sign up, upgrade their subscription, reset their password, or complete checkout.

What I would rather see is a simple map of your important product functionality and the automated tests covering it.

Something like:

| Functionality | Automated | Last Tested | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sign up | Yes | Today | Passing |
| Log in | Yes | Today | Passing |
| Upgrade subscription | Yes | Today | Passing |
| Cancel subscription | No | - | Gap |
| Reset password | Yes | Yesterday | Passing |
| Invite team member | No | - | Gap |

The traditional QA term for this is a **Requirements Traceability Matrix**, or RTM.

But you don't need to turn it into an enterprise bureaucracy project.

For most SaaS companies, a lightweight feature-to-test coverage matrix is enough.

The point is that you should be able to look at the product and answer:

**What important functionality isn't protected by automated tests?**

That's much more useful than knowing you have 4,312 tests.

## 3. Can test automation keep up with the sprint?

This might be my favorite metric.

Imagine your engineering team finishes 15 meaningful product changes during a sprint.

How many of those changes have the appropriate automated tests by the end of that sprint?

If the answer is five, your test automation isn't really keeping up with development.

You're accumulating quality debt.

And eventually someone schedules a "QA automation sprint" to catch up.

Then development continues.

Then QA falls behind again.

I've seen organizations focus on how many Selenium or Playwright scripts their automation engineers produce. Sometimes they'll even indirectly measure productivity through commits or lines of code.

I think that's backwards.

I'd replace the KPI

> How much automation code did we write?

with

> Are we continuously keeping the product covered as it changes?

A great automation engineer who writes very little code but keeps every important sprint feature covered is doing a better job than someone who builds thousands of lines of framework code while the test backlog keeps growing.

This is also where tooling choices start to matter.

If creating a test requires writing a few hundred lines of code, debugging locators, configuring dependencies, reviewing pull requests, maintaining CI infrastructure and keeping framework versions working, you're spending a lot of your automation capacity on the automation itself.

That's time that isn't being spent increasing product coverage.

## 4. Test maintenance cost

Automated tests are often described as if they have two states:

Created.

Not created.

But creation is only the beginning.

Every automated test becomes something you own.

The UI changes. An API changes. A locator stops working. Authentication changes. A browser update behaves differently. A dependency breaks. A test becomes flaky.

Someone then has to figure out whether the product is broken or the test is broken.

This is why I'd track the engineering hours spent maintaining automated tests.

Not perfectly. You don't need everyone running timers.

Even a rough monthly estimate can be eye-opening.

If three engineers spend a combined 100 hours every month maintaining your test infrastructure and fixing test scripts, that's part of the cost of your test automation strategy.

Which leads to another metric CTOs should care about.

## 5. The true cost of test automation

Selenium is free. Playwright is free. And both are excellent open-source projects. But your test automation isn't free.

Someone has to build the framework. Someone has to maintain it. Someone has to handle reporting, parallel execution, test data, browser infrastructure, retries, screenshots, logs, CI integrations, authentication, secrets, dependency upgrades, browser updates and flaky tests.

And eventually, someone has to understand the framework built by the person who left the company two years ago.

The license cost of your testing library might be $0 while the actual cost of operating your test automation program is tens of thousands of dollars per year.

This is the same mistake companies sometimes make when comparing an enterprise testing platform with an open-source library.

They compare:

**$0 vs. $15,000**

when the real comparison might be:

**$90,000 in engineering time and infrastructure vs. $15,000 for software that eliminates most of that work.**

The exact numbers will obviously vary by company.

But CTOs should be measuring total cost of ownership, not license price.

A tool is expensive when it consumes a lot of your team's time, not when it has a price.

## 6. Time to understand a failed test

A test failing is only useful if someone can understand why it failed.

If a test fails at 2:13 AM in CI and an engineer spends 45 minutes the next morning looking through logs, screenshots and source code trying to determine what happened, that investigation time is part of your QA cost.

Multiply it across hundreds of failures.

This is one reason flaky tests become so damaging.

Eventually the team stops treating a red test as information.

They treat it as noise.

"Probably flaky. Run it again."

At that point, you technically have automated testing.

But you don't have much release confidence.

I'd track how quickly the team can go from:

**Test failed**

to:

**We understand what happened.**

AI can be particularly useful here because screenshots, page source, test context and error information can be analyzed together instead of requiring someone to manually reconstruct the failure.

The goal is to save engineering time, not to make an impressive AI demo.

## 7. Team adoption

Here's another underrated one:

**Who can actually create and maintain your automated tests?**

If your 50-person engineering organization has one automation engineer who understands the Selenium framework, you don't really have broad test automation adoption.

You have a dependency on one person.

This creates two problems.

First, that person becomes a bottleneck.

Every sprint produces functionality faster than one person can possibly automate it.

Second, the system becomes fragile organizationally.

What happens when that person is on vacation? Or moves to another team? Or leaves?

I think a healthy automation program should gradually increase the number of people capable of contributing to it.

That can include QA engineers, developers, product people and other technical team members.

This is one of the ideas behind the [Endtest AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent).

Instead of requiring every contributor to understand a testing framework, selectors, browser drivers and all of the code surrounding the test, they can describe the scenario and generate an editable automated test.

The resulting test is a set of understandable steps that the team can inspect, modify and reuse, rather than something hidden inside a giant AI-generated codebase.

That makes team adoption a much more realistic KPI.

## 8. Release confidence

This one isn't as easy to put into a database column.

But it's arguably the metric everything else is trying to improve.

Before a deployment, ask the team:

**How confident are we that this release hasn't broken an important customer workflow?**

If the answer depends on whether Sarah manually clicked around staging for two hours, you have a problem.

If the answer is:

"We automatically tested every critical workflow affected by this release across the environments we care about, and everything passed."

That's a very different situation.

The point of automated testing is confidence, not the automation itself.

## The metrics I wouldn't obsess over

There are a few numbers I'd treat carefully.

**Lines of test automation code.**

More code means more code to maintain. It is not a measure of quality.

**Number of automated tests.**

10,000 bad tests aren't better than 1,000 meaningful tests.

**Percentage of tests automated.**

Automating low-value tests just to increase this number doesn't help anyone.

**Number of bugs discovered by QA.**

A QA team finding fewer bugs can mean quality improved. Or it can mean they're missing bugs. The number alone doesn't tell you much.

**Automation engineer output.**

Counting scripts, commits or tickets completed encourages the wrong behavior. Measure whether automation coverage keeps pace with product development instead.

## A better CTO quality dashboard

If I were building a simple quality dashboard for a CTO, I'd probably keep it to something like this:

- Serious production defects
- Critical functionality covered by automation
- Sprint features receiving automated coverage
- Flaky test rate
- Test maintenance effort
- Time to understand failures
- Total cost of automation
- Number of people actively contributing tests

You can add more metrics later.

But those eight already answer some pretty important questions.

Are we protecting the right things? Are we keeping up with development? Does the team trust the tests? And how much are we actually spending to get that confidence?

## The goal isn't more test automation

Your company isn't in the business of producing Selenium scripts. Or Playwright scripts. Or even Endtest tests.

You're trying to build a product and ship improvements to customers without constantly breaking what already works.

Testing infrastructure should make that easier.

When the testing framework itself becomes a significant engineering project, with its own architecture, dependencies, infrastructure, maintenance backlog and a handful of people who understand it, you should include all of that in the ROI calculation.

Modern testing platforms can remove a lot of that framework tax.

With Endtest, for example, teams can create and run automated tests without maintaining their own browser automation framework, while AI can accelerate test creation and help with maintenance and failure analysis.

That doesn't make Selenium or Playwright bad tools.

It just means "free" isn't the metric a CTO should optimize for.

There are better questions. How quickly can we cover new functionality? How much does that coverage cost us? Can the whole team contribute? And when the product changes again next week, can our automated tests keep up?

And if you're comparing the cost of building and maintaining your own automation stack with using a managed platform, don't just compare license prices.

Compare the actual resources required to get the same outcome.

You can see how [Endtest pricing](https://endtest.io/pricing) compares once engineering time, infrastructure and ongoing maintenance are part of the equation.
