# What Is the Easiest Way to Automate Tests?

Learn when manual testing stops being enough, why AI-generated Playwright and Selenium suites become costly, and how to automate tests more easily.

Published July 27, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/what-is-the-easiest-way-to-automate-tests

---
The easiest way to automate tests is not necessarily the method that produces the first test fastest.

That distinction matters more than ever in 2026.

Today, almost anyone can open an AI coding tool, ask it to generate a Playwright test, and get something that looks convincing a few minutes later. The test may even pass. That creates a powerful first impression: test automation has finally become easy.

But producing the first test was never the hard part.

The hard part is building a test suite that your team still understands, trusts, uses, and maintains six months later.

After working in test automation for nearly a decade, I have seen the same pattern repeat across companies of different sizes. Teams rarely fail because they cannot create an automated test. They fail because the system around those tests becomes too expensive, too specialised, or too opaque for the rest of the company to adopt.

So the real question is:

> What is the easiest way to own a reliable test suite over time?

For most growing software teams, the answer is an intelligent test automation platform where AI helps create and maintain tests, but the tests themselves remain visible, structured, and human-readable.

## You may not need automated tests yet

There is a point in the life of a small software business where not having functional end-to-end tests can be a rational decision.

Imagine a small team with:

- A relatively simple product
- A limited number of user journeys
- A small customer base
- Infrequent releases
- Direct access to users
- A founder or developer who still knows the entire product

At that stage, someone can manually check the registration flow, log in, create a record, process a payment, and verify the most important screens before a release.

You may already have unit tests. Those are useful, but they usually do not provide enough confidence that the complete product still works from a user's perspective. A passing unit test does not prove that a user can sign up, receive a verification email, enter a payment method, and reach the correct dashboard.

Still, when the product is small enough, manual checking may be good enough.

Test automation is an investment. It consumes money, attention, and implementation time. Early-stage companies have many competing uses for those resources: talking to customers, improving onboarding, closing sales, reducing churn, or shipping the feature that makes the product viable.

Automating everything too early can be as wasteful as automating nothing for too long.

## The economics change as the company grows

The point where test automation begins to make sense is determined by the growing cost of uncertainty, more than by team size.

As the company grows, several things happen at once:

- The product develops more features, roles, integrations, and edge cases.
- More developers change different parts of the system.
- Releases become more frequent.
- Manual regression takes longer.
- The number of customers affected by a defect increases.
- The team becomes less able to keep the entire product in one person's head.

A defect that affected three early adopters may have been an embarrassing support ticket. The same defect affecting thousands of paying users can cause a flood of complaints, lost renewals, emergency engineering work, and damage to the company's reputation.

The cost goes beyond the time required to fix the bug.

It can include:

- A poor user experience
- Customer churn
- Refunds or service credits
- Lost deals
- Support time
- Interrupted roadmap work
- Developer context switching
- Delayed releases
- Reduced confidence inside the team

A simple way to think about the decision is:

**Automated testing starts to make economic sense when the recurring cost of manual regression and escaped defects becomes greater than the cost of creating and maintaining reliable automated tests.**

The calculation does not have to be perfect. You can use the framework in our guide on [calculating test automation ROI](https://endtest.io/blog/how-to-calculate-roi-for-test-automation) to estimate it more formally.

In practice, the transition often becomes obvious. Releases feel increasingly stressful. Manual regression becomes a checklist no one has time to finish. The same bugs return. Developers avoid changing fragile areas. Customers discover important defects before the team does.

That is usually the moment when automated end-to-end testing stops being an optional engineering improvement and becomes part of running the business.

## The most difficult way to automate tests

Around ten years ago, the default answer was to build an internal automation framework.

A company would choose Selenium, Cypress, or another code-based library. One or two engineers would create a repository, establish conventions, build helper functions, configure environments, connect a browser cloud, and write the first group of tests.

The early demo usually looked promising.

Then reality arrived.

The framework needed:

- Authentication helpers
- Test data management
- Reporting
- Screenshots and videos
- Parallel execution
- Retry logic
- Environment configuration
- Browser and driver updates
- CI/CD integration
- Secrets management
- Email and SMS testing
- File handling
- Debugging tools
- Cross-browser infrastructure

At some point, writing automated tests had turned into building and operating an internal test automation product.

This is where the ROI frequently collapsed.

The framework remained "almost ready" for months or years. The team could run some tests, but not consistently enough to trust them. Flaky failures trained developers to ignore the results. Maintenance work competed with product development. Documentation lagged behind the code.

When the original approach became difficult to extend, the proposed solution was often to rebuild it.

Maybe Selenium was the problem. Maybe the programming language was the problem. Maybe the architecture was the problem. Perhaps Cypress, Playwright, a new page-object pattern, or a new set of AI-generated helpers would finally solve it.

The rewrite created another burst of activity, followed by another framework that was almost ready.

## Low adoption is the clearest warning sign

The best indicator of a failing internal test framework is the number of people who regularly use and contribute to it, not the number of tests in the repository.

When only one or two people understand the framework (and those are usually the people who built it), the company does not have a shared testing system. It has a specialised internal project with concentrated knowledge.

This creates several problems:

1. Test coverage grows only when those specific people have time.
2. Every failure needs to be routed through them.
3. Product managers, business analysts, and manual testers cannot easily review what is covered.
4. Developers see the test repository as another maintenance obligation.
5. The framework becomes vulnerable when its creators change roles or leave.

Developers generally do not want another repository to maintain. They already have the product, infrastructure, deployment pipelines, internal tools, integrations, and production incidents competing for their attention.

An automation framework may be technically impressive and still be a business failure.

If the broader team cannot use it, understand it, or trust its output, the framework is moving the cost of quality into a less visible part of the engineering organisation instead of reducing it.

## Intelligent test automation changed the trade-off

Test automation became much easier when intelligent platforms such as [Endtest](https://endtest.io/product) began handling the framework and infrastructure layer.

These products have been described as no-code testing tools, codeless testing tools, low-code testing tools, and more recently, AI test automation tools. The labels have changed, but the central idea has remained consistent:

**Your team should spend its time defining and validating product behaviour, not rebuilding browser automation infrastructure.**

That shift accelerated and democratised test creation.

A manual tester could create a meaningful regression suite without first learning a programming language, a browser automation library, a design pattern, and a CI configuration format. In the right product, a focused tester could build a substantial set of tests in a day.

When a question came up, the team could ask the vendor's support team through chat or email instead of spending hours searching old Stack Overflow threads and debugging differences between package versions.

That support is easy to underestimate when comparing a paid platform with a free open-source library.

The library may be free, but every hour spent diagnosing browser drivers, CI containers, authentication state, flaky waits, or reporting infrastructure is paid for with someone's salary and attention.

An easier tool removes entire categories of work.

## Human-readable tests change who can participate

One of the most important improvements had nothing to do with AI, self-healing, or cloud execution. It was storing tests in a human-readable format instead of hiding their intent inside application code.

A test should make it obvious that the user:

1. Opens the registration page.
2. Creates an account.
3. Confirms the verification email.
4. Selects a subscription.
5. Completes the payment.
6. Reaches the dashboard.

A developer can understand that. So can a manual tester, product manager, business analyst, support specialist, or founder.

When tests are readable, more people can answer important questions:

- Are we testing the correct behaviour?
- Is this scenario still relevant?
- Which business rule is being validated?
- What changed after the latest release?
- Can this flow be reused elsewhere?
- Is a failure caused by the product or the test?

Readable tests create shared ownership.

They also make test coverage easier to review. A code repository may contain tens of thousands of lines while still leaving the team unsure about which customer journeys are protected. A structured test suite makes the relationship between business behaviour and automation much clearer.

This is one reason [no-code testing](https://endtest.io/product/capabilities/no-code-testing) helps more than non-programmers. It can improve communication across the entire product team.

## Cross-browser testing should not be a future project

Internal frameworks also tend to treat cross-browser coverage as a "nice to have."

The Chrome tests come first. Firefox is planned for later. Edge appears on the roadmap. Safari requires different infrastructure and becomes something the team will address when there is more time.

There is rarely more time.

A complete cross-browser setup requires more than changing a browser name in a configuration file. Teams need access to the operating systems, browser versions, parallel capacity, debugging artifacts, and reliable execution environments.

Safari is the clearest example. Testing real Safari means running on macOS rather than a WebKit-based browser inside a Linux container.

Intelligent platforms make this infrastructure part of the product. The same test can run across Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and [real Safari in a managed cross-browser cloud](https://endtest.io/product/validate/cross-browser-testing) without turning browser coverage into another internal engineering project.

That matters because "easy test automation" should include executing the tests where your users actually are.

Creating a test quickly but running it only in one convenient browser is not the same as having useful coverage.

## AI made the first five minutes misleading

Over the last two years, AI has made coding dramatically faster.

You can now describe a login flow to an AI coding agent and receive a Playwright or Selenium test almost immediately. The generated code may include selectors, assertions, fixtures, helper functions, and comments.

That is useful.

But it mainly improves the cheapest phase of the test's lifecycle: initial creation.

Things often become more difficult from there.

The application changes. A locator stops working. Authentication is redesigned. Test data becomes inconsistent. A helper function affects thirty files. The generated architecture no longer matches how the product evolved.

Now the team asks the AI to fix the tests.

That means providing the coding agent with more files, more context, more execution logs, and more instructions. Each small change becomes another AI session. Tokens go into modifying the test and into repeatedly rediscovering how the generated framework works.

Model usage is only part of the cost.

Someone still has to:

- Explain the problem
- Select the correct context
- Review the generated changes
- Run the suite
- Investigate new failures
- Confirm that the AI did not weaken an assertion
- Check that unrelated tests were not changed

AI can write code quickly, but it does not automatically create organisational understanding.

Our article on [AI-generated Playwright tests](https://endtest.io/blog/ai-playwright-testing-useful-shortcut-or-maintenance-trap) explores this maintenance trap in more detail.

## AI-generated test code can become a black box

A code-based test suite maintained primarily through AI can create an unusual situation: the repository contains a huge amount of executable detail, but very little shared understanding.

No one deliberately designed every part of it. No one has time to read all of it. The team sees passing or failing tests, but cannot always explain exactly what each test validates or why the framework behaves as it does.

That is effectively a black box.

This matters because a test that passes for the wrong reason is more dangerous than a test that fails loudly.

An AI agent may replace a precise assertion with a broader one to make the test pass. It may introduce a fallback that hides a product defect. It may duplicate helpers, misunderstand state, or change behaviour outside the requested scope.

The larger the generated codebase becomes, the more context the AI needs to process. More context can mean more irrelevant information, more stale assumptions, higher token usage, and more opportunities for hallucinated changes.

You can reduce some of this risk through careful prompting, smaller context windows, and disciplined review. We cover those tactics in [our guide to reducing AI hallucinations in test automation](https://endtest.io/blog/ai-hallucinations-in-test-automation) and our article on [reducing AI token usage](https://endtest.io/blog/how-to-reduce-ai-token-usage-in-test-automation).

But the deeper question remains:

Why should AI repeatedly read and rewrite thousands of lines of framework code when the test could be represented as a concise sequence of human-readable actions?

## The better model: AI creates, humans can inspect

"AI writes all the test code" is not the ideal scenario. The ideal is:

**AI accelerates test creation while the resulting test remains understandable and editable by humans.**

This is the model used by intelligent test automation platforms such as Endtest.

You can describe a scenario in plain English. The [AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) inspects the application and creates the test. But the result does not disappear into an opaque code repository.

The generated test is stored as regular, visible steps.

You can inspect the actions, locators, values, waits, and assertions. You can modify them directly. You can reuse existing test cases, parameterise values, add new checks, or hand the test to another member of the team.

AI handles the acceleration. The structured test remains the source of truth.

This changes the maintenance model.

When the product changes, the team does not need to ask a general-purpose coding agent to rediscover an entire custom framework. A person can open the test, understand the affected flow, and make a targeted change. AI can assist without owning the only understandable representation of the system.

There is no conflict between AI and human-readable testing. They work better together.

## What is actually the easiest approach in 2026?

There are now three common approaches:

| Approach | Initial creation | Long-term maintenance | Team accessibility | Infrastructure burden |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manual regression | Easy at small scale | Becomes expensive as coverage grows | High | Low |
| AI-generated Playwright or Selenium framework | Very fast first demo | Can become code-heavy and opaque | Usually limited to technical users | High |
| Intelligent test automation platform | Fast | Structured, visible, vendor-supported | Broad | Low |

The correct choice still depends on the company.

A highly specialised engineering organisation may have strong reasons to own every line of its automation infrastructure. A small product with very little regression risk may continue with manual testing for a while.

But most growing software companies do not gain a competitive advantage from building a custom test framework.

Their advantage comes from shipping a reliable product, learning from customers, and moving quickly without repeatedly breaking important workflows.

For those teams, the easiest path is usually:

1. Identify the user journeys whose failure would cost the business the most.
2. Automate those journeys first.
3. Store the tests in a format the wider team can understand.
4. Use AI to accelerate creation and maintenance, not to hide complexity.
5. Run the same tests across the browsers and environments that matter.
6. Measure whether the suite reduces regression time and escaped defects.
7. Expand coverage only when the economics justify it.

This approach avoids both extremes: automating everything too early and building an internal framework that never becomes dependable.

## Start with the business risk, not the tool

The best first automated test is the workflow where a failure would hurt the business, not necessarily the easiest screen to automate.

That might be:

- Account creation
- Login
- Checkout
- Subscription upgrades
- Password reset
- Email verification
- A critical dashboard
- A customer-facing report
- A core integration
- A recurring production monitor

Start with one of those.

Build a small group of tests that protect real customer value. Run them consistently. Make sure the team pays attention when they fail. Then expand based on observed risk rather than an abstract target such as "80% automated coverage."

The easiest test suite to maintain is usually the one where every test has a clear reason to exist, and it is rarely the largest one.

## The real measure of ease

An impressive demo does not make a tool easy.

It is easy when:

- A new team member can understand the tests.
- A manual tester can contribute without waiting for an automation engineer.
- A product manager can review what behaviour is covered.
- A failed test provides enough information to act.
- Browser infrastructure does not become an internal project.
- Small product changes do not require large AI coding sessions.
- The suite is still trusted after hundreds of releases.
- The cost remains lower than the defects and manual work it prevents.

That is the standard teams should use in 2026.

AI-generated Playwright and Selenium code can be useful. Open-source frameworks can be the right choice for teams that want to own and maintain them. Manual testing can remain rational while a product is small.

But for a growing business that wants reliable end-to-end coverage without creating another software product inside the company, an intelligent platform such as Endtest is typically the fastest, easiest, and most affordable way to create and maintain automated tests.

You can [start a free trial](https://endtest.io/pricing) and create your first human-readable test without setting up a framework, installing browser drivers, or generating thousands of lines of code.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the easiest way to automate website tests?

For most teams, the easiest approach is to use an intelligent test automation platform that can create tests from plain-English instructions and store the result as editable, human-readable steps. This removes much of the framework, infrastructure, and maintenance work associated with Selenium or Playwright.

### When should a small company start test automation?

A small company should consider test automation when manual regression begins delaying releases, recurring defects consume engineering time, or failures in important customer journeys become materially expensive. Start with a few high-risk end-to-end flows rather than trying to automate everything.

### Is AI-generated Playwright testing easy to maintain?

AI can generate Playwright tests quickly, but maintenance may become difficult as the codebase grows. The AI needs increasing amounts of context, engineers must review the generated changes, and the wider team may struggle to understand the test coverage.

### Are no-code tests a black box?

They do not have to be. In a transparent platform, each action, locator, value, and assertion is visible and editable. AI may help generate or maintain the test, but the team can still inspect exactly what the test does.

# AI Hallucinations in Test Automation: 8 Fixes

Reduce AI hallucinations in test automation with specialized models, smaller context, clearer prompts, validation checks, and safer self-healing.

Published July 21, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/ai-hallucinations-in-test-automation

---
AI hallucinations are usually discussed as a chatbot problem.

You ask a question, the model invents a fact, and someone notices that the answer sounds confident but wrong.

In test automation, the failure mode is more dangerous.

The AI can create a test that looks reasonable, runs successfully, and still verifies the wrong thing. It can click the wrong button, extract a locator for a nearby element, accept an invalid visual state, or quietly replace a broken selector with one that points somewhere else.

The result is often not a red build but a green one that gives the team false confidence.

That is why reducing AI hallucinations in test automation is a system-design problem more than a prompt-writing exercise. The model, the context, the output format, the validation layer, and the review process all matter.

Here are the practical ways to make AI-assisted testing more reliable.

## What AI hallucinations look like in test automation

A hallucination does not always mean the AI invents an entire feature that does not exist. More often, it makes one plausible but incorrect decision inside a larger workflow.

| AI task | Example hallucination | Why it is risky |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Creating tests from specifications | The model invents a confirmation message or skips a required precondition | The generated test no longer represents the actual requirement |
| Extracting element locators | The model selects a similar button, label, or hidden element | The test may interact with the wrong part of the page |
| Performing AI assertions | The model decides that a page is correct based on incomplete visual or textual evidence | A real defect can be classified as a pass |
| Generating random values | The model creates data with the wrong format, length, locale, or business rules | The test fails for irrelevant reasons or exercises an unrealistic path |
| Finding alternative locators | A self-healing system replaces a broken locator with a nearby but incorrect element | The test continues passing while testing a different behavior |

These mistakes become more likely when the model receives vague instructions, excessive context, no permission to express uncertainty, and no deterministic checks around its output.

## 1. Give clear and granular instructions

Do not assume the AI will infer the test intent from a short feature description.

A human tester may understand that "test the checkout flow" means using an existing customer, selecting a specific shipping method, applying a valid coupon, confirming the tax calculation, and verifying the order in the account history.

An AI model sees many possible checkout flows. Unless you define the important details, it has to fill the gaps.

This instruction is too broad:

```text
Create a test for checkout.
```

A better instruction defines the preconditions, actions, boundaries, and expected outcome:

```text
Create a test for a signed-in customer purchasing one in-stock product.

Preconditions:
- The customer has a saved delivery address.
- The product price is $49.00.
- The coupon SAVE10 is valid and provides a 10% discount.

Actions:
- Add the product to the cart.
- Apply the coupon.
- Select standard shipping.
- Complete the purchase with the test card.

Assertions:
- The subtotal is $49.00.
- The discount is $4.90.
- The order confirmation page displays an order number.
- The same order appears in the customer's order history.

Do not add steps that are not supported by these instructions.
```

Nobody wants to write a novel for every test. The point is to remove the places where the model would otherwise have to guess.

Smaller tasks also help. Asking AI to identify one locator, generate one assertion, or convert one requirement at a time is usually more reliable than asking it to design an entire regression suite in a single response.

## 2. Use a model specialized for test automation

A more expensive model is not automatically the best model for every testing task.

General-purpose foundation models are built to handle a huge range of requests: writing, research, programming, summarization, brainstorming, and many other activities. That breadth is useful, but it does not make them specialists in test intent, locator quality, browser behavior, assertion design, or self-healing decisions.

Test automation has its own rules.

A useful model needs to understand that a locator should be stable and unique, that a hidden element should not be preferred over an interactable one, that an assertion must verify business intent rather than merely confirm that some text exists, and that changing a locator can silently change what a test is testing.

At Endtest, we do not simply route every AI task through a generic model and hope that a larger prompt will solve the problem. We use models specialized for test automation. In our experience, that is one of the main reasons the hallucination rate is extremely low.

Specialization matters more than price.

Specialized models are also not always available as a simple option inside general AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude. A team building an internal framework may have access to excellent general-purpose models while still lacking a model trained or optimized for the narrow decisions required by reliable test automation.

This is also why "Which AI model is smartest?" is the wrong question. A better one is "Which model is most reliable for this exact testing operation?" We discussed that distinction in more detail in our article about the [best AI model for test automation](https://endtest.io/blog/best-ai-model-for-test-automation).

## 3. Send less data, not more

When an AI model makes a mistake, the instinct is often to give it more context.

Sometimes that helps. Often it creates more opportunities for confusion.

A full page source can contain thousands of elements, hidden templates, duplicate mobile and desktop navigation, old modal content, analytics markup, SVG paths, dynamic IDs, and components that are not relevant to the current test step.

If the task is to find the locator for the visible **Submit Order** button, the model probably does not need the entire HTML document.

It may only need:

- The relevant form or component.
- A small amount of parent context.
- Nearby labels and attributes.
- Information about visibility and interactability.
- A screenshot or accessibility representation when useful.

This reduces both token consumption and ambiguity.

The same principle applies to test generation. Do not send a 70-page specification when only two paragraphs describe the workflow being automated. Retrieve the relevant section, remove unrelated material, and send the smallest context that still contains the required evidence.

## 4. Ask the AI to reason through a defined process

"Think step by step" can help, but it is more useful when the steps are specific to the task.

For locator generation, the model can be instructed to follow a process such as:

```text
1. Identify the intended element from the instruction.
2. List the visible candidate elements that could match.
3. Reject candidates that are hidden, disabled, duplicated, or semantically different.
4. Prefer stable attributes over generated classes or dynamic IDs.
5. Verify that the proposed locator matches exactly one interactable element.
6. Return the locator and a short explanation of the supporting evidence.
```

For an AI assertion, the process may be:

```text
1. Restate the expected condition.
2. Identify the evidence required to prove that condition.
3. Check whether that evidence is present in the supplied data.
4. Distinguish between a pass, a failure, and insufficient evidence.
5. Do not infer missing information.
```

This reduces internal logic gaps and makes the output easier to inspect.

The explanation should be concise. You do not need pages of reasoning. You need enough structure to verify that the model evaluated the right evidence and did not jump from "this looks similar" to "the test passed."

## 5. Give the model permission to be uncertain

Many AI workflows accidentally reward guessing.

The system expects a locator, a pass/fail answer, or a generated value. The model therefore produces one, even when the evidence is weak.

Explicitly give it another valid response:

```text
If you are not completely certain about something, say you don't know rather than guessing.
```

For production systems, make uncertainty part of the output schema:

```json
{
  "status": "uncertain",
  "confidence": 0.54,
  "reason": "Two visible buttons match the supplied instruction.",
  "result": null
}
```

The surrounding automation must respect that answer.

If the model reports insufficient evidence, the system should request more context, use a deterministic fallback, or send the decision for review. It should not quietly convert "uncertain" into "good enough."

This matters especially for self-healing. A system that always returns an alternative locator is not necessarily intelligent. It may simply be incapable of admitting that it cannot identify the original element safely.

## 6. Separate generation from validation

Do not ask the same AI response to generate an answer and certify that the answer is correct.

Add a validation layer after generation.

Some checks can be deterministic:

- Does the locator match exactly one visible element?
- Is the element interactable?
- Does the generated step type exist in the automation platform?
- Does a generated email address match the required format?
- Is a random date inside the allowed range?
- Does the expected value appear in the specification?
- Did a self-healed locator preserve the element's role, label, and surrounding context?

Other checks can use a second model pass with a narrower instruction. The validator should receive the proposed output and ask whether it is fully supported by the available evidence.

The principle is the same one used in reliable software systems: do not trust input merely because it came from a sophisticated component.

The AI proposes, and the validation layer decides whether the proposal is safe to use.

## 7. Constrain the output

Free-form text gives the model many ways to be creative. Test automation usually benefits from the opposite.

Use structured outputs with:

- A fixed list of allowed step types.
- Required fields for each action.
- Explicit assertion operators.
- Defined locator strategies.
- Valid data types and ranges.
- Rejection of unknown properties.
- Confidence and uncertainty fields.

For example, a test creation model should not be able to invent a new step called `VerifyEverythingLooksGood`. It should select from known actions such as click, write text, send an API request, switch to an iframe, or assert an exact value.

This is one reason editable, structured test steps are safer than receiving a large block of generated code. The system can validate each step independently, and a human can see what the test is supposed to do.

Endtest's [AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) creates tests as structured, editable actions rather than leaving the team with an opaque conversation and a pile of generated automation code.

## 8. Never let AI change test intent silently

AI can help repair a locator. It should not silently redefine the test.

A self-healing system should preserve evidence about:

- The original locator.
- The replacement locator.
- The old and new elements.
- The attributes and context used for matching.
- The confidence score.
- The screenshot or page state at the time of healing.
- Whether the change was applied automatically or requires approval.

High-confidence repairs can be useful for predictable changes, such as a generated ID being replaced while the element's label, role, and position remain consistent.

Low-confidence repairs should stop.

Consider a checkout page with two buttons: **Continue Shopping** and **Continue to Payment**. A self-healing system that selects the first visible element containing "Continue" has technically fixed the broken locator. It has also changed the test.

The requirement is to preserve the original test intent, and "something similar" does not meet it.

For more detail, see our guide to [self-healing test automation](https://endtest.io/blog/self-healing-test-automation-what-it-is-and-how-it-works).

## The Playwright + Claude maintenance trap

There is nothing wrong with using Playwright or Selenium. Both can be useful foundations for browser automation.

The problem starts when a team assumes that adding Claude or another general-purpose AI model will turn an internal framework into an autonomous testing platform.

The first demo can look impressive. The AI reads a requirement, writes a Playwright test, fixes a selector, and explains a failure. It feels like the maintenance problem has disappeared.

Then the suite grows.

The model needs more repository context. It needs page objects, fixtures, helper methods, test data, environment rules, previous failures, application HTML, screenshots, and parts of the product specification. Token consumption increases, prompts become infrastructure, and every generated change still requires review.

Three problems appear quickly.

### Token consumption becomes an operating cost

Large codebases and page sources must be repeatedly selected, sent, and interpreted. Even when model prices decrease, someone still has to build and maintain the context pipeline, control retries, store traces, and investigate inconsistent output.

### Nobody is completely sure what the tests are testing

Generated code can be syntactically valid while representing the wrong business intent. When the AI changes selectors, assertions, waits, or helper methods, reviewers must determine whether it repaired the implementation or changed the meaning of the test.

That uncertainty compounds over time.

### A general model is being asked to make specialist decisions

Claude and other foundation models are capable programming assistants. But test maintenance is more than code generation. It requires narrow judgment about intent, evidence, element identity, browser behavior, and the acceptable boundary of a repair.

A Playwright + Claude or Selenium + Claude setup can therefore become expensive and unreliable: high token usage, heavy review requirements, uncertain coverage, and more hallucinations than teams expect from the initial prototype.

These models are not bad. The problem is using a broad model as though it were a specialized test automation system.

We covered the broader maintenance tradeoff in [AI Playwright Testing: Useful Shortcut or Maintenance Trap?](https://endtest.io/blog/ai-playwright-testing-useful-shortcut-or-maintenance-trap).

## How we reduce hallucinations at Endtest

Our approach is to keep AI powerful but bounded.

That means using specialized models for test automation, giving each model a narrow task, trimming the supplied context, validating structured outputs, allowing uncertainty, and keeping the resulting tests readable and editable.

The AI should accelerate test creation and maintenance without becoming an invisible layer that continuously rewrites the suite.

A useful rule is this:

> The more important the decision, the less freedom the model should have to improvise.

Generating a realistic first name can tolerate more variation than changing the locator for a **Delete Account** button. A visual suggestion can tolerate more uncertainty than declaring a payment flow correct. The system should treat those operations differently.

## A practical hallucination-reduction checklist

Before letting an AI-generated decision affect a test, ask:

- Is the instruction specific enough to define the expected behavior?
- Is the model specialized for this testing task?
- Did we send only the relevant context?
- Is the model following a defined evaluation process?
- Can it return "uncertain" or "insufficient evidence"?
- Is the output constrained by a schema?
- Can deterministic checks validate the result?
- Will a human be able to understand what changed?
- Can a self-healing action be reversed and audited?
- Did the AI preserve the original test intent?

If several answers are no, the system is not reducing maintenance so much as moving it somewhere less visible.

## Frequently asked questions

### What causes AI hallucinations in test automation?

The most common causes are vague instructions, missing requirements, excessive or irrelevant context, general-purpose models being used for specialized tasks, unconstrained output, and systems that force the model to return an answer even when evidence is insufficient.

### Can AI-generated tests be trusted?

They can be useful and reliable when the output is structured, reviewable, validated, and tied to clear requirements. AI-generated tests should not be trusted merely because they compile or pass once.

### Do larger and more expensive models hallucinate less?

Not necessarily for every task. Model quality matters, but specialization, context selection, prompting, output constraints, and validation often matter more than simply selecting the most expensive general-purpose model.

### Is Playwright with Claude enough for AI test automation?

It can be useful for experiments and developer assistance. It is not automatically a complete maintenance system. Teams still need context management, validation, browser infrastructure, reporting, review workflows, and safeguards that prevent generated changes from altering test intent.

## The goal is not blind trust

AI can make test automation dramatically faster. It can turn instructions into tests, identify elements, create realistic data, evaluate complex conditions, and reduce repetitive maintenance.

But reliability comes from boundaries: clear instructions, a specialized model, a small context, a defined reasoning process, permission to be uncertain, a schema on the output, deterministic validation, and an audit trail for every self-healing change. If a decision matters, the model should have less room to improvise, and someone on the team should be able to see exactly what it changed.

# AI Test Automation: Practical Guide

Learn where AI helps in test automation, where it fails, and how to use Playwright, Selenium, and Endtest without wasting tokens or time.

Published July 7, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/ai-test-automation-practical-guide

---
## AI is useful, but not magical

AI is going to change test automation.

That part is obvious.

AI belongs in test automation. The more important question is where it belongs, where it does not, and how to use it without creating a fragile, expensive mess that nobody on the team wants to touch after six weeks.

That distinction matters because test automation has always had a graveyard problem.

Teams get excited. A new framework gets started. A few impressive demos happen. A login test runs in CI. Someone says, "This is almost ready." Then three months later, one person is still maintaining everything, the rest of the team avoids it, and the tests are either flaky, ignored, or commented out.

AI can make that better.

AI can also make that worse, faster.

The useful approach is to keep judgment with humans and put AI in the parts of testing where it is strong: interpreting messy inputs, converting vague human instructions into structured steps, helping with locators, generating specific test data, and assisting with assertions that are hard to express with simple code.

The dangerous approach is to ask AI to invent your entire testing strategy, generate a large codebase, and maintain it forever while nobody on the team understands what is happening.

That is debt with a nice demo.

## Where AI actually helps in test automation

AI is good at dealing with unstructured data.

That is the main idea.

Traditional automation is strongest when the world is structured. A selector points to an element. A database query returns a value. An API response has a predictable schema. A test step has a clear expected result.

AI is useful when the input is messier than that.

For example, AI can help when a user describes a flow in plain English:

> Create a test that signs up as a new user, verifies the email, creates a project, invites a teammate, and confirms the teammate can access it.

A good AI-assisted testing tool can convert that instruction into a structured automated test that the team can review, edit, and run. That matters because the output is operational rather than plain text.

AI can also help with certain assertions.

A normal assertion might check that a specific string exists on the page. But sometimes you want to validate something more flexible: whether a generated summary is accurate, whether a chatbot response stays within policy, whether a recommendation looks relevant, or whether an error message is understandable.

Those are not always binary checks. They involve meaning. AI is useful there.

AI can also help find or repair locators, especially when the page structure is complicated or when multiple attributes need to be considered together. Humans are good at knowing what they want to click. AI can help translate that intent into a usable locator.

And AI is very useful for generating specific random data.

Libraries like faker.js are excellent when you need a random name, address, company, or email-like value. But they are limited when you need something more specific, such as:

- a realistic Japanese company name in the construction industry
- a support ticket written by an angry but polite customer
- a product description for a vegan protein bar
- a fake invoice line item with unusual tax language
- a list of realistic search queries for a travel website

That kind of data is where AI shines.

| Use AI for | Why it works |
|---|---|
| Turning human instructions into tests | AI is good at interpreting intent and mapping it to structure |
| Generating specific test data | AI can create realistic data beyond simple faker.js templates |
| Helping with flexible assertions | AI can evaluate meaning, tone, relevance, and semantic correctness |
| Suggesting or repairing locators | AI can reason about messy DOMs and human intent |
| Explaining failures | AI can summarize logs, screenshots, and error patterns |

The pattern is simple: use AI when the input is vague, messy, or semantic.

Do not use AI when the problem is already structured and deterministic.

## Where AI should not be used

AI is not a good substitute for testing judgment.

This is where many teams get disappointed.

AI can generate a list of test cases. Some of them will sound reasonable. Some will be generic. Some will be redundant. Some will miss the actual risk in your product.

That is because AI's creativity is limited by the context you give it and the patterns it has seen before. It does not know which bugs cost your company money. It does not know which flows your support team hates. It does not know which customer segment is most important this quarter. It does not know that the finance team panics every time invoices are wrong.

You do.

That is why AI should not be treated as the person responsible for test strategy.

A useful workflow is to let AI help express a test. A risky workflow is to let AI decide what matters.

The best test case ideas usually come from product knowledge, customer pain, production incidents, support tickets, analytics, release risk, and the ugly little details that only your team knows.

AI can help organize that knowledge.

It cannot replace it.

## The new cost of AI: tokens, time, and maintenance

For a while, many AI features felt almost free. That is changing.

More AI providers and AI-powered tools are moving toward token-based pricing or usage-based billing. That means every prompt, every page summary, every code update, and every AI-assisted repair can have a real cost.

But money is only one part of efficiency.

There are three kinds of waste you want to avoid.

| Waste type | What it looks like | Better approach |
|---|---|---|
| Token waste | Sending large files, long test histories, or entire codebases to AI for every small change | Keep tests structured and only use AI where it adds value |
| Execution waste | Using AI to find every element during every run, even when stable locators already exist | Store reliable locators and use AI only for creation, repair, or semantic checks |
| Engineering waste | Building an internal AI testing framework from scratch and maintaining it forever | Use a mature platform where AI is part of a larger testing system |

The second point is especially important.

If a test already has reliable locators, there is usually no reason to call AI every time the test clicks a button. That makes the test slower, more expensive, and harder to reason about.

AI should not be in the hot path unless it needs to be.

A stable test should mostly run like a normal deterministic automated test. AI should help create it, improve it, repair it, or validate things that cannot be checked with a simple assertion.

That is how you get the benefit without turning every test run into a token-burning exercise.

## Selenium and Playwright are tools, not an AI strategy

Selenium and Playwright are excellent tools.

But when teams ask, "Should we use AI with Selenium or Playwright?", the answer is often: neither, at least not in the way they are imagining.

Selenium and Playwright are fine. The problem is that the output is code.

When AI creates Selenium or Playwright tests, it creates code. Then the code changes. Then more code gets added. Then helpers appear. Then fixtures appear. Then custom retry logic appears. Then page objects drift from the real product. Then CI fails. Then someone asks AI to fix it.

At first, this feels productive.

But after a few weeks, the AI needs more and more context to make safe changes. It may need to understand the test file, the helper functions, the page objects, the fixtures, the environment setup, the CI configuration, and the previous failures.

That context costs tokens.

It also costs understanding.

The strange thing is that code can become a black box in this situation. Not because code is inherently unreadable, but because nobody fully knows what the AI changed, why it changed it, and what other flows were affected.

Some teams describe this as a death spiral with AI-generated Playwright tests.

A test fails. They ask Claude or another AI coding tool to fix it. The AI makes a plausible change. Another flow breaks. They prompt again. The AI adds a workaround. The helper becomes more complicated. The test suite becomes harder to understand. The team still does not have enough context to explain the real failure, so the next prompt is also incomplete.

That is painful in any codebase.

It is especially painful when tests are holding up a release.

## Responsibility does not disappear because AI wrote it

Someone has to be responsible for the tests.

That does not change because Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or another AI tool generated part of them.

Developers are still responsible for code generated by AI. They need to understand it, review it, and own the consequences when it breaks. QA teams need the same mindset for AI-powered tests.

You cannot really blame a bad release on a prompt.

You cannot say, "The AI wrote the test, so nobody knows what it checks."

That is a risk.

Every important automated test should have a clear owner or at least a clear owning team. People should know what it checks, why it exists, what risk it protects, and how to debug it when it fails.

That is one reason human-readable tests matter.

When tests are expressed in a format that product managers, QA engineers, developers, and support people can understand, the whole team can participate. When the test is buried in an AI-generated codebase that only one person touches, you are back to the old test automation trap.

## A framework is more than generated code

Another common mistake is underestimating what a real end-to-end testing system requires.

You can ask Claude to generate a Playwright test.

That does not mean you now have a mature test automation framework.

A serious end-to-end testing setup needs reliable execution infrastructure. Ideally, that includes real browsers on Windows and macOS machines, not only Linux containers running headless browsers.

It needs parallel execution.

It needs video recordings, screenshots, logs, and historical results.

It needs ways to test email flows with real email infrastructure, not only by reading values directly from the database.

It needs SMS testing with real phone number providers when the product uses phone verification.

It needs API requests, database checks, file downloads, secrets management, environment configuration, user permissions, reporting, and alerting.

It needs role-based access control if a large team is using it.

It needs audit trails if an enterprise customer asks who changed a test before a failed release.

It needs support when something breaks at the worst possible time.

AI can help generate code for one layer of that system. But the code is only a small part of what makes test automation work in a real company.

This is why so many internal frameworks get stuck in the "almost ready" phase.

The first passing test is the easy part.

The hard part is making the system boring, repeatable, understandable, and used by the whole team.

## The most efficient approach: AI inside a real testing platform

The most efficient way to use AI in test automation is to use an intelligent test automation platform where AI is part of a broader system, instead of building everything from scratch.

A mature platform should already have the pieces you need for serious end-to-end testing: a cross-browser cloud, reliable execution infrastructure, email testing, SMS testing, API requests, database validation, reporting, permissions, logs, screenshots, videos, and support.

AI then becomes an accelerant.

It helps create tests from human-readable instructions, suggest locators, write specific assertions, generate realistic data, and explain failures.

But the output should still be a test that people can read, edit, debug, and own.

That is one reason Endtest fits naturally into this category. It gives teams a way to build and run end-to-end tests without turning every test into a custom code project. The AI capabilities are useful, but they sit inside a platform that already handles the infrastructure and workflow pieces that most teams underestimate.

That also makes the economics better.

You are not burning tokens every time a test runs. You are not asking AI to re-understand an entire codebase for a small change. You are not relying on one internal framework maintainer to keep a fragile project alive.

This is the kind of workflow the [Endtest AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) is built around: describe the scenario in plain English, generate a working test, and keep the result editable and reviewable by the team.

For enterprise teams, the difference is even larger.

They need role-based access to tests, reporting, activity logs, security expectations such as ISO 27001-style controls, uptime commitments, and technical support. They also need confidence that the test automation project will not become a hobby project that gets thrown away after a few months.

Endtest's long list of enterprise customers and strong independent reviews are useful signals here. They show that teams can actually use the system in production-like workflows, which matters more than the AI feature list.

## How to know if your AI testing approach is working

The simplest signal is adoption.

If your AI testing approach is working, the team uses the tests.

The whole team, not only the automation person or the person who wrote the framework.

Developers look at failures. QA people update flows. Product people can understand what is covered. Managers trust the reports. New team members can make small changes without needing a two-week onboarding session into a custom framework.

That is the healthy version.

The unhealthy version is easy to recognize:

- one person owns everything
- the tests are always "almost ready"
- nobody else wants to edit them
- failures require a long debugging session
- AI keeps making changes that nobody fully understands
- the test suite is impressive in a demo but ignored during releases

That is a warning sign.

It means the AI moved the complexity somewhere harder to see instead of removing it.

## A practical rule for using AI in test automation

Use AI when it makes the test easier to create, easier to understand, or better at checking meaning.

Do not use AI when it makes the test slower, more expensive, or harder to own.

That rule sounds simple, but it catches most mistakes.

AI should help a team move faster without losing responsibility: turn human intent into structured tests, handle unstructured data, reduce maintenance, and make debugging clearer.

It should not become the invisible person responsible for quality.

The teams that win will be the ones that build the most useful feedback loops: tests that run reliably, explain failures clearly, protect important user flows, and are understood by the people shipping the product. The amount of generated test code has nothing to do with it.
