# How to Stabilize Automated Tests

Stabilize flaky automated tests with better waits, reliable locators, isolated data, useful logs, and dependable cross-browser infrastructure.

Published July 2, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/how-to-stabilize-automated-tests

---
Flaky automated tests are expensive in a way that rarely appears in a budget.

A test fails, so someone runs it again. It passes the second time, so the failure is ignored. After this happens often enough, a red test result no longer means that the release should stop. It means that someone should click **Retry**.

At that point, you do not really have an automated test suite. You have a notification system that may or may not be telling the truth.

Teams often blame the framework. Selenium is flaky. Playwright is flaky. Cypress is flaky. The testing platform is flaky.

Framework and browser bugs do happen. But in my experience, most flaky tests are caused by something less dramatic: waits that are not synchronized with the application, locators that are too fragile, test data that depends on a previous run, an overloaded environment, or settings that were never configured for the real behavior of the application.

Changing tools without fixing those problems usually moves the same instability into a new syntax.

## Define what a stable test actually is

A test that passes is not necessarily a stable test.

If the product is broken, a good test should fail. Stability means that the test reaches the same conclusion when the relevant conditions are the same.

My practical definition is simple: if you run a test 5,000 times under the same conditions, the result should be the same 5,000 times.

When the feature works, it should pass consistently. When the feature is broken, it should fail consistently and at the correct step.

Even a 99.9% consistency rate produces roughly five questionable results across 5,000 executions. That might sound acceptable until those failures appear in the middle of release pipelines, wake people up during monitoring runs, or cause the team to stop trusting the entire suite.

The goal is to make every result believable rather than to make the dashboard green.

## Optimize waits instead of adding delays

Poor synchronization is probably the most common cause of flaky browser tests.

Modern applications rarely load in one clean event. The page may appear before a request finishes. A button may be visible before it is enabled. A dropdown may exist in the DOM while an animation still prevents a click. A React component may render, disappear, and render again.

The tempting fix is to add a five-second pause.

That can make the test pass, but it does not make the test stable. It only assumes that the application will always finish within five seconds. It also makes every fast execution wait longer than necessary.

A better test waits for the condition it actually needs:

- The element is visible and enabled.
- The loading indicator has disappeared.
- The expected URL or text is present.
- A network request has completed.
- The number of results has changed.
- The animation or background job has finished.

Hardcoded pauses still have a place when you intentionally need to test a duration, such as a session timeout. They should not be the default solution for ordinary synchronization.

This is also why increasing every timeout globally is usually the wrong first move. It can hide the real issue while making the entire suite slower. As discussed in [our guide to speeding up test executions](https://endtest.io/blog/5-ways-to-speed-up-test-executions), the best waits continuously check for the required condition and continue as soon as it is met.

## Use locators that describe intent

A locator can be technically correct and still be unreliable.

Long XPath expressions, `nth-child` selectors, generated CSS classes, and exact matches against frequently edited text can all work today and fail after a harmless UI change tomorrow.

Whenever possible, prefer locators based on stable application intent:

- Unique IDs created for testing
- `data-testid` or similar dedicated attributes
- Stable names and labels
- Accessible roles combined with reliable accessible names
- Small, deliberate relationships between nearby elements

The best locator is the one that the development and testing teams can look at six months later and immediately understand, which is rarely the cleverest one.

Self-healing can reduce maintenance when an element changes, but it should not be used to excuse ambiguous selectors. If three buttons look almost identical to the automation, the underlying test is still unclear. AI cannot reliably infer intent that was never expressed.

Reliable locators should also be unique. A selector that sometimes matches one element and sometimes matches three is not stable, even if the framework happens to click the correct one during your local run.

## Make every test own its state

Many flaky tests are not actually flaky in isolation. They are dependent on invisible state left behind by another test.

A sign-up test assumes the email address has never been used. A checkout test assumes the cart is empty. A project-creation test assumes no project already has that name. The first run passes, and the second run fails.

The most reliable testing flows create the users, accounts, projects, orders, and other data they need. They use unique values, verify that setup succeeded, and clean up afterward when cleanup is practical.

This makes the flow independent from previous executions and from the order in which tests run.

Sometimes reusing existing data is unavoidable. In that case, the flow should be designed for the states it may encounter. It might need to detect that a user is already verified, empty an existing cart, remove an old project, or restore the application to a known starting point.

The key is determinism. The test should not be surprised by a state that the team already knows can exist.

This principle matters even more when tests run in parallel. Two tests should not modify the same user, order, inbox, or shared record unless the collision is part of the scenario being tested.

## A stable test needs a stable environment

You cannot build stable automation on top of an environment that changes behavior from minute to minute.

A staging server with insufficient CPU may respond quickly during the day and time out when the full suite runs. Shared databases can accumulate bad data. Background workers can fall behind. Email and SMS providers can throttle requests. Rate limits can turn parallel execution into random failures.

Before changing the test, check whether the environment is giving the test a consistent application to evaluate.

The same applies to browser infrastructure. Browser and driver versions should be compatible. Operating systems, fonts, permissions, viewport sizes, locale, and time zone should be controlled. Parallel workers need enough CPU and memory. Test sessions should be isolated from one another.

Running on your laptop can hide these problems because your local environment is familiar and lightly loaded. CI and cross-browser execution expose the assumptions.

This is one reason we invested heavily in Endtest's [cross-browser testing infrastructure](https://endtest.io/product/validate/cross-browser-testing). A managed platform does not eliminate the need for good test design, but dependable browser machines, real operating systems, and consistent session configuration remove a major source of unnecessary variance.

## Collect enough evidence to explain every failure

A screenshot is useful, but it is rarely enough.

To diagnose stability problems, collect the evidence that explains what happened before and during the failure:

- The failing step and its duration
- Screenshots and video
- Browser console messages
- Network requests and response codes
- Browser, driver, operating system, and viewport details
- Test data identifiers
- Retry history
- Relevant application and server logs

The most important evidence is often the difference between a passing run and a failing run.

Did the failing run receive a slower API response? Did the locator match a different element? Did the browser console report a JavaScript exception? Did a previous test leave the user in a different state?

A test that passes on retry should still be investigated. The retry is proof that the original result was not deterministic. Retries are a useful safety net for infrastructure incidents, but they are not a stabilization strategy.

Endtest's [test insights and analytics](https://endtest.io/product/analyze/test-insights) are designed around this idea: a failure should include enough context to classify it instead of forcing someone to reproduce it blindly.

## Use a repeatable stabilization loop

When a test is unreliable, avoid making several speculative changes at once. Use a small loop:

1. Reproduce the failure with the same browser, data, environment, and configuration.
2. Classify it as synchronization, locator, data, environment, infrastructure, configuration, or a real product defect.
3. Fix the root cause rather than increasing delays or retries.
4. Run the test repeatedly and under parallel load.
5. Track whether the same failure pattern returns.

Temporary quarantine can be reasonable when one test is blocking the entire pipeline, but quarantine needs an owner and an expiration date. Otherwise, the flaky-test folder becomes the place where useful coverage goes to disappear.

The same is true for broad exception handling. A test that catches every error and continues may look stable, but it is only hiding failures.

## Stability is a property of the whole system

Stable automation comes from the combination of clear test logic, condition-based waits, reliable locators, controlled data, dependable environments, consistent browser infrastructure, and useful diagnostics, rather than from one framework feature.

At Endtest, we have seen teams replace one framework with another and carry the same flaky tests with them. The syntax changed, but the waits, selectors, shared data, and environment assumptions did not.

AI, self-healing, and managed infrastructure can remove a great deal of repetitive maintenance. They work best when the underlying flow is deterministic and the expected behavior is clear.

A good automated test should be boring. It should run thousands of times, reach the same conclusion, and give the team a signal they can act on without first asking whether the test itself is telling the truth.

---

# Speed Up Test Executions: 5 Practical Ways

Speed up Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, and Endtest runs by fixing waits, reducing artifacts, sizing staging correctly, and running tests in parallel.

Published June 23, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/5-ways-to-speed-up-test-executions

---
A slow automated test suite rarely becomes slow because of one dramatic technical mistake.

It usually happens one harmless-looking decision at a time.

Someone adds a five-second pause because a dropdown occasionally loads late. Then another person enables screenshots after every step. The staging environment gets moved to a smaller container to save money. Test cases start depending on whatever state the previous test left behind. Eventually, the suite takes 90 minutes, nobody wants to run it before a pull request, and the CI pipeline becomes something the team works around instead of something it trusts.

I have seen versions of this pattern across Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, custom testing frameworks, and intelligent test automation platforms. The syntax changes, but the bottlenecks are remarkably consistent.

The good news is that you usually do not need to rewrite the entire test suite. You need to identify where time is being spent, remove unnecessary work, and make the tests easier to distribute.

Here are the five changes that usually produce the largest improvement.

## First, measure where the time is going

Before changing the framework, browser, or cloud provider, split the total execution time into a few basic categories:

1. Time spent waiting in a queue for a browser
2. Time spent starting the browser session
3. Time spent preparing test data or authenticating
4. Time spent performing browser actions
5. Time spent waiting for application conditions
6. Time spent capturing and uploading artifacts
7. Time spent cleaning up after the test

This matters because teams often optimize the wrong layer.

A test that spends 40 seconds waiting for a report to appear will not become meaningfully faster because you replaced Selenium with Playwright. A suite that waits two minutes for every browser worker to start will not be fixed by changing a locator. A staging environment that takes eight seconds to return a basic API response will make every testing tool look slow.

Enable timestamps for individual steps whenever your testing tool supports them. Without step-level timing, you are guessing.

I usually start with the slowest ten tests, then inspect the slowest steps inside those tests. This gives you a much clearer picture than looking at the average duration of the entire suite.

## 1. Replace fixed pauses with condition-based waits

Hardcoded pauses are one of the most common sources of wasted test execution time.

Imagine that a test contains this instruction:

```python
time.sleep(10)
```

The page may be ready after 800 milliseconds, but the test will still wait the full ten seconds. Multiply that by 30 pauses across 200 tests and you have created hours of waiting that produce no additional coverage.

A fixed pause is appropriate when the passage of time is actually part of the scenario. For example, you might intentionally wait to verify that a user session expires after a defined period. It can also be acceptable as a temporary debugging measure while you are figuring out which condition should be observed.

It should not be the default way to synchronize a test with the application.

The better pattern is:

1. Define the condition that means the application is ready.
2. Check that condition repeatedly.
3. Continue immediately when it becomes true.
4. Stop with a useful error after a maximum timeout.

The maximum timeout is important. Without it, a broken application can leave a test waiting for an unreasonable amount of time.

### Selenium

In Selenium, use an explicit wait for a specific condition:

```python
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait

wait = WebDriverWait(driver, 10, poll_frequency=0.25)

checkout_button = wait.until(
    EC.element_to_be_clickable((By.ID, "checkout"))
)

checkout_button.click()
```

This does not mean the test always waits ten seconds. Ten seconds is the upper limit. If the button becomes clickable after 400 milliseconds, the test continues at that point.

Selenium's own [waiting documentation](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/) describes explicit waits as polling loops that continue until a condition becomes true or the timeout is reached.

Be careful with a global implicit wait that is much larger than necessary. It can make every missing element expensive to diagnose, especially when combined with helper methods that perform multiple lookups.

### Playwright

Playwright already performs actionability checks before many actions. For example, a locator click waits for the element to be visible, stable, enabled, and able to receive events.

That means this is often enough:

```typescript
await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Checkout" }).click();
await expect(page.getByText("Order confirmed")).toBeVisible();
```

Playwright's [auto-waiting](https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability) and web-first assertions are useful precisely because they avoid the need for arbitrary sleeps.

The mistake I still see is adding `waitForTimeout()` around actions that already wait intelligently. That turns a fast, condition-based test back into a fixed-duration test.

### Cypress

Cypress queries and assertions have built-in retry behavior. A chain such as this will keep retrying until it passes or reaches the configured timeout:

```javascript
cy.get("[data-testid='order-status']")
  .should("contain.text", "Completed");
```

The Cypress documentation on [retry-ability](https://docs.cypress.io/app/core-concepts/retry-ability) explains how queries and assertions are retried together.

The practical lesson is the same across all three libraries: wait for an observable result, not for a guessed number of seconds.

### Endtest

In Endtest, use condition-based steps such as **Wait Until** or **Wait For Element** instead of adding a **Pause** after every navigation or click. You can also define a maximum wait time, so the test continues as soon as the condition is met and fails clearly when it is not.

The [Endtest waits documentation](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/waits) covers the available options.

Endtest also records timestamps for test steps. Those timestamps are one of the fastest ways to identify a locator, page transition, API response, or assertion that is consuming more time than expected.

A practical rule is to review every pause longer than one second. For each one, ask: *What exact condition are we really waiting for?*

## 2. Collect fewer artifacts during routine runs

Artifacts are useful. They are also work.

Every screenshot requires the browser to render and capture pixels. Page source extraction requires the browser and driver to serialize the DOM. Network logs have to be collected, stored, transferred, and sometimes processed. Video recording adds encoding and upload work. Cookies, console logs, traces, and accessibility data all have a cost.

The bottleneck is not always the test framework. Often, the browser is doing exactly what you asked it to do.

A common overcorrection is to collect everything during every test:

- Screenshot after every step
- Full-page screenshot after every navigation
- Page source after every action
- Complete network log
- Browser console log
- Video
- Trace
- Cookies
- Performance data

That might be reasonable for a short diagnostic run. It is usually excessive for a large regression suite that runs on every commit.

A better approach is to create artifact profiles.

### Fast CI profile

Use this for pull requests and frequent regression runs:

- Capture screenshots only on errors or failed assertions
- Save page source only when a test fails
- Keep essential console errors
- Disable video unless it provides unique value
- Record traces only on the first retry or failure
- Avoid collecting full network traffic unless the test is specifically investigating network behavior

### Diagnostic profile

Use this when reproducing an intermittent issue:

- Screenshots at important checkpoints
- Page source on selected steps
- Full browser and console logs
- Network capture
- Video or trace
- Additional timing information

Playwright explicitly recommends avoiding traces on every test because tracing every run is performance-heavy. A common Playwright configuration is to collect a trace only on the first retry:

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from "@playwright/test";

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    screenshot: "only-on-failure",
    video: "retain-on-failure",
    trace: "on-first-retry",
  },
});
```

Cypress automatically captures screenshots on failures during `cypress run`, while video recording can be enabled or disabled through configuration. Its [screenshots and videos documentation](https://docs.cypress.io/app/guides/screenshots-and-videos) also describes how teams can avoid retaining videos for successful specs.

In Selenium, artifact collection is usually implemented by the framework around WebDriver. The same principle applies: put screenshot, DOM, and network capture in failure hooks instead of calling them after every action.

In Endtest, artifact and logging behavior can be adjusted through the test suite's [advanced settings](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/advanced-settings). The right configuration depends on the purpose of the run.

Do not minimize artifacts at all costs. Collect the smallest set that still lets you understand a failure.

## 3. Give development and staging enough resources

Test automation is often blamed for application slowness that the test merely exposes.

Suppose the staging environment is running on a tiny container with aggressive CPU throttling, a cold database, limited memory, and background jobs competing for the same resources. A checkout flow that takes two seconds in production may take 15 seconds in staging.

The team then adds longer waits to the tests.

Now the tests are slower, the staging environment is still unrealistic, and genuine performance regressions become harder to distinguish from infrastructure noise.

Development and staging do not need to match the full production scale. They do need enough capacity to behave consistently and realistically for the traffic generated by the test suite.

Things worth checking include:

- CPU throttling and memory pressure
- Database connection limits
- Cold starts
- Autoscaling delays
- Shared services used by multiple teams
- Rate limits
- Slow third-party sandbox APIs
- Large debug builds or unoptimized frontend assets
- Background jobs competing with tests
- Test data that has grown far beyond normal production patterns

Using the smallest possible virtual machine or container can look like cost optimization. In practice, it can cost more through slow pipelines, false failures, repeated reruns, and engineering time spent investigating problems that do not occur in a properly sized environment.

There is also a trust problem. When everybody knows staging is slow and inconsistent, failures become easy to dismiss as "probably the environment." That is how real defects survive.

I recommend tracking basic application response times alongside test duration. If a test suddenly becomes slower, you should be able to see whether the time was spent inside the browser automation layer or waiting for the application itself.

For important end-to-end paths, keep the infrastructure profile reasonably close to production. You do not need to reproduce every production server, only to avoid testing under conditions so artificial that the results stop being useful.

## 4. Make tests independent, then run them in parallel

Parallel execution can turn a 60-minute suite into a 10-minute suite, but only when the tests are designed to run independently.

This is the part that gets skipped.

Teams sometimes enable ten workers on a suite whose tests share the same account, modify the same records, and assume that test case 7 will begin where test case 6 ended. The result is a faster way to create nondeterministic failures, not a faster suite.

A parallel-friendly test should be able to start without knowing what another test did before it.

For example, you should be able to run test cases 2, 6, 9, 10, and 13 at the same time without them changing each other's state.

That usually means each test should:

- Navigate to a known starting location
- Establish its own authentication state
- Create or reserve the data it needs
- Avoid modifying records used by another test
- Clean up temporary data when appropriate
- Use a separate browser session
- Avoid depending on execution order

A checkout test might begin by opening the application, checking whether the user is authenticated, and logging in when necessary. It should not assume that a previous test already completed the login flow.

Do not duplicate the login logic in every test. Reuse it.

In Endtest, shared setup flows can be reused through [imported test cases](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/importing-test-cases). Conditional logic can handle situations such as "log in only when the user is not already authenticated" through [IF statements](https://endtest.io/docs/web-tests/if-statements-for-web-tests).

In Selenium, create a new WebDriver instance for each independently executed test and avoid shared mutable test data. Selenium's own guidance on [avoiding shared state](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/avoid_sharing_state/) recommends isolated tests and separate driver instances.

In Playwright, test files already run in parallel by default, and worker count can be configured:

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from "@playwright/test";

export default defineConfig({
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : undefined,
  fullyParallel: true,
});
```

For tests that modify server-side state, use separate accounts or data partitions for parallel workers. Reusing one authenticated state across tests is fast until two tests change the same user setting at the same time.

Cypress can distribute specs across parallel CI machines when configured with Cypress Cloud, but the same isolation rules apply. The orchestration layer cannot repair shared-state assumptions inside the tests.

One more point: if you started automating tests a few weeks ago, it is fine if the first tests are not perfectly independent. You are learning the application and the tool. Just treat independence as an architectural direction, not as something to postpone forever.

A useful migration approach is:

1. Make the ten slowest or most important tests independent.
2. Run those in parallel.
3. Measure the reduction.
4. Convert the rest of the suite in batches.

This produces value earlier than pausing all automation work for a large framework rewrite.

## 5. Use a cross-browser cloud built for execution

You can run browser tests on a developer laptop. You can also build your own Selenium Grid, provision CI containers, maintain browser images, install drivers, patch operating systems, manage queues, and investigate why a worker stopped accepting sessions at 2:00 a.m.

Sometimes self-hosting is the correct choice. It is not free.

The total test duration includes more than the time between the first click and the last assertion. It also includes:

- Waiting for a worker
- Starting the machine or container
- Starting the browser
- Establishing the remote session
- Downloading dependencies
- Uploading results
- Replacing unhealthy workers

A setup that creates a fresh Windows worker for every test job can spend 30 to 60 seconds provisioning before the first test step runs. Across many short tests, startup time becomes a large percentage of the pipeline.

A mature cross-browser cloud keeps browser capacity ready, manages session allocation, and removes much of that provisioning delay.

It also makes parallel execution practical across browser and operating system combinations. That matters because production users do not all use the same headless Chromium build on Linux. Depending on your audience, reliable coverage may require Chrome and Edge on Windows, Safari on macOS, Firefox, mobile browsers, different resolutions, and different geographic locations.

Selenium Grid exists specifically to route tests to remote browser instances and run them in parallel across machines. Building and operating that Grid yourself, however, is a separate infrastructure project.

With Endtest, executions are routed to an always-available cross-browser cloud. In our internal launch-time measurements across the services and setups we benchmark, Endtest has delivered the fastest browser session startup we have measured, with many executions beginning in under one second.

That is internal product telemetry, not an independent industry benchmark, so I would not present it as a universal law. But startup time is measurable, and teams should measure it when comparing platforms.

Do not compare only how fast a single test runs after the browser is already open. Compare the complete CI experience:

1. How long does the session wait in a queue?
2. How long does browser startup take?
3. How quickly can the suite scale from one to 20 parallel sessions?
4. Does startup time become worse during busy periods?
5. How much infrastructure maintenance is required?
6. Can the same tests run on realistic browser and operating system combinations?

A fast cross-browser cloud does not fix slow test logic. It removes infrastructure overhead after the test logic has been cleaned up.

You can learn more about Endtest plans and parallel execution capacity on the [pricing page](https://endtest.io/pricing).

## A practical speed audit for your test suite

If your suite feels slow, do this before switching frameworks:

### Day 1: Establish the baseline

Record:

- Total suite duration
- Queue time
- Browser startup time
- Average test duration
- Ten slowest tests
- Ten slowest individual steps
- Artifact upload time
- Retry count

### Day 2: Remove obvious waiting

Search the suite for:

- `sleep`
- `waitForTimeout`
- `cy.wait` with a numeric duration
- Pause steps
- Global timeouts that are much larger than necessary

Replace each fixed delay with a condition when possible.

### Day 3: Reduce default artifacts

Create a fast CI profile that captures screenshots, DOM, video, traces, and network logs only when they provide diagnostic value.

### Day 4: Check the application environment

Compare application response times in staging and production-like environments. Look for resource throttling, cold starts, database contention, and slow sandbox services.

### Day 5: Parallelize a clean subset

Choose tests that already have good isolation. Run them with two workers, then four, then more. Watch for shared data collisions and diminishing returns.

Do not assume that doubling the number of workers will always cut the duration in half. The application, database, test data service, or account limits may become the new bottleneck.

## Speed should improve feedback, not hide problems

Faster test execution should shorten the time between a code change and a trustworthy answer, not produce an impressive dashboard.

A five-minute suite that misses failures is not better than a 20-minute suite that catches them. A highly parallel suite that fails randomly because tests share state is noisy, not fast. A test that skips artifacts entirely may be quick, but expensive to investigate when it fails.

The best optimization is usually a balance:

- Wait only as long as the application needs
- Collect enough evidence to debug failures
- Test against a stable and realistic environment
- Design tests to run independently
- Use execution infrastructure that starts quickly and scales predictably

Framework debates tend to focus on syntax and benchmark examples. In real projects, the biggest gains usually come from removing fixed waiting, reducing unnecessary browser work, improving test isolation, and eliminating infrastructure startup delays.

Those changes help whether your tests are written in Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, or built with an intelligent testing platform.

And unlike a rewrite, you can start applying them today.

# How to Handle Defects in Production

A practical response plan for production defects: isolate the issue, patch safely, communicate clearly, and prevent regressions with real E2E tests.

Published June 18, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/how-to-handle-defects-in-production

---
At some point, every software company gets the message nobody wants to receive:

> Something is broken in production.

Sometimes it comes from an automated alert. Sometimes it comes from support. And sometimes it comes from a customer who has already spent 20 minutes trying to understand whether they are doing something wrong.

The technical defect might be small. The damage rarely is.

A production bug interrupts someone while they are trying to get work done. It can make them question whether their data is safe, whether an important operation completed successfully, and whether they can continue relying on your product.

For a software company, reliability is part of the product.

Customers do not separate your features from your uptime, browser compatibility, error messages, and response to incidents. It all becomes part of the same judgment:

**Can I trust this product?**

The way your team responds to a production defect can either reinforce that trust or make the situation worse.

## First, determine what is actually broken

The first report is usually incomplete.

A customer might say that a page does not work, a button does nothing, or their data disappeared. That is enough to start investigating, but not enough to start changing production code.

Before discussing causes, determine the scope of the problem.

Try to answer a few basic questions:

- Which users are affected?
- Which workflows are affected?
- When did the issue begin?
- Does it happen consistently or intermittently?
- Is it limited to a browser, operating system, account type, region, or configuration?
- Was there a recent deployment or infrastructure change?
- Is data being lost or corrupted?
- Is there a security or privacy impact?

This is the isolation stage.

The goal is to reduce the size of the unknown.

A defect affecting one browser version requires a different response from a defect corrupting data for every customer. A cosmetic problem on an internal settings page is different from a broken checkout, login flow, or deployment process.

Teams often lose time because they jump immediately to the first plausible explanation. Someone remembers a recent frontend change, so everyone assumes that change caused the problem. Another engineer sees a database timeout and concludes that the database is responsible.

Those clues may be useful, but they are not conclusions.

Reproduce the issue using the same conditions as the affected user whenever possible. Use the same browser, operating system, permissions, account state, feature flags, and data.

The closer your reproduction environment is to the customer's real environment, the less likely you are to spend hours fixing the wrong problem.

## Contain the damage before finding the perfect fix

When a defect is actively harming customers, the first objective is containment.

That might mean rolling back a release, disabling a feature flag, temporarily blocking a specific operation, restoring a previous configuration, or routing traffic away from a failing service.

A rollback is a tool for reducing the consequences of failure, not an admission that the team failed.

The temptation is to keep the new release live while the team works on a clean fix. That can make sense when the impact is minor and well understood. It makes much less sense when customer data, billing, authentication, or a critical workflow is involved.

A useful question is:

**If we do nothing for the next two hours, what happens?**

If the answer includes more corrupted records, more failed payments, more locked-out customers, or more support tickets, containment should happen before a detailed root-cause investigation.

The elegant solution can come later. Stop the damage first.

## Reproduce the defect before patching it

A patch created without a reliable reproduction is partly a guess.

It may work. It may also hide the original symptom while leaving the underlying problem in place.

Before changing the implementation, create the smallest repeatable scenario that demonstrates the failure. Ideally, that scenario should become an automated functional test.

This gives the team three things:

1. Proof that the defect exists.
2. A way to verify that the patch fixes it.
3. Protection against the same defect returning later.

The test should fail before the patch and pass after the patch.

This sounds obvious, but it is frequently skipped during urgent incidents. Someone changes a condition, refreshes the page twice, sees the expected result, and declares the problem fixed.

That is a promising observation, not verification.

A production defect has already demonstrated that the system behaved differently from what the team expected. That is exactly when assumptions deserve more scrutiny, not less.

## Find the root cause, not only the visible symptom

The root cause is not always the line of code where the error appeared.

Suppose a customer cannot save a form because a new validation rule rejects an empty optional field. The immediate fix might be to change the condition.

But the deeper questions are more useful:

- Why was the optional field treated as required?
- Why did the existing test suite not detect the change?
- Was the requirement unclear?
- Did the developer test only the most common path?
- Was the frontend tested without the real API response?
- Did different browsers serialize the value differently?
- Was the affected workflow missing from the release checklist?

The root cause might be a coding error. It might also be a missing test, an inaccurate assumption, an incomplete specification, a browser difference, or a review process that focused on implementation details while overlooking user behavior.

Stopping at "the condition was wrong" makes it likely that a similar problem will appear somewhere else.

Root-cause analysis should not become a search for the person who made the mistake. That encourages people to hide uncertainty and defend their decisions.

The better question is:

**What allowed this defect to reach users?**

That question can produce an actionable answer.

## Apply the smallest safe patch

Urgency creates a dangerous incentive to rewrite too much.

An engineer sees the defect, notices that the surrounding code is messy, and decides to clean up the entire area while fixing it. The resulting change becomes larger, harder to review, and more likely to introduce another problem.

During an incident, prefer the smallest change that safely corrects the behavior.

That does not mean inserting a random workaround and forgetting about it. The idea is to separate immediate risk reduction from broader architectural work.

A good production patch should be:

- Narrow enough to understand quickly
- Easy to review
- Covered by a regression test
- Reversible if the result is unexpected
- Tested against adjacent workflows
- Monitored after deployment

The regression test should cover the exact scenario that failed in production. The team should also test nearby paths that could be affected by the patch.

A change to authentication should not be verified only by logging in once. Check failed logins, password resets, sessions, permissions, and any related account flows.

A change to checkout should not be verified only with one successful payment. Check declined payments, retries, discounts, taxes, duplicate submissions, and confirmation messages.

The patch solves the known defect. Regression testing helps ensure that it does not purchase one fix by creating three new problems.

## Test the patch like a real user

One of the most dangerous phrases during an incident is:

> It works on my machine.

That statement is not useless, but it is incomplete.

The software does not exist only on the developer's machine. It exists on the combinations of browsers, operating systems, screen sizes, network conditions, permissions, and account states used by customers.

Testing a patch with unit tests and component tests is important. It is not sufficient.

At Endtest, we see aggregate patterns from millions of automated test executions performed through the platform each year. One pattern remains consistent: defects still appear at the functional level even when lower-level tests pass.

This is not an argument against unit or component testing. Both are useful. Unit tests provide fast feedback about isolated logic. Component tests help verify individual pieces of the interface.

But neither can fully replace a functional end-to-end test that opens the application, interacts with it through the browser, sends requests to real services, and verifies the outcome from the user's perspective.

There are always defects that appear only when the pieces are connected.

A button can render correctly while sending the wrong payload. An API can return the correct response while the frontend fails to display it. Two components can work independently but fail when they share state. A workflow can pass in Chrome and break in Safari.

The closer the test gets to actual user behavior, the more of these integration boundaries it can verify.

## A headless Linux container is not the entire internet

Headless browsers running in Linux containers are convenient. They are fast, inexpensive, and easy to add to a CI pipeline.

They are also only one testing environment.

It is extremely risky to treat a passing headless test suite inside a Linux container as proof that a release works for all users.

A production release should also be tested in real browser processes running on full operating-system environments similar to the ones used by customers. Those machines may be physical or properly virtualized, but they should reproduce the browser and operating-system combinations that matter to the product.

Headless testing can miss differences involving:

- Browser rendering
- Fonts and layout
- File downloads and uploads
- Permissions
- Popups and new tabs
- Clipboard behavior
- Authentication flows
- Video and audio
- Browser extensions
- Operating-system dialogs
- Focus, scrolling, and keyboard input
- GPU-dependent behavior

The answer is to understand what headless tests prove, not to stop using them.

A headless Chrome test on Linux proves that the tested scenario worked in headless Chrome on Linux under those conditions. It does not prove that it works in Safari on macOS, Chrome on Windows, Firefox, or Edge.

That distinction matters when a release can affect paying customers.

## Safari is not the same thing as WebKit

Cross-browser testing is often reduced to running Chrome and then running a WebKit-based test in a container.

That is better than testing only Chrome, but it is not the same as testing Safari.

WebKit is the rendering engine used by Safari. Safari is the complete browser, with its own networking behavior, privacy features, media handling, permissions, browser interface, and integration with macOS and iOS.

A WebKit build running on Linux can help identify compatibility problems. It should not be presented as a complete substitute for testing the real Safari browser on an Apple operating system.

This distinction becomes especially important for products with a meaningful number of Safari users.

Teams should not choose browsers based on personal preference or convenience. Look at real production analytics and determine what customers actually use.

That might include:

- Chrome on Windows
- Chrome on macOS
- Safari on macOS
- Mobile Safari on iOS
- Edge on Windows
- Firefox on Windows or Linux

The exact matrix will vary by product.

A B2B application used primarily by corporate customers may have a large Edge and Windows audience. A consumer product may have significant mobile Safari traffic. A developer tool may have more macOS and Firefox users than expected.

Your test strategy should follow your customers, not browser market-share headlines.

For a practical way to choose that browser matrix, see [What Browsers Should You Test Your Website On?](https://endtest.io/blog/what-browsers-should-you-test-your-website-on).

## Functional tests must belong to the whole team

Many companies technically have functional tests, but only one person understands them.

That creates a fragile system.

The tests live in a separate repository. They use a custom framework. They require specialized setup. Most developers avoid touching them. Product managers cannot read them. Manual testers have to ask an automation engineer to update a simple workflow.

Eventually, the test suite falls behind the product.

New functionality is released every sprint, while test updates remain in a permanent state of "almost ready." The suite gradually becomes less representative of the application. Failures are ignored. Tests are disabled. The CI job remains green because fewer meaningful things are being tested.

For functional tests to remain useful, all relevant team members should be able to contribute to them.

That includes developers, testers, and, where appropriate, product or support team members who understand the workflow being tested.

Not everyone needs to become an automation-framework specialist. The tests need to be understandable and editable without requiring one specific person to translate every product change into test code.

This is one of the reasons we believe functional automation should be accessible to the broader team. Tests that cannot be maintained during the sprint are unlikely to keep up with the product.

A large test suite that represents the application from six months ago is worth less than a smaller suite that accurately protects today's critical workflows.

This is also why test maintenance has to happen alongside product development rather than in a separate phase after the sprint. [How Testing Keeps Up With Development](https://endtest.io/blog/how-testing-keeps-up-with-development) explores that problem in more detail.

## Communicate with affected customers

When a production defect affects customers, silence creates its own damage.

Customers do not expect software to be literally incapable of failing. They do expect the company operating it to respond honestly and competently.

The communication should match the severity of the incident.

For a small issue affecting a few known users, direct communication may be enough. For a widespread outage, use the status page, in-app notifications, email, or the channels customers already rely on.

A useful incident update explains:

- What users are experiencing
- Which users or workflows are affected
- Whether there is a temporary workaround
- What the team has done so far
- Whether data or security is affected
- When the next update will be provided

Avoid speculation. Do not announce a root cause before it has been confirmed.

Also avoid empty language such as "some users may be experiencing degraded performance" when the application is clearly unavailable. Customers recognize language designed to minimize the appearance of a problem.

Trust is better served by accuracy.

After the issue has been resolved, tell affected customers what changed. The explanation does not need to expose sensitive implementation details, but it should demonstrate that the team understood the problem and took steps to prevent a recurrence.

For serious incidents, a service credit or other concrete gesture may be appropriate. The correct response depends on the impact, the contract, and the relationship with the customer.

## Production defects create brand damage

A defect is not only an engineering cost.

It creates support tickets, interrupts sales conversations, distracts product teams, delays other releases, and forces leadership to explain what happened.

Repeated defects also change how customers use the product.

They begin double-checking results manually. They avoid recently released features. They keep backup tools available. They hesitate before expanding usage to another team.

At that point, the product may still technically retain the account, but trust has already started eroding.

For subscription software, this can eventually increase churn.

Customers rarely cancel because of one harmless visual issue. They do cancel when recurring defects make the product feel unreliable, especially when those defects affect core workflows.

Reliability compounds in the same way product quality does.

A company that responds well, communicates clearly, and prevents repeated failures can strengthen customer trust after an incident. A company that repeatedly ships avoidable defects and provides vague explanations teaches customers not to depend on it.

## Run a blameless post-incident review

After the patch is deployed and customers are no longer affected, the team should review what happened.

Do this while the details are still fresh.

A useful review covers:

- The incident timeline
- The initial customer impact
- How the issue was detected
- How it was isolated
- The confirmed root cause
- Why existing tests did not catch it
- What slowed down the response
- What limited the impact
- Which preventive actions will be taken
- Who owns each action and when it should be completed

Avoid turning the review into a document that says "be more careful."

That is not a preventive action.

Useful actions might include adding a functional test, changing a deployment check, improving browser coverage, adding monitoring, clarifying ownership, updating a feature flag, or making a critical workflow easier to test.

The best post-incident actions change the system so that future teams do not need to remember the lesson manually.

## Build the regression test into the release process

A production defect should leave behind a permanent test whenever the scenario can be automated.

The test should not sit on someone's laptop or in a branch that will be merged later. It should become part of the normal release process.

For critical workflows, functional tests should run automatically before deployment or immediately after deployment in a controlled environment.

A green check mark has no value when the test avoids the conditions that real customers face. It should not exist merely so that the team can say, "The pipeline was green," after something breaks in production.

The purpose of an automated test is to reduce uncertainty about the product.

That means interacting with the application like a real user, in a real browser, on representative machines, and verifying meaningful outcomes.

Did the order actually get created?

Did the user receive the correct permissions?

Was the file really uploaded?

Did the confirmation appear?

Was the record stored correctly?

Does the workflow still work in Safari?

These questions matter more than the number of tests in the dashboard.

For a deeper explanation of how these tests protect complete workflows, see [What Is End-to-End Testing?](https://endtest.io/blog/what-is-end-to-end-e2e-testing).

## A practical production-defect checklist

When a defect reaches production, use this sequence:

1. **Confirm the report.** Capture the exact symptoms and affected workflow.
2. **Assess severity.** Determine the impact on users, data, security, and revenue.
3. **Contain the issue.** Roll back, disable, or isolate the affected functionality when necessary.
4. **Reproduce it.** Match the user's browser, operating system, account state, and data.
5. **Create a failing test.** Preserve the scenario before changing the implementation.
6. **Identify the root cause.** Explain both the technical failure and why the process allowed it through.
7. **Apply a narrow patch.** Avoid unrelated rewrites during the incident.
8. **Run regression tests.** Cover the exact defect and adjacent workflows.
9. **Test representative browsers.** Include the real browser and operating-system combinations used by customers.
10. **Communicate clearly.** Inform affected users without minimizing or speculating.
11. **Monitor the release.** Verify that the patch behaves correctly under production conditions.
12. **Review the incident.** Assign specific preventive actions with owners and deadlines.
13. **Keep the regression test.** Add it permanently to the automated release process.

## The real goal is confidence, not perfect software

No testing strategy can guarantee that production will never contain another defect.

The goal is to reduce the number of avoidable failures, limit their impact, respond quickly, and prevent the same defect from returning.

Unit tests, component tests, monitoring, and code review all help.

But none of them removes the need to test the complete product from the perspective of a real user.

That means opening the application in actual browsers, interacting with real workflows, and checking the outcome that matters to the customer.

It also means making those tests accessible enough that the whole team can keep them current throughout each sprint.

When functional tests become an outdated side project owned by one specialist, they stop protecting the release. When they become part of everyday product development, they provide evidence that the software customers depend on still works.

That is worth more than another green icon.

That is also the principle behind [Endtest](https://endtest.io/): functional tests should reflect real user behavior, run in the environments customers actually use, and remain maintainable by the wider team.

# The 5 Stages of Test Automation Maturity

A practical framework for judging test automation maturity, from fragile local scripts to reliable, shared, cross-browser release confidence.

Published June 17, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/the-5-stages-of-test-automation-maturity

---
Most teams talk about test automation as if it were binary.

You either have automated tests or you do not.

A manager asks, "Do we have automated testing?" Someone says yes because there is a Playwright repository with 180 test files in it. A dashboard exists. A few green screenshots were shown in a demo six months ago. The box gets checked.

But the team still spends two days manually testing every release.

The automated suite is not part of the deployment pipeline. Only one person understands it. Half the tests are skipped. Nobody trusts the results enough to delay a release. Production defects continue to appear in workflows that were supposedly covered.

Technically, the company has test automation.

Operationally, it does not.

Test automation maturity is a progression. A team can have thousands of automated steps and still be at an early stage. Another team can have a smaller suite that reliably protects its most important customer journeys and be much further ahead.

A better question than "Do we have automated tests?" is:

> What stage is our test automation in, and what would move it to the next one?

I have worked in software testing since 2012, first as a manual tester and later building Endtest. Over that time, I have seen the same progression repeat across small startups, growing SaaS companies, and large organizations.

The tools change. Selenium gives way to Cypress. Cypress gives way to Playwright. AI gets added to the conversation. But the organizational problems remain surprisingly consistent.

Here is the five-stage framework I use to think about test automation maturity.

## The five stages at a glance

| Stage | Description | CI/CD integration | Ownership | Browser coverage | Release confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Almost Ready** | Tests exist, but they do not influence releases | None | One person | Inconsistent | Very low |
| **2. Useful on Demand** | Tests occasionally provide useful feedback | Partial or scheduled | One or two people | Usually Chrome | Low |
| **3. Part of the Pipeline** | Critical tests run automatically with deployments | Yes | Small automation group | Mostly Chrome | Moderate |
| **4. Broad Release Confidence** | Reliable coverage extends across browsers and teams | Strong | Shared across QA and development | Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari | High |
| **5. Automation as a Team Capability** | Testing is a dependable part of how software is built | Continuous | Broad, shared ownership | Full relevant coverage | Very high |

These stages are not formal industry standards. The indicators are intentionally practical rather than academic.

A team can also sit between stages. You might have Stage 4 browser coverage but Stage 2 ownership. You might have excellent CI integration but poor failure analysis. The goal is to find the weakest part of the system, the one limiting confidence, rather than to obtain a perfect label.

## Stage 1: Almost Ready

This is the most common stage.

The team has automated tests, but the tests live beside the real development process rather than inside it.

### Typical indicators

- Automated tests are not required in the CI/CD pipeline.
- One person created and maintains most of the suite.
- Tests are run manually before selected releases.
- A large percentage of failures require rerunning the suite.
- The automation project is described as "almost ready."
- The team still performs broad manual regression testing.
- Production defects regularly escape from supposedly covered areas.
- Most automation conversations are about tools, frameworks, and architecture.

### What it looks like

There is usually a repository.

It may contain Playwright, Selenium, Cypress, or a mix of older experiments. There are page objects, helper functions, environment files, custom fixtures, reporting libraries, and a README that has not been updated since the second developer joined the project.

The suite appears substantial when measured by files or lines of code.

But it does not reliably answer the question the business actually cares about:

> Can we release this version safely?

The tests may work on the automation engineer's laptop. They may even work in a dedicated environment after a few retries. But they are not dependable enough to become part of the release process.

Only one team member knows how to investigate failures. When that person is on vacation, the suite effectively stops existing.

Meanwhile, manual testers carry the real release risk. They repeat login checks, account creation, checkout flows, subscription upgrades, permissions tests, and other regression scenarios by hand.

The organization tells itself that automation will soon reduce this work.

It has often been telling itself that for a year.

### What to focus on

The goal at Stage 1 is to make a small number of tests operationally useful rather than to add more tests.

Start by identifying five to ten workflows that would cause meaningful customer or business damage if they stopped working. Examples might include:

- A new customer creating an account
- An existing customer logging in
- A payment completing successfully
- A subscription being upgraded
- A user inviting a colleague
- A critical report being generated
- A customer receiving a confirmation email

Get those tests running automatically in a stable environment.

The suite does not need to cover everything. It needs to produce a result that another team member can understand and trust.

Stage 1 teams often make the mistake of treating framework completeness as progress. They spend weeks deciding how page objects should inherit from base classes, how fixtures should be organized, or whether the company should move from Selenium to Playwright.

Those decisions are not meaningless. But they are secondary.

A mediocre test that runs on every deployment and catches a real regression is worth more than a beautifully abstracted test framework that is still "almost ready."

### Common traps

**Debating Playwright versus Selenium instead of shipping useful coverage**

Tool debates feel productive because they are technical and measurable. But choosing the perfect framework does not solve unclear ownership, unstable environments, missing test data, or the absence of CI integration.

**Automating low-value scenarios first**

Teams often begin with whatever is easiest to automate rather than what is most important to protect. A hundred tests for settings screens can create impressive numbers while checkout remains manual.

**Building an internal platform too early**

At this stage, the team needs reliable feedback, not a generalized testing framework capable of serving every future project.

**Treating manual testing as the problem**

Manual testing is carrying the release because automation is not ready. Removing manual coverage before automation becomes dependable only increases risk.

## Stage 2: Useful on Demand

At Stage 2, the suite sometimes earns its keep.

It is still not a dependable release gate, but it catches real issues and saves time in specific situations.

### Typical indicators

- Tests run nightly, on demand, or for selected pull requests.
- One or two people maintain most of the suite.
- The team has a small set of reasonably stable critical tests.
- Failed tests still generate a meaningful number of false alarms.
- Results are reviewed, but they do not automatically block deployment.
- Browser coverage is usually limited to Chrome or Chromium.
- Manual regression remains the final source of release confidence.

### What it looks like

The team has moved beyond experimentation.

A developer can trigger the suite. A scheduled run produces a report. Some failures are real and lead to bugs being fixed before release.

This is an important improvement.

For the first time, test automation is producing visible outcomes rather than only code.

But trust is inconsistent.

When the suite is green, everyone feels better. When it is red, the first assumption is often that the test is wrong.

The tests may also be disconnected from normal development timing. A nightly run that fails at 2:00 a.m. might not be investigated until the afternoon. By then, several unrelated changes have been merged and identifying the cause becomes slower.

The team has automation, but feedback arrives too late or too inconsistently to shape daily behavior.

### What to focus on

The next step is to shorten the distance between a code change and a trustworthy test result.

Move the most important and stable tests into the CI/CD pipeline. They do not need to run after every small commit if execution is still slow, but they should run automatically at a meaningful point before release.

At the same time, establish simple ownership rules:

- Who investigates a failure?
- How quickly should a failed test be reviewed?
- When is a flaky test fixed?
- When is a test removed?
- Who can update tests after a product change?

A test suite with no response process is only a notification system.

Teams should also begin measuring outcomes instead of activity. Useful indicators include:

- How many releases received automated feedback?
- How long did failures take to investigate?
- How many real defects were caught before production?
- Which critical workflows remain entirely manual?
- How often was a failure dismissed as flaky?
- How much manual regression time was actually removed?

The number of automated test cases can be useful, but it is not the primary measure of maturity.

### Common traps

**Moving every test into CI at once**

This often creates a wall of red failures that developers learn to ignore. Start with the tests that deserve trust.

**Using retries to hide instability**

Retries can help with intermittent infrastructure problems. They can also make an unreliable suite look healthier than it is.

**Keeping automation isolated inside QA**

Developers do not need to write every test, but they should understand how product changes affect the suite. If automation remains a separate department's problem, maintenance will always lag behind development.

**Assuming Chrome coverage means web coverage**

Chrome may represent most of your users, but it does not prove that the application works correctly in Safari, Firefox, or Edge.

That becomes the central limitation of the next stage.

## Stage 3: Part of the Pipeline

At Stage 3, automated testing becomes part of how the team ships software.

Critical tests run automatically. Failures are investigated. A red result can delay a deployment.

This is where automation begins to create real release confidence.

### Typical indicators

- Critical end-to-end tests run in CI/CD.
- Failures can block or delay releases.
- Results are available soon enough to influence development.
- Several team members can investigate common failures.
- Test data and environments are more predictable.
- The team has reduced some manual regression work.
- Most automated browser coverage still runs in Chrome.
- Complex workflows involving email, SMS, or third-party systems remain manual.

### What it looks like

The tests are no longer a side project.

A pull request or deployment triggers a meaningful set of checks. Developers know when they have broken a critical journey. Product managers and testers can look at a result and understand which customer flow failed.

The organization starts to rely on the suite during sprints.

This changes behavior.

Developers become more careful about breaking stable selectors. Product changes include test updates more often. Test failures are discussed alongside build failures rather than after them.

Manual testers also gain time for exploratory work, new-feature analysis, usability, edge cases, and risks that are difficult to automate.

But there is often a hidden confidence gap.

The suite runs almost entirely in Chrome.

The team knows that Chrome works. It assumes the rest.

Safari bugs are discovered by customers. Firefox problems are dismissed as uncommon. Edge is treated as Chrome with a different icon, even when enterprise policies, extensions, permissions, or browser-specific behavior create differences.

At this stage, automation protects a significant part of the product, but only through a narrow technical lens.

### What to focus on

The goal at Stage 3 is to broaden confidence without destroying execution speed.

Start by identifying the browsers and devices that matter to your actual users. You do not need to run every test in every browser after every commit.

A sensible strategy might look like this:

- Run a fast Chrome suite on pull requests.
- Run critical flows in Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari before deployment.
- Run the broader cross-browser suite on a schedule.
- Add targeted browser-specific tests for known risks.
- Review production analytics to decide where coverage is justified.

This is also the point where the team should make failures easier to understand.

A useful failure result should include enough context to answer basic questions quickly:

- Which step failed?
- What was visible on the page?
- Was the expected element missing or merely delayed?
- Which browser and environment were used?
- What network or console errors occurred?
- Did the same test pass in other browsers?
- Was the failure caused by the application, test data, infrastructure, or the test itself?

The faster the team can classify a failure, the more willing it will be to rely on automation.

### Common traps

**Running the entire suite in every browser on every commit**

This can make feedback too slow and expensive. Cross-browser maturity is about meaningful risk coverage, not brute force.

**Treating WebKit emulation as identical to real Safari**

Browser engines provide useful coverage, but real operating systems, devices, permissions, fonts, networking, and browser behavior can still matter.

**Leaving test readability behind**

A suite can become technically sophisticated while becoming inaccessible to most of the team. If only specialists can understand a failed scenario, ownership remains narrow.

**Measuring pass rate without measuring trust**

A 98% pass rate sounds excellent. It means less if the remaining 2% fails unpredictably and is routinely ignored.

## Stage 4: Broad Release Confidence

At Stage 4, the test suite protects the product across the environments customers actually use.

Automation is integrated into delivery, browser coverage is deliberate, and ownership is no longer concentrated in one person.

### Typical indicators

- Critical tests run in all relevant major browsers.
- Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari are covered intentionally.
- Test failures are usually investigated by the same day.
- Developers, testers, and other team members contribute.
- Tests are readable enough for non-authors to modify.
- Manual regression is narrower and risk-based.
- The suite covers important API interactions and external dependencies.
- Automated results are trusted during release decisions.

### What it looks like

The suite has become a shared product asset.

A developer changing a workflow updates the relevant tests. A tester can add coverage without redesigning the framework. A failed Safari scenario is not postponed indefinitely because only one person knows how to reproduce it.

The team has also stopped thinking about automation purely as browser clicking.

Real customer journeys cross system boundaries.

A signup flow may involve:

1. Submitting a form in the browser
2. Creating a record through an API
3. Sending a verification email
4. Opening a link from that email
5. Receiving an SMS code
6. Confirming the account
7. Displaying the correct permissions after login

At Stage 4, the team starts automating these journeys as complete business processes rather than isolated pages.

This produces a different kind of confidence.

The question becomes whether the customer can achieve the outcome the product promises, rather than whether a button can be clicked.

### What to focus on

The focus now shifts from creating coverage to keeping the system understandable and economical.

As suites grow, teams should regularly review:

- Which tests protect important risks?
- Which tests duplicate lower-level coverage?
- Which scenarios are slow without providing unique value?
- Which tests fail often enough to create fatigue?
- Which flows should run on every change?
- Which flows can run before release or on a schedule?
- Which manual checks still exist because automation is difficult?
- Are those manual checks useful, or merely habitual?

Stage 4 teams should also reduce key-person dependencies.

Readable test design matters here. So does documentation, but documentation alone will not solve ownership. The test itself should communicate intent clearly enough that another person can understand what business behavior it protects.

This is one reason no-code and low-code tools can be a good fit for some teams, while code-first frameworks remain better for others. The right choice depends on who needs to contribute and how much low-level control the organization requires.

Whether the test is code matters less than whether the right people can safely maintain it.

### Common traps

**Automating every possible variation**

More coverage eventually creates diminishing returns. A large suite can become slower, more expensive, and harder to maintain without materially improving release confidence.

**Confusing broad participation with no ownership**

Shared ownership does not mean nobody is accountable. Someone still needs responsibility for suite health, standards, and long-term direction.

**Replacing all manual testing**

Exploratory testing, usability review, visual judgment, and investigation of new risks still matter. Mature automation makes manual testing more focused. It does not make human testing obsolete.

**Ignoring execution economics**

A cross-browser suite that takes four hours and blocks every deployment may be comprehensive but operationally unusable.

## Stage 5: Automation as a Team Capability

At Stage 5, automated testing is part of the company's software delivery system rather than a project owned by QA.

### Typical indicators

- Tests run multiple times per day.
- Critical checks are fully integrated into CI/CD.
- Most relevant team members can contribute or make safe updates.
- Tests are easy to read, understand, and modify.
- Failures contain enough evidence for fast diagnosis.
- Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari are covered based on real risk.
- Native mobile coverage is included when the product requires it.
- End-to-end tests verify email, SMS, API, file, payment, and other external workflows.
- Manual testing is focused on exploration and new risk.
- Releases are faster because confidence arrives earlier.
- Production defects still happen, but recurring critical regressions are uncommon.

### What it looks like

The organization no longer celebrates the existence of automated tests.

It expects them to work.

A product change and its test coverage are usually delivered together. The suite runs throughout the day and provides feedback while the change is still fresh in the developer's mind.

Instead of being hidden inside an automation specialist's personal framework, the tests are visible, understandable, and connected to business behavior.

When a test fails, the team can usually determine whether it is:

- A product regression
- An intentional product change
- A test-data problem
- An environment failure
- A browser-specific issue
- A third-party service problem
- A genuine flaky test

The suite also reflects how the product actually works.

It can verify that an email arrived, that an SMS contained the correct code, that an API response changed after a UI action, that a downloaded file contains the expected information, and that a user can complete the same critical journey in the browsers the company supports.

No single person is holding the system together.

That may be the clearest sign of maturity.

### What to focus on

Stage 5 is not the end.

A mature suite can still decay if the organization stops paying attention.

The focus becomes preserving speed, trust, and maintainability as the product and team grow.

Useful practices include:

- Reviewing slow and flaky tests regularly
- Removing coverage that no longer protects meaningful risk
- Keeping fast checks separate from broader release suites
- Monitoring browser and device usage
- Updating tests as part of product changes
- Maintaining clear ownership for suite health
- Making failure evidence easy to access
- Tracking production escapes and adding coverage when patterns emerge
- Evaluating whether new tools reduce or merely relocate maintenance work

AI can help at this stage by creating initial tests, suggesting assertions, explaining failures, and helping repair outdated steps.

But AI does not replace the operating model.

A suite with weak ownership remains weak even if an AI agent writes more of it. A flaky test does not become trustworthy because its locator was generated by a language model. A test that never runs in CI provides little release confidence, regardless of how it was created.

Maturity comes from the whole system: people, process, coverage, execution, diagnosis, and maintenance.

### Common traps

**Assuming maturity is permanent**

A fast-growing suite can move backward. New products, acquisitions, team turnover, and architectural changes can reintroduce fragile ownership and unreliable coverage.

**Optimizing the test suite instead of the delivery system**

Automation exists to help the organization deliver reliable software with less wasted effort, not to produce beautiful reports.

**Adding AI everywhere without measuring the result**

The relevant question is whether tests are created faster, maintained with less effort, and trusted more often, not whether AI is present.

**Allowing success to create bloat**

Once automation becomes respected, every team wants more of it. Mature teams remain selective.

## Test automation maturity is not the number of tests

Many teams try to measure progress with test counts.

They report that the company has:

- 2,000 automated test cases
- 14,000 automated steps
- 93% automation coverage
- A 97% pass rate

Those numbers can be useful, but they can also hide weak maturity.

Two thousand tests that run once per month and require one engineer to interpret them may provide less value than 100 critical tests that run on every deployment and are trusted by the entire team.

A better maturity assessment looks at outcomes.

Ask:

- How quickly does the team learn that a critical flow is broken?
- Can the result stop a bad release?
- How many people can understand and update the test?
- How much repetitive manual regression has actually been removed?
- Which customer environments are covered?
- Do tests verify complete customer outcomes?
- How much time is lost investigating false failures?
- Are production defects becoming less repetitive?
- Can the suite keep working when its original author leaves?

These questions are harder to place on a dashboard.

They are also much closer to the reason test automation exists.

## A note about tools

Every stage can be reached with several tools.

You can build a mature system with Playwright, Selenium, Cypress, WebdriverIO, or a commercial platform. You can also build an unusable system with any of them.

Tools influence the cost of moving between stages, but they do not determine maturity by themselves.

A code-first framework may be ideal when developers own automation, unusual workflows require low-level control, and the company is willing to maintain the infrastructure.

A platform such as [Endtest](https://endtest.io/product) may be a better fit when the team wants broader participation, built-in cross-browser execution, and less framework maintenance.

The honest comparison is the total cost of producing and maintaining release confidence, not open source versus paid.

That includes engineering time, infrastructure, debugging, adoption, training, execution, and the risk of a suite that never becomes dependable.

For teams evaluating code-first options, the article on [Playwright alternatives](https://endtest.io/blog/top-7-playwright-alternatives-2026) covers the tradeoffs in more detail. Teams considering a managed approach can also compare the current [Endtest pricing](https://endtest.io/pricing) with the ongoing cost of an internal framework.

## Where is your team?

The point of this framework is to decide what work matters next, not to award yourself a maturity badge.

If you are at Stage 1, stop expanding the framework and get a few critical tests running automatically.

If you are at Stage 2, improve trust, ownership, and feedback speed.

If you are at Stage 3, broaden browser coverage and make failures easier to diagnose.

If you are at Stage 4, extend automation across real customer journeys and reduce key-person dependencies.

If you are at Stage 5, protect the speed and clarity of the system as it grows.

Every stage has a different bottleneck.

Trying to solve a Stage 4 problem while you are still at Stage 1 creates impressive architecture and very little confidence.

The goal is to make automated testing a reliable part of how your team delivers software.
