# Top 7 Playwright Alternatives in 2026

Compare seven Playwright alternatives for web testing, including Endtest, Cypress, Selenium, WebdriverIO, Puppeteer, Katalon, and TestCafe.

Published June 17, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/top-7-playwright-alternatives-2026

---
Playwright is a very good testing framework.

That is worth saying at the beginning, because articles about "alternatives" often pretend the popular option is secretly terrible. Playwright is not terrible. It has a clean API, useful auto-waiting, solid debugging tools, and support for Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

But a good framework can still be the wrong choice for a particular team.

Whether Playwright can click a button is rarely the problem. The problem is who will maintain the test six months from now, how much infrastructure the team wants to own, whether non-developers can contribute, and whether the testing scope includes real Safari, native mobile apps, APIs, accessibility, or visual regression.

This guide compares seven credible Playwright alternatives from that perspective.

## The quick answer

Here is the practical version before we get into the details:

| Tool | Best for | Coding required | Native mobile | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Endtest** | Teams that want fast creation and lower maintenance | Low or none | Yes | Less framework-level control |
| **Cypress** | Front-end teams and component testing | Yes, JavaScript or TypeScript | No | Different browser architecture and workflow constraints |
| **Selenium** | Maximum browser, language, and infrastructure flexibility | Yes | Through Appium | More engineering and maintenance work |
| **WebdriverIO** | JavaScript teams that also need mobile automation | Yes, JavaScript or TypeScript | Through Appium | Configuration and ecosystem complexity |
| **Puppeteer** | Chrome and Firefox automation close to browser internals | Yes, JavaScript or TypeScript | No | It is a browser automation library, not a complete QA platform |
| **Katalon** | Larger teams wanting no-code, low-code, and full-code options | Optional | Yes | A heavier platform and IDE experience |
| **TestCafe** | Straightforward JavaScript end-to-end testing | Yes, JavaScript or TypeScript | No | Smaller ecosystem and less momentum than the leading frameworks |

My overall recommendation is Endtest for teams trying to reduce the amount of test infrastructure and code they own, Cypress for front-end developers who care deeply about the local debugging experience, and Selenium for organizations that need maximum control or already have a mature WebDriver ecosystem.

## How I evaluated these Playwright alternatives

A testing tool should not be judged by how elegant the first login test looks.

Nearly every framework looks good in a ten-minute demo. The differences appear later, when the application changes, the suite reaches hundreds of tests, the original author moves to another project, and a failed CI run blocks a release.

I used seven criteria for this comparison:

1. Time to the first useful test
2. Long-term maintenance effort
3. Browser and platform coverage
4. Debugging and failure analysis
5. Accessibility to the wider QA and product team
6. CI/CD and parallel execution
7. Freedom to handle unusual workflows

These are editorial assessments, not laboratory benchmarks. There is no honest universal score for "maintainability" because the answer changes with the application, the team, and the quality of the implementation.

To make the tradeoffs easier to scan, the scores below use a five-point editorial scale. A higher score means a stronger general fit in that category, not a measured speed advantage.

| Tool | Fast setup | Lower maintenance | Platform coverage | Wider team access | Low-level control |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Endtest** | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 3 |
| **Cypress** | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| **Selenium** | 2 | 2 | 5 | 1 | 5 |
| **WebdriverIO** | 3 | 3 | 5 | 2 | 5 |
| **Puppeteer** | 4 | 3 | 3 | 1 | 5 |
| **Katalon** | 4 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 3 |
| **TestCafe** | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 4 |

There is also an important disclosure: I am the founder of Endtest, which is ranked first in this article. I know that creates an obvious conflict of interest. I have tried to handle it by making the selection criteria explicit, describing where Endtest is not the best fit, and recommending competing tools when they make more sense.

## 1. Endtest: best for reducing test maintenance

[Endtest](https://endtest.io/product) takes a different approach from Playwright.

Instead of giving your team another browser automation library, it provides a complete platform for creating, running, maintaining, and analyzing automated tests. Tests are represented as clear, editable steps rather than a large codebase that only automation engineers can safely modify.

You can create tests with a recorder, build them manually, or use the [AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) to turn a scenario into an executable test. The important part is that the result remains visible and editable. The AI is helping create the test, not hiding the test inside a black box.

Endtest also includes [self-healing tests](https://endtest.io/product/execute/self-healing-tests), cross-browser execution, visual testing, accessibility checks, API steps, email and SMS testing, CI/CD integrations, and native mobile testing.

### Why it is a strong Playwright alternative

Playwright can already automate a button click very well, so that is not where Endtest wins.

The advantage is that your team does not need to build and maintain the surrounding framework. There is no custom reporting layer to assemble, no browser grid to operate, no retry system to invent, and no internal abstraction library that gradually becomes the responsibility of one person.

That changes the economics of test automation.

A Playwright project may have no license fee, but it is not free. The cost shows up in engineering time, framework maintenance, CI infrastructure, code reviews, flaky-test investigations, and the opportunity cost of pulling developers away from product work.

Endtest is strongest when the team wants automated testing to be a shared operational capability rather than a software project inside the software project.

### Where Endtest is weaker

A platform cannot offer the same degree of low-level control as a general-purpose code framework.

A senior automation engineer who wants to build custom fixtures, intercept unusual browser behavior, create deeply specialized abstractions, or control every detail of the runtime may prefer Playwright, Selenium, or WebdriverIO.

Endtest is also a commercial product. Teams that have more engineering time than budget, and enjoy owning their testing infrastructure, may prefer an open-source framework.

### Best fit

Choose Endtest when:

- Test maintenance is consuming too much engineering time.
- Manual testers and product specialists need to contribute.
- You want web, mobile, API, visual, and accessibility testing in one place.
- You need real cross-browser execution without maintaining the infrastructure.
- You care more about reliable coverage than framework customization.

You can review the current [Endtest pricing](https://endtest.io/pricing) before comparing the subscription cost with the engineering cost of an internal framework.

## 2. Cypress: best for front-end developer experience

[Cypress](https://www.cypress.io/) became popular for a good reason: it made browser testing feel approachable to front-end developers.

Its interactive runner, automatic reloading, command log, screenshots, videos, and time-travel-style debugging create a tight feedback loop. When a test fails locally, the path from "something broke" to "I understand why" is often pleasantly short.

Cypress is especially compelling for component testing. Teams working heavily with React, Vue, Angular, or other front-end frameworks can mount components in a real browser and test them without running the entire application.

### Why it can be better than Playwright

For a front-end team that wants component and end-to-end testing to feel like part of the normal development workflow, Cypress remains one of the strongest choices.

Its conventions can also be an advantage. Playwright gives developers considerable freedom, which is useful, but that freedom can produce inconsistent patterns across a larger organization. Cypress encourages a more recognizable structure.

The product has also expanded beyond its original open-source runner with cloud reporting, test recording, orchestration, and AI-assisted capabilities.

### Where Cypress is weaker

Cypress has architectural constraints that can matter in unusual workflows. Multi-tab and multi-browser scenarios do not map as naturally as they do in tools designed around multiple independent browser sessions.

It is also primarily a web testing tool. It can test responsive web applications, but it is not a native mobile application automation solution.

Teams should also separate the experience of running Cypress locally from the complete cost of operating it at scale. Parallelization, analytics, recording, and team collaboration may involve paid cloud services or additional infrastructure.

### Best fit

Choose Cypress when:

- The test authors are primarily JavaScript or TypeScript developers.
- Component testing is a major requirement.
- Fast local feedback and visual debugging are top priorities.
- Your workflows fit comfortably within Cypress's browser model.
- Native mobile testing is outside the scope.

## 3. Selenium: best for maximum flexibility

[Selenium](https://www.selenium.dev/) is still the reference point for browser automation.

It supports several programming languages, works with the major browsers through the W3C WebDriver standard, and can run locally, through Selenium Grid, or through almost every major cloud testing provider.

Playwright feels more modern out of the box. Selenium feels more universal.

That distinction matters.

### Why it can be better than Playwright

Selenium is the safer choice when browser automation must fit into an existing Java, C#, Python, Ruby, or JavaScript environment. It is also attractive when an organization already has a large WebDriver suite, internal libraries, experienced engineers, and established grid infrastructure.

Its ecosystem is enormous. When a team encounters an obscure browser, proxy, authentication, enterprise policy, or legacy application problem, there is a reasonable chance that someone has solved a similar issue before.

Selenium also gives teams a high degree of control over architecture. You can choose the test runner, assertion library, reporting system, design patterns, cloud provider, and deployment model.

### Where Selenium is weaker

The freedom is also the cost.

Selenium is not a complete testing platform. It automates browsers. Your team still needs to decide how tests are structured, how waits are handled, how data is managed, how failures are reported, how screenshots and videos are stored, how parallel runs are coordinated, and how flaky tests are investigated.

A disciplined team can build an excellent Selenium framework. Many teams, however, build an internal framework that is permanently "almost finished."

That is why Selenium can be both the most flexible option and the most expensive option, depending on who maintains it.

### Best fit

Choose Selenium when:

- You need a language other than JavaScript or TypeScript.
- You have a significant existing WebDriver investment.
- Legacy browser or enterprise compatibility matters.
- Your team wants full control over the automation architecture.
- You have engineers dedicated to maintaining the framework and infrastructure.

For a more direct comparison, see [Playwright vs Selenium in 2026](https://endtest.io/blog/playwright-vs-selenium-2026).

## 4. WebdriverIO: best for JavaScript teams spanning web and mobile

[WebdriverIO](https://webdriver.io/) occupies a useful middle ground.

It gives JavaScript and TypeScript teams a modern test runner and a large plugin ecosystem while retaining compatibility with WebDriver-based browser automation. It can also work with Appium for native and hybrid mobile applications.

That makes it a practical option for teams that like Playwright's developer-oriented approach but need broader automation targets.

### Why it can be better than Playwright

The clearest advantage is scope.

WebdriverIO can automate modern web applications, native and hybrid mobile applications through Appium, Electron desktop applications, and browser-based components. It also supports multi-remote scenarios, which are useful for chat applications, video calls, multiplayer workflows, and tests involving two simultaneous users.

The framework is highly extensible. Reporters, services, integrations, and test frameworks can be assembled around the runner without starting completely from scratch.

### Where WebdriverIO is weaker

Flexibility creates configuration.

A WebdriverIO project can accumulate services, capabilities, plugins, cloud-provider settings, Appium configuration, hooks, reporters, and environment-specific logic. Experienced teams may see that as healthy modularity. Smaller teams may see another framework they have to understand and maintain.

Mobile support also does not remove the underlying Appium complexity. Device setup, platform tools, drivers, signing, emulators, simulators, and real-device infrastructure still need attention.

### Best fit

Choose WebdriverIO when:

- Your team is comfortable with JavaScript or TypeScript.
- Web and native mobile automation should share one ecosystem.
- Multi-user or multi-browser sessions are important.
- You want a framework rather than a managed platform.
- Your team is prepared to own configuration and infrastructure.

## 5. Puppeteer: best for browser automation close to Chrome

[Puppeteer](https://pptr.dev/) is a browser automation library maintained by the Chrome team. It controls Chrome and Firefox through the Chrome DevTools Protocol or WebDriver BiDi.

It is often compared with Playwright because the APIs feel familiar and both tools can automate modern browsers. But they are not identical products.

Playwright is designed as a complete end-to-end testing framework. Puppeteer is a focused browser automation library.

### Why it can be better than Playwright

Puppeteer is excellent when the task is close to the browser itself.

It is a natural fit for generating PDFs, taking screenshots, crawling pages, testing Chrome extensions, collecting performance data, automating DevTools-related workflows, or building a custom browser automation service.

The smaller conceptual surface can also be appealing. Teams that do not need a full test runner may prefer using Puppeteer as a building block inside their own system.

### Where Puppeteer is weaker

For a conventional cross-browser QA program, Playwright usually provides more out of the box.

With Puppeteer, teams may need to select or build the surrounding test runner, assertion library, fixtures, reporting, retries, parallelization, test management, and cloud execution. Firefox support exists, but Puppeteer remains closely associated with Chrome-centric automation.

It is also not a native mobile testing framework.

### Best fit

Choose Puppeteer when:

- Chrome-focused automation is the main requirement.
- You are building a custom browser automation product or service.
- PDF generation, screenshots, crawling, or performance instrumentation matters.
- You want a library rather than an opinionated test platform.
- Your use case is broader than software testing alone.

## 6. Katalon: best for organizations wanting multiple authoring modes

[Katalon](https://katalon.com/) combines no-code, low-code, and full-code testing in a desktop IDE and a broader cloud platform.

It covers web, mobile, API, and desktop testing. That breadth makes it attractive to larger QA organizations that do not want separate authoring tools for every test type.

### Why it can be better than Playwright

Katalon provides more structure around the complete testing lifecycle.

Teams can record tests, work with keyword-driven steps, add custom code, manage test objects, connect tests to cloud execution, and use built-in reporting and analytics. This can be easier to standardize across a mixed team than a collection of independent Playwright repositories.

It also supports native mobile testing and API testing, areas where Playwright alone is not a complete replacement for Appium or a dedicated API tool.

### Where Katalon is weaker

Katalon is a heavier environment than a code-first framework.

Developers who prefer a lightweight editor, plain source files, and direct control over every dependency may find the IDE and platform model restrictive. Teams should also examine which capabilities are included in each plan, especially when execution volume and collaboration grow.

The keyword-driven approach can become verbose if tests are not designed carefully. Low-code does not automatically mean low-maintenance.

### Best fit

Choose Katalon when:

- A mixed-skill QA team needs no-code, low-code, and scripted options.
- Web, API, mobile, and desktop testing should live in one ecosystem.
- Central governance and reporting matter.
- A desktop IDE fits the team's workflow.
- The organization prefers a commercial platform with broad coverage.

## 7. TestCafe: best for straightforward JavaScript web testing

[TestCafe](https://testcafe.io/) is an open-source end-to-end testing framework for JavaScript and TypeScript.

It supports the major desktop browsers and offers a relatively direct test authoring experience. The framework handles common browser interactions, screenshots, iframes, multiple windows, HTTP requests, and debugging without requiring teams to assemble every basic capability themselves.

### Why it can be better than Playwright

TestCafe can be appealing to teams that value simplicity and already have working TestCafe knowledge or suites.

The API is readable, the setup is approachable, and broad browser support is available without exposing developers to the lower-level WebDriver experience. For a modest web application and a small team, that may be enough.

Not every project needs the framework with the most features or the most online attention. A stable, understood tool can be worth more than a fashionable migration.

### Where TestCafe is weaker

The main concern is ecosystem momentum.

Playwright and Cypress currently receive more attention from many modern front-end and test automation teams. That affects community examples, third-party integrations, hiring, and the likelihood that new team members already know the tool.

TestCafe is also focused on web testing rather than native mobile applications. Teams with ambitious cross-platform requirements will likely need additional tooling.

### Best fit

Choose TestCafe when:

- You already have a productive TestCafe suite.
- The application is primarily web-based.
- The team wants a readable JavaScript or TypeScript framework.
- Simplicity matters more than having the newest ecosystem.
- There is no strong business reason to migrate.

## Which Playwright alternative should you choose?

The answer depends less on browser support than most comparison pages suggest.

Most serious tools can automate a login form. The harder question is what your organization wants to own.

### Choose Endtest if maintenance is the bottleneck

Endtest is the strongest alternative when the team wants coverage without turning test automation into another internal software product.

It is particularly useful when manual testers, product managers, support engineers, or other non-developers should be able to understand and contribute to tests.

### Choose Cypress if the front-end workflow is the center of gravity

Cypress is a strong choice for developer-led front-end testing, particularly when component testing and interactive local debugging are important.

### Choose Selenium if control and compatibility matter most

Selenium remains difficult to beat for language choice, ecosystem size, legacy compatibility, and infrastructure freedom.

Just enter that relationship with open eyes. Your team is choosing to own more of the system.

### Choose WebdriverIO if JavaScript and mobile must coexist

WebdriverIO is a practical framework for teams that want a modern JavaScript experience while retaining access to WebDriver, Appium, and multi-remote automation.

### Choose Puppeteer for browser automation products and Chrome-heavy workflows

Puppeteer is often the better building block when the goal is to create a custom automation service around the browser rather than to run an end-to-end test suite.

### Choose Katalon for a broad enterprise QA platform

Katalon makes sense when a larger organization wants multiple authoring modes and support for web, mobile, API, and desktop testing inside one commercial ecosystem.

### Choose TestCafe when it already works

A migration should solve a business problem. "Another framework is more popular" is usually not enough.

If TestCafe is producing reliable feedback at a reasonable maintenance cost, continuing to use it may be the most rational decision.

## When should you stay with Playwright?

An alternatives article should also tell you when not to switch.

Stay with Playwright when:

- The suite is reliable and maintenance is under control.
- The team is comfortable with JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, or .NET.
- Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit coverage meets your needs.
- Developers own the tests and actively contribute to them.
- The existing fixtures, reporting, CI setup, and debugging workflow work well.
- A migration would consume more time than it could realistically save.

Framework migrations are frequently underestimated.

The first ten tests are rewritten quickly, which creates optimism. Then the team reaches authentication helpers, data factories, visual baselines, file downloads, email confirmation, role-based access, third-party integrations, environment management, and the strange test that has been failing only on Fridays since 2023.

The old framework was carrying more institutional knowledge than anyone realized.

Switch when the current model is imposing a real cost, not because a comparison table gave another tool half a point more.

## Final verdict

Playwright is one of the best code-first testing frameworks available. Replacing it only makes sense when you need a different operating model.

For teams that want to reduce test code, infrastructure, and maintenance, Endtest is the best overall Playwright alternative.

For front-end developers, Cypress offers an excellent authoring and debugging experience.

For maximum control and compatibility, Selenium remains the most flexible option.

For JavaScript teams combining web and mobile automation, WebdriverIO deserves serious consideration.

For browser-centric automation products, Puppeteer is a focused and capable building block.

For larger mixed-skill QA organizations, Katalon provides broad platform coverage.

And for teams already succeeding with it, TestCafe may be a better business decision than an unnecessary migration.

The best tool is the one your team can still understand, maintain, and trust after the original excitement has worn off, not the one with the nicest five-line example.

# 5 Underrated Tools for Software Teams

Practical picks including Archbee, Bunnyshell, Pentest-Tools, Doppler, and Svix for docs, environments, security, secrets, and webhooks.

Published June 10, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/5-underrated-tools-for-software-teams

---
Most software teams already know the obvious tools: GitHub, Jira, Slack, Notion, the big cloud providers. They probably have too many dashboards, too many alerts, and at least one spreadsheet that everyone pretends is "temporary".

Some of the most useful tools never try to become the center of your entire company. They solve one painful problem really well.

The kind of tool where, after a few weeks, someone on the team says:

"Wait, why weren't we doing this before?"

Here are five underrated tools worth trying if your team builds, ships, documents, secures, or integrates software products.

## 1. Archbee

[Archbee](https://www.archbee.com/) is a documentation and knowledge base platform built for product and engineering teams.

Documentation is one of those things that every team says is important, but very few teams actually enjoy maintaining. The usual pattern is familiar: docs start clean, then product changes, APIs change, onboarding changes, and six months later nobody is sure which page is still accurate.

Archbee is interesting because it is built around structured product documentation, developer guides, API references, user guides, and internal knowledge, instead of being one more place to dump text. That makes it useful for teams that need docs to be more than a company wiki.

Where it can help:

* Product documentation for customers
* Internal engineering documentation
* API guides and technical references
* Onboarding docs for new team members
* Support articles that reduce repeated questions

The underrated part is that better docs also reduce interruptions inside the team: fewer repeated Slack questions, fewer "where is that written?" moments, fewer cases where only one person knows how something works.

Good documentation is not glamorous, but it compounds.

## 2. Bunnyshell

[Bunnyshell](https://www.bunnyshell.com/) focuses on Environments as a Service, which is a practical way of saying: your team can spin up production-like environments without fighting over staging.

This is a real problem for growing software teams.

At first, one shared staging environment seems fine. Then more developers join. More features are in progress. QA needs to test something. Product wants to review a flow. Sales needs a demo. Someone deploys over someone else's work. Suddenly, staging becomes less like a testing environment and more like a small battlefield.

Bunnyshell is useful because it helps teams create preview and ephemeral environments, often tied to pull requests. That gives developers, testers, and product people isolated spaces where they can review changes without stepping on each other.

Where it can help:

* Preview environments for pull requests
* Reducing staging conflicts
* Testing full-stack changes before merge
* Giving product and QA a realistic place to review work
* Making environment creation less dependent on DevOps tickets

This is especially useful for teams where the application has multiple services, databases, workers, queues, or integrations. The more complex the product gets, the more clean environments matter.

## 3. Pentest-Tools.com

[Pentest-Tools.com](https://pentest-tools.com/) is a security testing platform for vulnerability scanning, attack surface discovery, and penetration testing workflows.

A lot of teams treat security as something that happens late. Maybe before an enterprise deal, or a compliance audit, or after a customer asks for a security questionnaire.

That approach usually creates stress.

Pentest-Tools.com is useful because it makes security testing more accessible and repeatable. It gives teams a way to scan websites, networks, and exposed assets, then prioritize issues based on actual risk.

Where it can help:

* Website vulnerability scanning
* Network vulnerability scanning
* Attack surface discovery
* Security checks before major releases
* Preparing evidence for security reviews or reports

A tool like this does not replace a professional pentest. But it can help teams find obvious problems earlier, keep track of exposed assets, and avoid treating security as a once-per-year panic exercise.

For software teams, that is already a big improvement.

## 4. Doppler

[Doppler](https://www.doppler.com/) is a secrets management platform.

This is one of those categories that sounds boring until you have a real problem.

API keys in `.env` files. Shared credentials in Slack. Old secrets that nobody rotated. Different values across local, staging, and production. A developer leaving the company while still having access to things they should not have anymore.

Every software team eventually has to deal with secrets properly. Doppler gives teams a cleaner way to manage API keys, tokens, database passwords, environment variables, and other sensitive values across projects and environments.

Where it can help:

* Centralizing secrets across environments
* Managing local, staging, and production values
* Reducing secrets shared through Slack or spreadsheets
* Syncing secrets with CI/CD and infrastructure
* Improving visibility and access control

The nice thing about a good secrets workflow is that it protects the team without slowing everyone down too much. Developers still need fast access to the right values. Security still needs control. Doppler sits in that middle ground.

It is not the flashiest tool on the list, but it solves a problem that becomes painful very quickly.

## 5. Svix

[Svix](https://www.svix.com/) is webhook infrastructure for software products.

Webhooks seem simple at first.

You send an HTTP request when something happens. Done.

Then reality appears.

Customer endpoints are down. Retries need to be handled. Delivery attempts need to be logged. Events need to be signed. Users want replay functionality. Support needs to debug why a webhook did not arrive. Enterprise customers want reliability, security, and visibility.

Suddenly, "just send a webhook" becomes an entire product area.

Svix helps teams avoid building all of that from scratch. It provides infrastructure for sending webhooks reliably, with features around delivery, retries, security, and customer-facing webhook management.

Where it can help:

* Adding webhooks to a SaaS product
* Managing retries and failed deliveries
* Giving customers better webhook visibility
* Improving webhook security
* Avoiding custom internal webhook infrastructure

This is a good example of a tool that solves a hidden engineering problem. Your customers may not care what webhook infrastructure you use, but they will definitely care if integrations are unreliable.

## How to think about tools like these

The best tools remove recurring pain instead of adding another dashboard.

Archbee helps when knowledge is scattered. Bunnyshell helps when environments slow everyone down. Pentest-Tools.com helps when security testing is too late or too manual. Doppler helps when secrets are spread across too many places. Svix helps when webhooks become more serious than expected.

That is also a useful way to evaluate any software team tool:

* Does it remove a real bottleneck?
* Does it make the team faster without hiding too much?
* Does it reduce repeated manual work?
* Does it improve reliability, security, or collaboration?
* Would the team still care about it after the demo?

A lot of tools look good in a demo. Fewer tools stay useful after three months of real usage.

If your team is also evaluating test automation tools, you can review the [Endtest pricing](https://endtest.io/pricing) page to see how a no-code testing platform fits into the broader engineering stack.

## Final thoughts

None of these tools are mandatory.

A small team can survive with basic docs, one staging environment, manual security checks, `.env` files, and custom webhook logic.

But as the product grows, those shortcuts become expensive.

The best time to improve these workflows is before they become emergencies. That does not mean buying every tool immediately. Know what is available, try the tools that match your current bottlenecks, and be honest about what your team is repeatedly wasting time on.

# Affordable AI Test Automation

A practical look at AI test automation costs, from Playwright and Selenium maintenance to predictable pricing and unlimited AI in Endtest.

Published June 10, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/affordable-ai-test-automation

---
The most affordable way to automate tests with AI is not always the option with the lowest starting price.

That sounds obvious, but it is easy to forget when you are comparing tools.

A free open-source library looks cheap. A shiny AI assistant looks cheap. A vendor that says "contact sales" might look expensive, but maybe you assume there is a startup discount hiding somewhere.

The real cost usually shows up later.

It shows up when the framework needs maintenance. When only one person understands the setup. When the AI-generated code breaks after a UI change. When the team stops contributing tests because every small change feels like touching a fragile internal codebase. When cloud execution costs grow faster than expected.

AI did change a lot about test automation.

But it did not magically remove the boring parts.

## Free libraries are not free

Playwright and Selenium are excellent tools.

They are also free in the same way that a free puppy is free.

You do not pay a license fee, but you still pay for everything around it. Someone needs to design the framework. Someone needs to write the tests. Someone needs to review flaky failures. Someone needs to fix locators. Someone needs to maintain test data, retries, reporting, screenshots, video recording, browser versions, parallel execution, CI/CD integration, and environment issues.

That "someone" has a salary.

And their time has an opportunity cost.

Every week spent maintaining a custom automation framework is a week not spent testing important flows, improving product quality, or shipping customer-facing features.

This is where teams often miscalculate. They compare a paid testing platform against the monthly cost of Playwright, which is zero. But that is the wrong comparison.

The real comparison is:

* How much time will the team spend building and maintaining the automation layer?
* How many people will actually be able to contribute?
* How quickly can new tests be created and updated?
* How much debugging will be required when something breaks?
* How much infrastructure is needed to run tests reliably?
* What happens when the original framework owner moves to another project?

Those are the costs that matter.

## AI did not make code maintenance disappear

There is a popular idea that AI fixes the old Selenium and Playwright maintenance problem.

The thinking goes like this:

"Sure, maintaining test code was hard before, but now AI can write and update it."

Sometimes that is true.

For small examples, simple pages, and controlled demos, AI can generate useful code. It can create a Playwright test, explain an error, rewrite a selector, or add assertions.

AI can write code. The long-term problem is that the output is still code.

That means it still needs to live somewhere. It still needs structure, conventions, review, and debugging. It still needs to fit into the rest of your framework.

And when the app changes, the AI needs context.

It needs to process the test file. Maybe helper files, page objects, fixtures, and custom commands. Maybe CI logs and screenshots. Maybe the DOM. Maybe the product requirement. Maybe the previous attempt that failed.

The bigger the framework gets, the more context the AI needs. More context means more tokens, more time, more cost, and more chances for the AI to misunderstand something.

So yes, AI can help with test code.

But if your entire strategy is "we will generate a lot of Playwright code and ask AI to maintain it forever," you are still signing up to maintain a codebase.

Just with a more expensive autocomplete.

## Internal frameworks have a gravity problem

Most internal test automation frameworks start with good intentions.

A senior engineer or QA automation engineer builds a clean architecture. There are page objects, helpers, fixtures, custom commands, environment configs, naming conventions, maybe a nice README.

At the beginning, it looks professional.

Then the team grows. The product changes. New flows get added. Edge cases appear. People copy and paste old tests because they are not sure how the framework works. A few abstractions become too clever. A few helpers get overloaded. The original design no longer matches the product.

Eventually, contributing a test feels like contributing to another application.

That is when adoption drops.

Developers avoid it because they do not want to learn the internal testing framework. Product people cannot use it. Manual testers may not feel comfortable editing code. QA automation people become the bottleneck. And the whole thing starts to depend on a small number of people who understand the magic.

This has nothing to do with intelligence. Internal tools age this way.

The more complex the framework becomes, the fewer people want to touch it.

That is a bad place to be, because test automation only works long term when the team actually uses it.

## Pasting files into an AI chat is not a workflow

Another tempting shortcut is to keep the existing codebase and use a general AI chat as the maintenance layer.

You paste a test file. You paste an error. You ask it to fix the issue. Then you paste another file. Then a screenshot. Then the helper. Then the config. Then the logs.

This can work once or twice.

It does not scale well.

The context gets messy. The AI does not always know which files matter. It may fix the symptom instead of the test design. It may create code that looks correct but does not follow your framework. And the person using the chat becomes the glue holding the whole process together.

That is manual work with a chatbot in the middle, not automation.

AI is much more useful when it is built into the testing workflow itself, where it has access to the right test structure, the right execution data, and the right maintenance path.

## Beware of mysterious pricing

There is another side of the market that teams should be careful with: very expensive AI testing platforms with vague pricing.

Not every company that hides pricing is doing something bad. Enterprise sales can be complicated. Large customers need custom contracts, procurement, legal review, security review, and support terms.

But if you are a normal software team and the pricing page tells you almost nothing, you should at least be cautious.

Some heavily funded companies are under pressure to grow revenue quickly. That pressure often turns into expensive contracts, usage-based surprises, or plans that look reasonable until you need the features that actually matter.

AI can make this worse because token usage, cloud execution, premium features, and parallel runs can all become pricing levers.

The risk is that your team starts using a tool, builds part of the testing workflow around it, and only later realizes that the real cost is much higher than expected.

A good testing solution should not make you nervous every time someone creates more tests.

## Cloud execution has real costs too

Running automated tests in the cloud is incredibly useful.

You get parallel execution. You get different browsers. You get more reliable infrastructure than someone's laptop. You can run tests from CI/CD. You can collect screenshots, videos, logs, and reports.

But cloud testing is not free.

Browser sessions consume infrastructure. Parallel execution consumes infrastructure. Real operating systems, real browsers, and longer test suites all add cost.

The alternative is not free either.

Maintaining your own cloud infrastructure means dealing with machines, browser versions, drivers, scaling, crashes, queues, storage, networking, security, and monitoring. That takes time. And the people maintaining that infrastructure are usually not cheap.

So again, "can we do this ourselves?" is the wrong question.

Of course you can.

The question is whether doing it yourself is the best use of your team's time.

## Unit tests are not enough

Some teams try to control cost by reducing the problem.

They say:

"We will rely mostly on unit tests and component tests."

That is reasonable to a point. Unit tests and component tests are worth having. They are fast, cheap to run, and great for checking isolated logic.

But they do not replace functional end-to-end testing.

They do not prove that a real user can sign up, verify an email, complete onboarding, invite a teammate, make a payment, or recover from an error state.

A product can have excellent unit test coverage and still fail in production because two systems did not work together.

That is why functional testing matters.

Not every tiny thing needs an end-to-end test.

But the critical user journeys need to be tested the way users actually experience them. Otherwise, the cost moves somewhere else: support tickets, churn, emergency fixes, broken releases, and lost trust.

## What "affordable" really means

The affordable solution is the one that gives you the best outcome for the total cost, not the one with the lowest single line item.

That means:

* Tests are easy to create
* Tests are easy to maintain
* The whole team can contribute
* Execution is reliable
* AI helps without creating token anxiety
* Pricing is predictable
* The tool does not require a second internal tool to manage the first tool

This is the part that matters most.

A testing tool should reduce the amount of test automation work your team has to do. It should not move that work somewhere else.

If the tool gives you AI, but you still spend your week feeding it files, reviewing generated code, fixing framework abstractions, and worrying about usage limits, the cost is still there.

It just has a different shape.

## Why we built Endtest this way

[Endtest](https://endtest.io/) has been around for almost 10 years.

We have seen a lot of test automation trends come and go. Selenium frameworks. Cypress frameworks. Playwright frameworks. Recorders. Self-healing. Low-code tools. No-code tools. AI agents. AI-generated test code.

The pattern is usually the same.

The demo looks easy.

The real question is whether the team can keep using it after the first month, the first product redesign, the first flaky release, and the first person who built the setup moving on to something else.

Our philosophy has always been simple: test automation should be powerful enough for serious teams, but affordable and approachable enough that people actually use it.

That is why Endtest focuses on making tests easy to create, easy to maintain, and easy to run across browsers and environments without requiring teams to build and maintain their own automation infrastructure.

It is also why we offer [Unlimited AI](https://endtest.io/pricing).

We do not want teams thinking about token consumption every time they create or update a test. That is the wrong thing to optimize for.

The goal is to test the flows that matter, catch real bugs, and give the team confidence before every release.

## The bottom line

AI test automation can be affordable.

But only if you look beyond the obvious price tag.

A free framework, a code-generating AI workflow, a cloud setup, and a vendor with vague pricing can all become expensive. So can skipping end-to-end tests, just in a way that shows up later.

The best approach is usually the practical one.

Use a tool that your team can actually adopt. Make maintenance easy. Avoid overcomplicated internal frameworks. Keep costs predictable. Use AI where it removes work instead of creating more of it.

That is the kind of test automation that stays affordable after the demo is over.

# Manual Testing Is Still a Great Career

Manual testing is still a strong career path because it connects product, users, business context, and intelligent no-code automation.

Published June 5, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/manual-tester-career-option

---
A lot of people in software testing are being told the same thing: manual testing is going away, everything will be automated, and if you do not become an SDET, Test Automation Engineer, or AI-Powered Test Automation Architect, you will be left behind.

That sounds convincing at first.

After all, automation is everywhere. AI is writing code. Testing tools are becoming smarter. Companies want faster releases. Nobody wants to manually repeat the same regression checklist every sprint.

But the conclusion is wrong.

Manual testing is not a dead-end career.

In many companies, being a strong manual tester can actually give you a better long-term career path than becoming a narrow test automation specialist.

Automation is incredibly valuable. But the most valuable people in a software company are not always the ones who write the most code. They are the ones who understand the product, the customer, the business process, the risks, the edge cases, and the places where everything can quietly fall apart.

That is exactly where a great manual tester can become irreplaceable.

## The problem with the "everything will be automated" mindset

There is a simple version of the future that sounds something like this:

Developers write the product.
Automation engineers write the tests.
Manual testers disappear.

But real software teams do not work like that.

Real products are messy. Real users behave unpredictably. Real business flows have exceptions, permissions, old data, partial migrations, third-party integrations, strange browser behavior, and confusing UX decisions that technically "work" but still create frustration.

A script can check whether a button exists.

A manual tester can notice that the button is in the wrong place, appears at the wrong moment, uses confusing wording, creates anxiety for the user, or sends someone into a workflow that technically passes but practically fails.

That difference matters.

Manual testing is product investigation, not clicking buttons.

It is the act of putting yourself in the shoes of the user and asking: would this make sense to a real person? Could someone misunderstand this? What happens if the user has incomplete data, or is in a hurry, or does something slightly unexpected but completely reasonable? What happens if this flow works technically, but feels broken emotionally?

That is not something you fully automate.

## Manual testing is closer to the business than most people realize

One of the biggest advantages of manual testing is that it naturally sits between the technical side and the business side.

A good manual tester talks to developers, product owners, support teams, implementation teams, and sometimes even customers. They understand how the product is supposed to work, how it actually works, and where the gap appears.

That position is extremely valuable.

Developers often know their own area very deeply. They may understand the billing service, the authentication module, the frontend component library, or the API they maintain.

But manual testers often understand the full journey.

They know what happens before the user reaches that screen. They know what happens after the user clicks the button. They know which systems are connected. They know which customer scenarios are common. They know which "small" bug will create a huge support problem.

At a previous job where I worked as a manual tester, our QA team also handled second-level support for people inside the organization. We were the ones who understood how all the systems connected together, technically and from a business perspective.

A developer might have known one service better than anyone else. But the testers knew the end-to-end flow. They knew how data moved from one system to another. They knew which department used which feature. They knew which workaround people were using when the software did not behave as expected.

That kind of knowledge is business-critical, not junior work.

## The awkward position of some test automation specialists

Moving from manual testing to test automation does not automatically make your career safer.

In some companies, it can place you in an awkward middle position.

You are in a highly technical role, but you may not be as technically fluent or flexible as your developer colleagues. You write code, but often inside a narrow testing stack. You may spend most of your time in Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, Appium, or a custom internal framework.

From the outside, executives may struggle to understand the value of that role.

And when companies start cutting costs, that can become dangerous.

A high-level manager might look at a test automation specialist and think:

This person is not building product features, not fixing production issues, not talking to customers, and not driving product strategy. They are maintaining tests.

That is not always fair, but it happens.

From the R&D side, some test automation engineers can also be seen unfairly as "somewhat like a junior developer, but only knows one library: Playwright or Selenium."

Again, that is not a fair description of a good automation engineer.

But if the automation work is isolated from product impact, business context, and team adoption, the perception can become a real problem.

This is one reason why we are seeing so many SDETs, Test Automation Architects, and AI-Powered Test Automation Engineers with the #OpenToWork badge on LinkedIn.

That is not because they lack intelligence. Many of them are very smart.

The problem is that executives often have a hard time understanding the business value of a role that sits somewhere between QA and development, especially when the output is a test framework that is always "almost done."

## The internal framework trap

A common story in software teams looks like this:

The company decides that manual regression testing takes too long. Someone proposes building an internal Playwright or Selenium framework. A few technical QA people start building it. The first demo looks great. The framework can log in, click around, run in CI, generate reports, and maybe even record a video. Everyone is impressed.

Then reality starts.

The application changes. Selectors break. Test data becomes difficult to manage. Developers do not contribute because they do not want to learn another internal framework. Manual testers do not contribute because the tests are too technical. Product owners cannot read the tests. The automation team becomes a bottleneck. The framework needs more abstractions, more helpers, more utilities, more documentation, more maintenance.

Two years later, the framework is still in a constant state of "almost done." And the company quietly realizes that it has not really solved the testing problem. It has created another codebase to maintain.

This is the old-school test automation problem. The goal was to reduce manual effort, but the result was often a private engineering project that only a few people understood.

## Manual testers should not feel inferior because they do not write code

A lot of manual testers feel pressure to move into automation because they believe that writing code makes them more valuable.

They want to feel equal to developers.

They want to be able to say:

I also write code.

That feeling is understandable.

Software companies often reward technical confidence. Developers usually have higher status. Automation roles sound more modern. Manual testing can sometimes be unfairly treated as basic work.

But the conclusion is wrong.

A manual tester is not less valuable because they do not write code.

In many organizations, a strong manual tester can be more valuable than another developer because they understand the product from a wider angle.

They understand the flows, the users, and what the business is trying to achieve. They understand enough of the technical side to know where things might break, without being trapped inside one technical implementation. They can see the whole picture. That is rare.

And the more complex a product becomes, the more valuable that perspective becomes.

## Manual testing is not repetitive clicking

Bad manual testing is repetitive clicking. Good manual testing is thinking. There is a huge difference.

If your role is only to click the same button 10 times every release, then yes, that work should probably be automated.

But that is not what a great manual tester does.

A great manual tester explores. They compare the product against the user's intent. They notice awkward flows. They challenge assumptions. They ask uncomfortable questions. They discover what happens when a user is confused, distracted, impatient, or working with unusual data. They find issues that are hard to define in a test case, but obvious once you see them.

For example:

- The confirmation message appears, but it does not clearly explain what happened.
- The flow works, but it requires too many steps.
- The error message is technically correct, but useless to the user.
- The page loads, but the user has no idea what to do next.
- The feature works for a clean account, but fails for accounts with older data.
- The button is visible, but the user would not know when to use it.
- The happy path passes, but the real workflow feels fragile.

These are product quality issues, and exactly the type of issues that scripts usually miss.

## Manual testers have strong paths into better roles

One of the best arguments for manual testing as a career is that it can lead to many different roles.

A manual tester who understands the product deeply can move into:

- Product Owner
- Business Analyst
- UX Researcher
- Product Manager
- Customer Success
- Implementation Specialist
- QA Lead
- Release Manager
- Solutions Consultant
- Technical Support Lead
- Test Manager

These are strong career paths, not fallback options, and many of them can lead to even better roles later.

Manual testers already spend their time understanding how the product works, what users need, where confusion appears, and how different teams think about quality.

That experience transfers extremely well.

A developer might know the codebase better. But a manual tester may understand the product experience better. That is a powerful advantage.

## Automation is still important, but it should not be locked away

None of this means test automation is bad. Automation is essential for modern software teams.

But the way we approach automation matters.

The old model said automation belongs to technical specialists. They build the framework. Everyone else waits. That model is broken for many teams.

The better model says automation should be understandable by the entire team. Manual testers should be able to contribute. Developers should be able to review. Product owners should be able to understand what is being tested. QA should not be trapped behind a codebase that only one or two people can maintain.

This is where modern no-code and intelligent test automation tools have changed the situation completely.

With tools like [Endtest](https://endtest.io/), teams can create automated tests without having to build and maintain an internal Selenium or Playwright framework from scratch.

That matters because the problem with many internal frameworks was never only technical. The bigger problem was adoption. Nobody wanted to maintain another codebase. Nobody wanted to learn a custom test syntax. Nobody wanted to debug fragile helper functions created two years ago by someone who no longer works at the company.

No-code test automation removes many of those barriers. It allows manual testers, developers, and product owners to understand the tests and contribute to them.

## Intelligent no-code automation gives manual testers more power

The rise of intelligent no-code test automation tools has democratized automation. It has removed many of the gatekeepers and fences that used to separate "manual QA" from "automation QA."

In the past, a manual tester might have found a critical flow and then had to ask an automation engineer to automate it.

That created delays and translation problems. The manual tester understood the business risk. The automation engineer understood the framework. But the final test often ended up somewhere in the middle, shaped more by technical convenience than by product importance.

With intelligent tools, manual testers can participate directly. They can automate the flows they understand best. They can help decide what should be covered. They can review tests in a format that actually makes sense. They can maintain tests without becoming full-time framework engineers.

This is an upgrade of manual testing, not the end of it. The best manual testers will not be replaced by automation. They will use automation to remove the boring parts of their work, so they can spend more time on the valuable parts: exploration, risk analysis, user empathy, product understanding, business flows, edge cases, and quality strategy.

## The future is not manual versus automation

The debate is often framed as manual testing versus automation, manual testers versus SDETs, no-code versus code. That is not the right way to think about it. The real question is how the team produces better software with less waste.

Sometimes the answer is automation. Sometimes it is exploratory testing. Sometimes it is better requirements, or a product conversation, or a simple automated regression test that everyone can understand. And sometimes the answer is a manual tester saying: this works, but no real user will understand it.

That sentence can be more valuable than 500 passing automated tests.

## What manual testers should focus on today

If you are a manual tester, the best career move is not necessarily to rush into becoming a test automation engineer.

Instead, focus on becoming harder to replace.

That means developing skills that make you valuable across the entire product organization.

- Understand the business domain.
- Learn how users think.
- Learn basic technical concepts.
- Understand APIs, databases, browser behavior, logs, and integrations at a high level.
- Learn how to write clear bug reports.
- Learn how to explain risk.
- Learn how to talk to product owners.
- Learn how to challenge unclear requirements.
- Learn how to prioritize testing based on business impact.
- Learn how to use modern automation tools without turning yourself into a framework maintainer.

That combination is extremely powerful. You do not need to become a developer to be respected. You need to become someone who understands quality better than anyone else in the room.

## The companies that win will involve the entire team in testing

The best software teams do not treat testing as a department that receives work at the end. They treat quality as a shared responsibility. Developers write unit tests and review technical risks. Product owners clarify expected behavior. Manual testers explore the product and identify gaps. Automation tools cover the important repeatable flows. Support teams share real customer pain. Everyone contributes.

That is where intelligent test automation tools become especially useful. When tests are readable and maintainable, they become part of the team's shared understanding. They are no longer hidden inside a technical framework. They become living documentation of how the product is supposed to work.

Automation like that gives testers more power instead of replacing them.

## Manual testing is still a great career option

Being a manual tester is still a great career option because the core skill is understanding, not clicking. Understanding users, flows, risk, and the business. Understanding where the product can fail, not only technically, but practically.

A narrow automation role can sometimes become fragile if it is disconnected from business value. But a strong manual tester who understands the product deeply can become one of the most valuable people in the organization.

That person can move toward product, business analysis, UX, leadership, customer success, or quality strategy.

And with modern tools like Endtest, they can also participate in automation without needing to spend years building and maintaining a fragile internal framework.

Manual testing is evolving, not disappearing. The testers who understand both the human side of software and the power of intelligent automation will have some of the strongest careers in the industry.
