# What Is the Best AI Model for Test Automation?

Compare GPT, Claude, and specialized AI for test automation by speed, reliability, hallucinations, and cost before choosing a model.

Published May 20, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/best-ai-model-for-test-automation

---
Choosing the best AI model for test automation is not a matter of taste.

It should not be based on which chatbot gave the most impressive demo, which model is currently trending on social media, or a few prompts that worked well in a proof of concept.

The best AI model for test automation has to be measured.

And it has to be measured against the realities of software testing:

- Can it create useful automated tests quickly?
- Can it identify the right web elements?
- Can it understand element states?
- Can it choose reliable selectors?
- Can it avoid hallucinating actions, locators, assertions, or expected results?
- Can it maintain tests when the application changes?
- Can it do that at a cost that makes sense at scale?
- Can it produce output that humans can inspect, edit, and trust?

That last part matters.

A model can look impressive in a chatbot window and still be a poor fit for production-grade test automation.

## The best model depends on the task

There is no universal "best AI model" for every test automation task.

A model that is strong at writing long explanations may not be the best model for identifying the correct button in a complex DOM. A model that is good at generating Playwright code may not be the best model for self-healing a broken locator. A model that produces beautiful reasoning may be too slow or too expensive for repeated testing workflows.

Test automation breaks down into many smaller tasks:

| Task | What the AI needs to do well |
| --- | --- |
| Test creation | Understand intent and convert it into clear steps |
| Element detection | Find the right element from HTML, screenshots, and page context |
| Locator generation | Choose stable selectors that survive UI changes |
| Assertion generation | Verify the right outcome rather than any visible text |
| Test maintenance | Repair broken steps without changing the test intent |
| Visual validation | Detect meaningful visual issues without excessive noise |
| Variable extraction | Capture dynamic values from pages, emails, SMS messages, APIs, and files |
| Failure analysis | Explain failures without inventing root causes |

A general-purpose foundation model may perform well in some of these areas and poorly in others.

That is why "Which model is smartest?" is the wrong question. The useful question is "Which model performs best on the exact test automation task we need to solve?"

## How to measure the best AI model for test automation

A useful benchmark should evaluate several dimensions at the same time.

If you only measure accuracy, you may choose a model that is too slow or too expensive. If you only measure cost, you may choose a model that creates unreliable tests. If you only measure speed, you may choose a model that produces hallucinations.

A serious benchmark should include at least four dimensions.

## 1. Speed

Speed matters because test automation is an interactive workflow.

When a user asks AI to create a test, update a step, identify an element, or repair a locator, the answer should arrive quickly.

Slow AI changes behavior.

If the AI takes too long, users stop relying on it. They go back to manual work. Or worse, they accept a lower-quality result because waiting for another attempt is painful.

Speed also matters during maintenance. If a locator breaks and AI assistance takes too long, the test suite becomes slower to debug and harder to trust.

General foundation models can be powerful, but they are often built to support a very wide range of tasks: writing, coding, reasoning, summarization, translation, image understanding, planning, customer support, and more.

That breadth comes with overhead.

A specialized model that only needs to solve test automation problems can often be much faster because it is optimized for a narrower domain.

## 2. Reliability

Reliability is more important than raw intelligence.

In test automation, the AI does not need to write a poem, debate philosophy, or generate a complete business strategy. It needs to do specific things correctly and repeatedly.

For example:

- Click the correct "Sign in" button, not another button with similar text.
- Verify that checkout succeeded, not merely that the page changed.
- Extract the actual SMS code, not a random number nearby.
- Repair a locator without changing the business intent of the test.
- Avoid selecting elements that are hidden, disabled, covered, or irrelevant.

A reliable model should behave consistently across many similar tasks.

That is different from a model that occasionally gives an impressive answer.

For testing, consistency wins.

## 3. Hallucination rate

Hallucinations are especially dangerous in test automation.

In a normal chatbot conversation, a hallucination might produce a wrong explanation or an imaginary fact. That is bad, but the user can sometimes notice it.

In test automation, hallucinations can create false confidence.

The AI might:

- Invent a selector that does not exist.
- Click an element that looks plausible but is not the right one.
- Add an assertion that checks the wrong outcome.
- Claim that a test passed for the wrong reason.
- "Fix" a broken step by changing the test intent.
- Treat a visual issue as acceptable when it is actually a defect.
- Produce a false positive and allow a real bug to reach production.

That last risk matters.

If AI is directly involved in deciding whether a test passed during execution, and the AI hallucinates, the result becomes harder to trust.

A safer architecture is to use AI during creation, maintenance, assertions, visual analysis, and failure investigation, while keeping the actual execution deterministic whenever possible.

When a test runs, the system should follow clear steps and expected outcomes. AI should assist when something needs interpretation or repair, not casually reinterpret the test on every run.

## 4. Cost

Cost is not a secondary detail.

Most AI providers price API usage based on tokens, including input tokens and output tokens. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and DeepSeek all publish token-based API pricing for their models.

That matters because test automation can become token-heavy very quickly.

If you ask a general model to modify a Playwright test, it may need to process:

- The test file
- Page object files
- Shared fixtures
- Helper methods
- Configuration files
- Previous failure logs
- Screenshots or traces
- Related selectors
- Package files
- CI logs

Even a small change can require a large amount of context.

That is expensive.

And as test suites grow, the cost grows with them. More files, more prompts, more retries, more debugging sessions, more AI calls.

This is one of the reasons why AI-generated test code can become surprisingly expensive to maintain. The first few tests may be cheap. The full workflow around them may not be.

A specialized AI test automation system can be more efficient because it does not need to process an entire general-purpose codebase for every small testing task.

It can operate on structured test data, page information, element metadata, execution history, screenshots, and test steps in a more focused way.

That is a major difference.

## General foundation models are broad by design

Models like GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and other foundation models are broad AI systems.

They are designed to help with many categories of work:

- Writing
- Coding
- Summarization
- Translation
- Reasoning
- Customer support
- Data extraction
- Brainstorming
- Image understanding
- Research assistance
- Agentic workflows

That breadth is useful.

It is also the reason they are not always the best fit for test automation.

Test automation has its own domain-specific requirements. The model needs to understand web pages, DOM structures, element states, selectors, waits, assertions, browser differences, test data, execution context, and maintenance patterns.

A general model may know about these topics. But knowing about them is not the same as being optimized for them.

This is why a general model can sound confident while still making a poor testing decision.

It may choose a selector that is technically valid but unstable. It may prefer visible text when a more reliable attribute is available. It may click the wrong element because two buttons look similar. It may generate code that works for the demo but becomes difficult to maintain after a few months.

These models are not bad. They are not specialized enough for every testing task.

## Why general models often hallucinate in testing workflows

General foundation models are trained to predict useful responses across many contexts.

That makes them flexible, but it can also make them too willing to fill gaps.

In test automation, filling gaps is dangerous.

If a model does not have enough information, it should not invent a selector. If the page source does not contain an element, it should not pretend it exists. If a screenshot is ambiguous, it should not guess with high confidence. If the test intent is unclear, it should not silently change the scenario.

But general models are often optimized to be helpful and conversational. That can create problems.

You have probably seen this behavior already outside of testing. A generated article may look polished but feel generic. A generated image may look impressive at first glance but have obvious flaws. A generated email may sound fluent but not quite human. A generated answer may begin with "You're absolutely right" even when the situation is more nuanced.

That is a meme, but it is also a symptom of a model trying to be broadly helpful.

In test automation, broadly helpful is not enough.

A testing model needs to be precise, skeptical, and constrained.

It should prefer saying "I cannot determine the correct element from this information" over confidently choosing the wrong one.

## Would you fly in a plane piloted by a general chatbot?

This is a useful way to think about specialization.

A general foundation model may be impressive. It may write code, summarize documents, explain architecture, and generate test ideas.

But would you want a plane piloted by a general chatbot?

Probably not, and not because the chatbot is useless or general AI is unimpressive. Aviation requires systems designed, tested, constrained, certified, and optimized for aviation.

The same principle applies at a smaller scale in test automation.

You do not need the broadest possible model. You need the model and system that are best suited for the job.

In testing, the job is more specific than "generate a plausible answer":

- Understand the page.
- Understand the user intent.
- Select the right element.
- Create a maintainable test.
- Avoid false positives.
- Avoid false negatives.
- Keep execution reliable.
- Help humans trust the result.

That requires specialization.

## Why specialized AI is faster and more reliable

A specialized AI model is not necessarily "smarter" in every possible way.

It may not be better at writing poetry. It may not be better at summarizing legal documents. It may not be better at discussing history, finance, or philosophy.

But it can be better at test automation because it is optimized for test automation.

That is the important distinction.

Specialization improves the system in several ways.

## It reduces irrelevant reasoning

A general model has to consider many possible interpretations of a prompt. A specialized testing model can operate inside a narrower context.

If the task is to identify a button, generate a locator, or repair a test step, the model does not need to reason about every possible domain. It needs to reason about web automation.

That narrower scope can make the result faster and more consistent.

## It improves selector decisions

Reliable selectors are one of the most important details in test automation.

A bad selector may work today and fail tomorrow. A good selector can survive layout changes, text changes, and component updates.

A specialized testing model can be tuned to prefer selector strategies that work better in real automation scenarios.

For example, it can learn to avoid fragile paths, ignore irrelevant generated classes when better attributes exist, and consider element visibility, state, role, text, surrounding context, and prior execution history.

## It reduces hallucinations

A specialized model can be trained and constrained to behave differently from a general chatbot.

It can be designed to avoid inventing elements, selectors, or assertions. It can be taught to return uncertainty when the page context is insufficient. It can use structured inputs and outputs instead of free-form guesses.

That matters because test automation does not reward creativity in the same way as content generation.

It rewards correctness.

## It improves cost efficiency

A specialized model can often solve the task with less context and fewer tokens.

Instead of feeding a general model an entire repository, a specialized testing system can provide the exact information needed for the task:

- Relevant page structure
- Element candidates
- Screenshot context
- Test step history
- Previous successful locators
- Execution logs
- Known backup locators
- Assertion targets

That makes the AI workflow more efficient.

Which model is used matters, and so does how the system around the model is designed.

## The architecture matters as much as the model

Choosing the right AI model is only part of the equation.

The engineering around the model can give it superpowers, or it can make it slower, more expensive, and less reliable.

A weak architecture asks a general model to do everything.

A strong architecture gives the model the right context, the right constraints, the right tools, and the right output format.

For test automation, this includes:

- How the page source is processed
- How screenshots are interpreted
- How candidate elements are ranked
- How selectors are generated
- How element visibility and state are evaluated
- How prior executions are used
- How backup locators are stored
- How assertions are represented
- How AI output is validated
- How humans review and edit the result
- How deterministic execution is preserved

This is where many AI test automation experiments fail. They focus only on the model, when the full system is the product.

## The problem with using Claude to generate Playwright code

A common workflow today looks like this:

1. Ask Claude, GPT, or another model to generate a Playwright framework.
2. Store the generated code in GitHub.
3. Ask the model to add more tests.
4. Ask the model to fix failing tests.
5. Ask the model to update selectors.
6. Ask the model to refactor the framework.
7. Repeat.

This can work in the beginning.

The first demo may look excellent.

But over time, several issues appear.

## The model needs more and more context

As the framework grows, the AI needs to understand more files before making safe changes.

A small request like "fix this checkout test" may require the model to inspect the test file, helper functions, page objects, fixtures, configuration, CI logs, and previous changes.

That increases token consumption.

And because most AI providers bill based on token usage, larger context means higher cost.

## The tests become harder for humans to read

AI-generated Playwright or Selenium code may be valid, but that does not mean the whole team can understand it.

A product manager cannot easily review the business intent of a generated test by reading code. A manual tester may not feel comfortable editing selectors, fixtures, or helper functions. A support engineer cannot quickly confirm whether the test covers the customer issue they reported.

The result is low adoption.

And low adoption is one of the classic reasons internal Selenium and Playwright frameworks struggle inside companies.

## Maintenance depends on AI again

If the team does not fully understand the generated code, they become dependent on AI to maintain it.

That creates a strange loop:

- AI creates the framework.
- The team does not fully understand the framework.
- The framework breaks.
- The team asks AI to fix it.
- The framework becomes more complex.
- The team understands it even less.

That is not a healthy long-term strategy.

AI should reduce maintenance burden, not create a system that requires constant AI intervention to remain usable.

## Code is not always the best output for test automation

Code is powerful.

But for many end-to-end testing workflows, code is not the most accessible output.

If the goal is to democratize test automation, the output should be understandable by more than just developers.

That is why generating tests as human-readable steps is often better than generating raw test code.

A human-readable test can be reviewed by QA, developers, product managers, support teams, and business stakeholders.

It can show the intent clearly:

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Open the signup page |
| 2 | Type a unique email address |
| 3 | Click "Create account" |
| 4 | Read the confirmation email |
| 5 | Open the confirmation link |
| 6 | Verify that the dashboard is displayed |

That is easier to understand than a generated code file with imports, fixtures, helper functions, selectors, waits, and assertions.

This is not an argument against code.

Developers should absolutely write unit tests, integration tests, API tests, and lower-level checks in code.

But for business-critical end-to-end workflows, human-readable automation often leads to better team adoption.

And adoption is what makes test automation successful long term.

## Why Selenium and Playwright frameworks often struggle in companies

Selenium and Playwright are useful technologies.

Selenium has been widely used for browser automation for many years. Playwright is a strong modern framework with good developer experience, auto-waiting, browser automation APIs, and useful debugging tools.

Selenium and Playwright are not the problem. Internal code-first frameworks are difficult to scale across a whole team.

Many companies follow the same pattern:

1. A proof of concept looks great.
2. A few tests are created quickly.
3. The team is excited.
4. The suite grows.
5. The application changes.
6. Locators start breaking.
7. Test data becomes messy.
8. CI failures become noisy.
9. Only one or two people understand the framework.
10. Other team members avoid touching the tests.
11. Maintenance becomes slower and more expensive.
12. The automation project loses trust.

This pattern has been discussed across industry research and quality engineering reports for years. The [DORA research on test automation](https://dora.dev/capabilities/test-automation/) frames automated testing as an engineering capability connected to delivery performance rather than a tooling choice. The [World Quality Report](https://www.capgemini.com/insights/research-library/world-quality-report-2025-26/) continues to show that quality engineering, automation, AI, and human-in-the-loop systems are deeply connected. The [State of Testing report](https://www.practitest.com/state-of-testing/) also tracks the growing role of AI and automation in testing, and the human side of the profession.

Test files existing does not make test automation successful. It succeeds when the team uses the tests, trusts the tests, maintains the tests, and keeps them in sync with development.

That requires adoption.

And adoption is much easier when tests are readable, editable, and accessible to the whole team.

## AI should not be involved in every execution decision

One of the most important architectural choices in AI test automation is deciding when AI should be used.

AI is useful for:

- Creating tests
- Suggesting steps
- Generating assertions
- Extracting variables
- Repairing broken locators
- Explaining failures
- Comparing visual differences
- Importing tests from other formats

But when a test is executing, AI should not casually reinterpret every step.

The test should run deterministically.

If the test says "Click the Submit button," the system should click the Submit button that was defined by the test logic. It should not ask an AI model to decide from scratch on every run, unless there is a failure or ambiguity that needs assistance.

That restraint matters because AI can hallucinate.

If AI is directly involved in deciding whether a test passed or failed on every execution, the team may not fully trust the result.

A false failure wastes time.

A false pass is worse.

A false pass can send a real defect to production.

That is why the safest approach is to combine AI assistance with deterministic execution.

AI helps create and maintain the test. The test itself remains stable, inspectable, and repeatable.

## The best AI model is not always the largest model

There is a common assumption that the largest or most expensive model must be the best model.

That is not always true.

For test automation, a smaller specialized model can outperform a larger general model on the specific tasks that matter.

This is normal in software engineering.

A specialized database can outperform a general storage system for a certain query pattern. A specialized image model can outperform a general model for a specific visual inspection task. A specialized static analyzer can outperform a general coding assistant for a narrow class of code quality checks.

The same principle applies to AI test automation.

The best model is the one that produces the best measured outcome for the task, not the one with the most impressive general benchmark.

For test automation, the outcome that matters is a reliable test, not a nice paragraph.

## How Endtest evaluates AI for test automation

Endtest has been focused on test automation since 2016.

We introduced AI-powered self-healing tests in 2017, long before the current wave of generative AI tools became mainstream. Since then, our approach has always been practical: AI should make test automation more reliable, not more mysterious.

Over the last two years, we have studied and benchmarked many AI models and approaches.

That included general foundation models, newer coding models, open models, commercial APIs, and specialized approaches. We have also continued to benchmark new foundation models as they appear, because the options change quickly.

Our conclusion has been consistent:

General-purpose models are impressive, but they are usually too imprecise, too slow, or too expensive for many production test automation workflows.

They are not bad models. The task is specialized.

Automated testing requires precision around web elements, selectors, browser behavior, page state, assertions, execution history, and maintenance. A model that is excellent for general reasoning may still be inefficient for those narrow, repeated tasks.

That is why Endtest uses AI models specialized in test automation.

We are not using the typical general models that people usually hear about in chatbot discussions. Endtest does not rely on OpenAI, Anthropic, or a public GitHub model as the core engine for its AI test automation capabilities.

We are not claiming that our AI is "smarter" in every possible area. The narrower, more useful claim is that Endtest AI is designed to be faster, more reliable, and more cost-efficient for creating and maintaining automated tests.

That specialization is what allows us to offer [Unlimited AI](https://endtest.io/pricing), so users do not have to think about tokens, credits, or surprise AI invoices every time they create, maintain, or improve tests.

## Why Unlimited AI matters

Unlimited AI is a pricing feature, but it also changes how users behave.

When AI usage is metered by tokens or credits, users naturally become cautious.

They may think twice before generating another test. They may avoid asking AI to improve an assertion. They may hesitate to run another maintenance attempt. They may worry that normal testing work will create an unexpected bill.

That is not ideal.

AI should make test automation easier, not introduce a new cost anxiety.

Endtest is built so users can rely on AI throughout the testing lifecycle:

- Creating tests
- Maintaining tests
- Generating assertions
- Working with variables
- Improving stability
- Importing existing tests
- Understanding failures
- Reducing repetitive work

Because our AI is specialized and the architecture is optimized around test automation, we can make that usage predictable.

That matters for teams that want to scale.

## How Endtest uses AI across the testing lifecycle

The best AI model for test automation is not useful by itself. It needs to be part of a complete testing platform.

Endtest uses AI across multiple areas of the product.

## AI Test Creation Agent

The [Endtest AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) can create automated tests from plain-English instructions.

The output is a normal Endtest test made of clear, editable steps, not an opaque code file.

That matters because the team can inspect the result, improve it, and understand what is being tested.

## AI Assertions

[AI Assertions](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-assertions) help users validate complex page conditions using natural language.

Instead of manually building every low-level check, users can describe what should be true.

This is useful for pages where the expected outcome is easier to express in business language than in selectors.

## AI Variables

AI Variables help extract dynamic values from pages, emails, SMS messages, documents, and other test artifacts.

This is useful for flows involving confirmation codes, order IDs, invoice numbers, temporary passwords, magic links, and other dynamic data.

## Visual AI

Visual AI helps detect meaningful visual differences.

Traditional assertions can confirm that text exists, but they may miss layout problems, broken components, overlapping elements, or visual regressions.

Visual AI helps cover that gap.

## Self-healing tests

Endtest includes self-healing capabilities powered by AI.

When an element changes, Endtest can use stored backup locators and AI-assisted repair to help keep tests stable.

This reduces the maintenance burden that often affects Selenium and Playwright suites.

## Email and SMS testing

Modern end-to-end testing often needs to go beyond the browser.

Endtest supports email testing and SMS testing, allowing teams to validate flows such as:

- Account confirmation
- Password reset
- Magic links
- User invitations
- Two-factor authentication
- SMS verification
- Notification workflows

This is important because real user journeys often involve more than clicking through a website.

## Cross-browser cloud execution

Endtest runs tests in the cloud on real browsers on Windows and macOS machines.

That includes real Safari on macOS machines.

This matters because browser behavior can differ in production. The official Playwright documentation says Playwright runs Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. WebKit support is useful, but it is not the same as testing on the branded Safari browser on real macOS machines.

If your customers use Safari, real Safari testing matters.

## The best AI testing system combines specialization with readability

The best AI model is only one ingredient.

A reliable AI test automation system also needs:

- Structured test steps
- Human-readable output
- Deterministic execution
- Reliable cloud infrastructure
- Strong debugging artifacts
- Cross-browser support
- Maintenance assistance
- Email and SMS testing
- Visual validation
- Team collaboration
- Predictable pricing
- Good customer support

This is why asking "Which model is best?" on its own can be misleading. The question to ask is "Which AI testing system produces the most reliable results for our team?"

A general model might generate a decent test once.

A specialized test automation platform should help your team create, run, maintain, debug, and improve tests every week.

That is the difference.

## How to choose the best AI model for your team

If you are evaluating AI models or AI testing tools, use a practical benchmark.

Do not only test with one happy-path example.

Use real workflows from your product.

## Test creation benchmark

Ask the AI to create tests for several real user journeys:

- Signup
- Login
- Password reset
- Checkout
- Subscription upgrade
- Account settings
- Email confirmation
- SMS verification
- File upload
- Report generation

Measure:

- How long it takes
- How accurate the generated test is
- How much editing is needed
- Whether the assertions are meaningful
- Whether non-technical team members can understand the output

## Locator benchmark

Give the AI real page sources and screenshots.

Ask it to identify target elements such as:

- Buttons
- Inputs
- Dropdowns
- Modals
- Hidden elements
- Disabled elements
- Similar-looking elements
- Elements inside dynamic components

Measure:

- Correct element selection
- Selector stability
- False positives
- Ability to say "not enough information"
- Performance on changed UI

## Maintenance benchmark

Break existing tests intentionally.

Change labels, move elements, update CSS classes, modify layout, or add new wrappers.

Then measure:

- Whether the AI repairs the test correctly
- Whether it preserves the original intent
- Whether it introduces new fragility
- How many attempts are needed
- How much human review is required

## Cost benchmark

Measure cost at the workflow level rather than the model call level.

Include:

- Test creation
- Revisions
- Debugging
- Maintenance
- Failure analysis
- Context loading
- Retries
- Prompt overhead
- Long-term usage

This gives a more realistic picture than comparing one prompt against another.

## Adoption benchmark

Ask people outside the automation team to review the generated tests.

Can QA understand them? Can product managers validate the business intent? Can developers debug failures? Can support teams confirm that customer issues are covered?

If the answer is no, the tool may not scale across the organization.

## The answer: the best AI model is specialized, measured, and productized

So, what is the best AI model for test automation?

The best model is not necessarily the largest, the most famous, or the one that performs best in a generic coding benchmark.

The best AI model for test automation is the one that performs best on the actual testing tasks your team needs:

- Fast test creation
- Accurate element detection
- Reliable selector generation
- Low hallucination rate
- Useful assertions
- Efficient maintenance
- Predictable cost
- Human-readable output
- Stable execution

In many cases, that means specialized AI models and specialized test automation systems will outperform general-purpose foundation models, not because they are more impressive in every domain but because they are built for this domain.

That is the same reason you use a database for structured queries, a browser engine for rendering pages, and a CI system for delivery pipelines.

## Final thoughts

General foundation models are remarkable.

They can write code, explain concepts, summarize documents, generate test ideas, and help developers move faster. For skilled programmers, AI-assisted coding can be useful.

But test automation has different requirements.

It needs speed, reliability, low hallucination rates, stable selectors, meaningful assertions, deterministic execution, readable output, maintainability, and predictable cost.

A generic model can help with parts of that workflow.

A specialized AI test automation system can be designed around the entire workflow.

That is the direction Endtest has taken.

We use AI models specialized in test automation, combined with a platform that turns AI output into clear, editable, deterministic tests that run on real browsers in the cloud.

What makes AI useful in practice is specialized AI, measured against real testing problems and built into a system that helps teams create, run, and maintain reliable automated tests.

If you want to see how that works in practice, explore the [Endtest AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) or compare plans on the [pricing page](https://endtest.io/pricing).

# Is AI Test Automation Reliable?

Learn when AI test automation helps, where it fails, and why Selenium, Playwright, and Endtest strategies differ in long-term reliability.

Published May 20, 2026 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/is-ai-test-automation-reliable

---
Is AI test automation reliable? Yes, it can be, but only when it is used inside a reliable testing strategy.

AI can create tests faster, help more people contribute to test automation, reduce repetitive work, and make assertions, variables, maintenance, and failure analysis easier.

But AI is still an accelerant.

If your test automation strategy is healthy, AI can help it move faster. If your strategy is fragile, AI will help you create fragile tests faster. If your team does not know what it is testing, AI will not magically fix that. If nobody owns maintenance, AI will not remove the need for ownership. If the output is hard to understand, AI can make the problem worse by producing more artifacts that the team cannot confidently review.

"Can AI create automated tests?" is the easy question.

The harder one is whether AI can help your team create, understand, run, maintain, and trust automated tests over the long term.

## What AI test automation actually means

AI test automation is not one single feature. Different vendors use the term in very different ways.

In practice, AI can be used for several parts of the testing lifecycle:

| Area | What AI can help with |
| --- | --- |
| Test creation | Turning plain-English scenarios into automated tests |
| Test maintenance | Updating locators or steps when the UI changes |
| Assertions | Checking complex page conditions using natural language |
| Variables | Extracting dynamic values from pages, emails, documents, or APIs |
| Visual testing | Detecting meaningful visual regressions |
| Failure analysis | Explaining why a test failed and whether it looks like a real bug |
| Test import | Converting Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, Postman, or manual test cases into another format |
| Coverage planning | Suggesting important user flows that should be covered |

This is why it is misleading to judge AI test automation only by asking whether a chatbot can write a Playwright script.

A generated Playwright script is one possible output. It is not the entire category.

Modern AI test automation is more useful when AI helps the team work inside a structured testing platform, where the generated result is visible, editable, reusable, and deterministic.

For example, the [Endtest AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) generates normal Endtest steps that can be inspected, edited, reused, and executed in the Endtest cloud. That is very different from asking an AI assistant to generate a folder of code that only a few engineers can comfortably understand.

## Why AI makes test creation faster

The most obvious benefit of AI test automation is speed.

Before AI, creating an end-to-end test often required someone to:

1. Understand the user flow.
2. Choose the right automation framework.
3. Set up the project structure.
4. Configure browsers and drivers.
5. Write selectors.
6. Add waits.
7. Add assertions.
8. Handle test data.
9. Integrate the test with CI/CD.
10. Debug failures across environments.

That is a lot of work before the test provides any value.

AI changes the starting point.

Instead of manually writing every command, a tester can describe the scenario:

"Create a test that signs up with a new user, confirms the email, logs in, upgrades to the Pro plan, and verifies that the dashboard shows the new subscription."

A good AI testing system can then produce a first version of that test much faster than a human would from scratch.

That matters because most companies that fail at test automation have plenty of ideas for what to test. What they lack is a fast way to convert those ideas into reliable, maintainable automation.

When test creation is slow, coverage always lags behind development.

The team ships a feature this sprint, but the automated regression test appears two sprints later. Or never.

AI can close that gap.

## AI democratizes test automation

The second major benefit is adoption.

Traditional test automation has often been limited to people who can write code. That usually means a small number of QA automation engineers, SDETs, or developers.

That creates a bottleneck.

Product managers know the expected behavior. Manual testers know the edge cases. Customer support knows the most common customer problems. Designers know what changed in the UI. Developers know the implementation details.

But if only one or two people can actually create and maintain automated tests, the organization never gets the full value of that knowledge.

AI changes that.

When test creation starts from plain English, more people can participate. They do not all need to become Selenium or Playwright experts before contributing to coverage.

This is one of the strongest arguments for AI in testing. It makes test automation more accessible.

But accessibility only works if the output is also understandable.

If a non-technical tester describes a scenario and receives a 300-line generated Playwright file, they still depend on an engineer or another AI prompt to understand it. That is dependency with a friendlier input box, not democratization.

The real breakthrough happens when the AI-generated test is displayed as clear, human-readable steps.

For example:

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Open the signup page |
| 2 | Type a unique email address |
| 3 | Click "Create account" |
| 4 | Read the confirmation email |
| 5 | Open the confirmation link |
| 6 | Verify that the dashboard is displayed |

That format can be reviewed by QA, developers, product managers, and support teams.

That is what drives adoption.

## AI is an accelerant, not a strategy

AI can make a good testing strategy faster.

It can also make a bad testing strategy fail faster.

If the team does not know which flows matter, AI may generate tests for low-value scenarios. If the application is unstable and nobody maintains test data, AI-generated tests will still fail. If the team treats end-to-end testing as a side project owned by one person, AI will not create a culture of quality by itself.

This is where many teams misunderstand AI test automation.

They expect AI to replace the hard parts of quality engineering. But the hard parts are not only technical.

The hard parts are strategic:

- Which user journeys matter most?
- Which failures are expensive?
- Which browsers and devices are used by real customers?
- Which flows involve email, SMS, payments, files, PDFs, APIs, or third-party systems?
- Who reviews the tests?
- Who maintains them?
- Who decides whether a failure blocks a release?
- How quickly does the team respond to failures?
- Are tests created in the same sprint as features?
- Can the whole team understand the automated coverage?

AI helps with execution. It does not remove the need for answers.

[DORA's research on test automation](https://dora.dev/capabilities/test-automation/) has long made the point that automated testing is a capability connected to software delivery performance rather than only a tooling decision. The same is true for [continuous delivery](https://dora.dev/capabilities/continuous-delivery/): reliable delivery depends on practices, feedback loops, and team behavior rather than scripts alone.

AI is powerful, but it works best when it supports a mature testing process.

## Why Selenium and Playwright projects often struggle long term

Selenium and Playwright are both useful technologies.

Selenium has been a standard browser automation project for years, and the official Selenium documentation correctly describes it as a project that enables and supports browser automation. Playwright is a modern framework with strong developer experience, fast execution, auto-waiting, and useful debugging tools.

Neither tool is the problem.

Internal code-first test automation frameworks are difficult to scale across a company.

Many teams have experienced the same pattern:

1. A proof of concept looks impressive.
2. A few tests are created quickly.
3. Management sees the demo and approves the initiative.
4. The suite grows.
5. The application changes.
6. Locators break.
7. Test data becomes messy.
8. CI failures become noisy.
9. Only one or two people understand the framework.
10. The team starts ignoring failures.
11. Maintenance becomes more expensive than test creation.
12. The automation initiative loses credibility.

The POC is usually not the problem. The demo almost always looks good.

The real test comes three to six months later.

That is when the team discovers whether the framework is maintainable, whether test ownership is distributed, whether new scenarios can be added quickly, and whether failures are trusted.

This pattern is visible across many public sources on test automation. The [World Quality Report 2025-26](https://www.capgemini.com/insights/research-library/world-quality-report-2025-26/) describes persistent barriers around scalable automation and AI-powered tooling. The [PractiTest State of Testing](https://www.practitest.com/state-of-testing/) tracks the growing role of AI and automation in testing, while also reflecting the human and organizational side of QA. Academic work such as [The State of Test Automation in DevOps](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3549206.3549321) also shows that automation in DevOps is a socio-technical problem rather than only a scripting problem.

In other words, success depends on more than picking a framework.

It depends on maintainability, ownership, adoption, infrastructure, data, execution speed, reporting, and trust.

## The Claude-generated internal framework problem

With modern AI coding tools, creating an internal Selenium or Playwright framework is easier than ever.

You can ask Claude, ChatGPT, or another coding assistant:

"Create a Playwright framework with page objects, reusable fixtures, CI integration, screenshots on failure, retries, environment support, and HTML reports."

A few minutes later, you may have a working framework.

That feels magical.

But it can also be dangerous.

Generating the first version is easy. Owning it is the hard part.

If the team does not understand the generated code, several problems appear:

- They cannot easily verify whether the test is checking the right behavior.
- They cannot confidently modify the test when requirements change.
- They cannot improve the framework without prompting AI again.
- They may accept fragile selectors without noticing.
- They may add unnecessary abstractions because the AI suggested them.
- They may not understand why a failure happened.
- They may create a system that looks professional but is difficult to maintain.

This creates a new kind of technical debt: AI-generated test automation debt.

The code exists. The test runs. The framework has folders, helpers, fixtures, screenshots, and reports.

But the team does not really own it.

That is risky.

And because most AI providers charge API usage based on tokens, the cost of AI-assisted maintenance can also grow as the framework grows. Both [OpenAI API pricing](https://openai.com/api/pricing/) and [Anthropic API pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) are structured around token usage for API-based model access. If every test change, debugging session, framework update, and failure analysis requires another long prompt with a large codebase, maintenance can become both slower and more expensive.

AI-generated code can be helpful. But generated code still needs human ownership.

## AI-assisted coding is better when you already know how to code

There is a big difference between these two workflows:

1. A skilled automation engineer uses AI to accelerate Playwright or Selenium work.
2. A non-programmer asks AI to generate an entire test framework they do not understand.

The first workflow can produce good results.

If you already understand programming, selectors, waits, test architecture, CI/CD, browser behavior, assertions, and debugging, AI-assisted coding can make you faster. You can review the code. You can reject bad suggestions. You can simplify over-engineered output. You can spot missing assertions. You can decide when generated logic is unreliable.

In that context, AI is like a junior assistant working with a senior engineer.

But in the second workflow, AI becomes the architect, implementer, and maintainer.

That is much riskier.

If the user does not understand the generated code, they cannot reliably judge whether the automation is correct. They may be able to run it, but they may not be able to trust it.

This does not mean AI coding tools are bad. They are extremely useful.

It means that AI-assisted coding does not completely eliminate the disadvantages of an internal Selenium or Playwright framework:

- The framework still has to be maintained.
- The team still needs coding skills.
- The tests still need infrastructure.
- Cross-browser execution still needs to be handled.
- Reporting still needs to be understood.
- Test data still needs to be managed.
- Flaky failures still need investigation.
- New team members still need onboarding.

AI reduces some friction. It does not remove the operating model.

## Generating tests as code can be contradictory

There is also a philosophical problem with using AI to generate end-to-end tests as code.

The promise of AI is simplicity:

"Describe what you want, and the system will create it."

But if the output is a code file, the result is often harder to understand than the input.

A plain-English instruction like this:

"Verify that a user can reset their password and log in with the new password."

May become a generated test with:

- imports
- fixtures
- page objects
- helper functions
- selectors
- environment variables
- custom waits
- test data factories
- assertions
- retries
- screenshots
- cleanup logic

For a developer, that may be acceptable.

For a QA tester, product manager, support engineer, or founder, it may be opaque.

That creates a contradiction.

The input was human-readable. The output is not.

This is one reason why intelligent test automation tools are becoming more important. The best AI testing systems should not only generate automation. They should generate automation that humans can inspect and improve.

That is why human-readable steps matter.

They create a shared language between AI, QA, developers, product managers, and business stakeholders.

## Reliable AI testing requires human-readable output

A reliable AI test automation strategy should make it easy for humans to answer these questions:

- What does this test do?
- What user journey does it cover?
- What data does it use?
- What does it assert?
- What browser does it run on?
- What environment does it target?
- What changed since the last successful run?
- Why did it fail?
- Can I edit it without asking a developer?
- Can someone else on the team understand it?

If the answer to these questions requires reading hundreds of lines of generated code, adoption will remain limited.

If the test is shown as human-readable steps, adoption improves.

That is why intelligent test automation platforms are increasingly important. They give teams a shared layer above raw automation code.

This does not mean code has no place in testing. Developers should still write unit tests, integration tests, API tests, and lower-level checks where code is the right format.

But for end-to-end business flows, human-readable automation is often a better fit.

Most people in the company care about behavior, not implementation.

They want to know:

"Can a user sign up, receive the email, confirm the account, complete checkout, receive the SMS code, and see the right dashboard?"

They do not want to decode test framework internals.

## Modern end-to-end testing is more than files with code

Another common mistake is treating automated testing as if it only means having a repository with test files.

That is not enough anymore.

Modern end-to-end testing usually requires:

- Real browser execution
- Cross-browser testing
- Parallel execution
- Cloud infrastructure
- Screenshots and videos
- Console logs
- Network logs
- Test data management
- Email testing
- SMS testing
- API calls inside UI flows
- File upload and download validation
- PDF validation
- Visual regression testing
- CI/CD integration
- Scheduling
- Failure triage
- Team collaboration
- Access control
- Historical reporting
- Reliable support when something breaks

This is where many internal frameworks become expensive.

The first five tests are easy. The full platform around those tests is not.

For example, a serious web application should not only be tested in one local Chrome instance. It should be tested on the browsers and operating systems your users actually use.

That includes Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari. And Safari matters.

Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, but the official Playwright documentation states that Playwright does not work with the branded version of Safari and instead uses its own WebKit build. For many teams, WebKit coverage is useful. But it is not the same as running tests on real Safari on macOS machines.

This distinction matters when browser-specific bugs affect checkout, signup, payments, forms, file uploads, or mobile-like behavior.

If your customers use Safari, testing only on WebKit is not always enough.

## When AI test automation is reliable

AI test automation is more likely to be reliable when it has these characteristics:

| Characteristic | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| The generated test is inspectable | Humans can verify what is being tested |
| The output is editable | The team can maintain it without regenerating everything |
| Execution is deterministic | The same test should behave consistently across runs |
| Assertions are explicit | The team knows what success means |
| Browser infrastructure is stable | Failures are less likely to come from the environment |
| Maintenance is built in | UI changes do not destroy the suite |
| Failure artifacts are clear | Screenshots, videos, logs, and traces reduce debugging time |
| The whole team can contribute | Test creation is not blocked by one specialist |
| AI is used where it adds value | AI supports the workflow instead of replacing judgment |

AI is especially useful when creating tests from plain English, generating assertions, suggesting locators, extracting dynamic values, importing old tests, and helping with maintenance.

It is less reliable when it is asked to make broad product decisions, invent expected behavior, or maintain a large codebase that nobody understands.

## When AI test automation is not reliable

AI test automation becomes unreliable when teams use it as a shortcut around strategy.

Warning signs include:

- The team generates many tests without prioritizing critical flows.
- Nobody reviews AI-generated tests.
- The expected behavior is vague.
- Tests contain weak assertions.
- Generated code is too complex for the team to maintain.
- The team uses AI to patch failures without understanding the root cause.
- Tests run only locally, not in reliable cloud infrastructure.
- The suite does not cover real browsers used by customers.
- The team ignores flaky failures.
- Test ownership belongs to one person instead of the whole team.

The biggest risk is false confidence.

A test can pass while checking the wrong thing.

For example, a generated test may verify that a confirmation message appears after checkout. But it may not verify that the order was actually created, that the email receipt was sent, that the SMS verification worked, or that the correct subscription was activated.

The test is green. The user journey may still be broken.

That is why AI-generated tests must be reviewed.

AI can propose coverage. Humans still need to decide whether the coverage is meaningful.

## The role of the whole team in successful test automation

Long-term test automation success depends heavily on team adoption.

If only one person can create tests, automation becomes a bottleneck. If only one person can maintain tests, automation becomes fragile. If only one person understands failures, automation becomes noise.

A healthy strategy involves multiple roles:

| Role | Contribution |
| --- | --- |
| QA testers | Define important scenarios, edge cases, and regression coverage |
| Developers | Improve testability, add stable attributes, fix failures quickly |
| Product managers | Clarify expected behavior and business-critical flows |
| Designers | Identify UI changes that may affect tests |
| Support teams | Surface real customer pain points |
| DevOps teams | Keep CI/CD and execution infrastructure stable |
| Leadership | Treat quality as a product investment, not a side task |

This is why human-readable test automation matters so much.

The more people can understand the tests, the more people can improve them.

And the more people contribute, the more likely automated testing can keep up with development.

## Pros of AI test automation

AI test automation has real advantages when used correctly.

## 1. Faster test creation

AI can dramatically reduce the time required to create a first version of a test.

This is especially useful for regression tests, smoke tests, onboarding flows, checkout flows, signup flows, and other repetitive business-critical journeys.

Instead of starting from a blank file or a blank test editor, the team starts from a generated draft.

## 2. Better access for non-programmers

AI allows people to describe behavior in natural language.

That gives manual testers, product managers, support engineers, and founders a more direct path into test automation.

The result is better coverage as well as speed, because more people can contribute their knowledge.

## 3. Easier assertions

Some assertions are simple:

"Verify that the text 'Payment successful' is visible."

Others are more complex:

"Verify that the invoice total matches the selected plan, includes VAT, and shows the correct billing period."

AI assertions can help with more flexible validation, especially when the expected outcome is easier to express in natural language than in selectors and code.

Endtest supports [AI Assertions](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-assertions), allowing teams to describe what should be true on the page instead of manually building every assertion from low-level checks.

## 4. Better handling of dynamic values

Many end-to-end tests need to extract values from one step and use them later.

Examples include:

- Order IDs
- Confirmation codes
- Email links
- SMS codes
- Invoice numbers
- Temporary passwords
- Usernames
- Values from PDFs
- Values from API responses

AI can make this easier by identifying and extracting values from messy or dynamic content.

That reduces brittle parsing logic and makes tests easier to maintain.

## 5. Faster maintenance

UI changes are one of the biggest causes of test maintenance.

A button moves. A label changes. A selector breaks. A form field gets wrapped in a new component. A modal appears before the next step.

AI-powered maintenance can help by finding alternative locators, updating broken steps, or explaining failures.

Endtest includes [Self-Healing Tests](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/self-healing-tests) that can help keep tests stable when the UI changes.

## 6. Better visual coverage

Not every bug is functional.

Sometimes the checkout still works, but the button is hidden. Sometimes a dashboard loads, but the chart is broken. Sometimes a page technically contains the right text, but the layout is unusable.

Visual AI can help detect meaningful visual differences that traditional assertions may miss.

This is especially useful for high-value pages like checkout, dashboards, reports, landing pages, onboarding flows, and account settings.

## 7. Easier migration from old tools

Many teams already have Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, or Postman tests.

The problem is that old suites may be difficult to maintain, poorly adopted, or tied to infrastructure the team no longer wants to own.

AI can help convert existing tests into a more maintainable format.

Endtest supports [AI Test Import](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-test-import), which can help teams migrate from older automation assets into Endtest.

## Limits of AI test automation

AI also has limits.

Ignoring those limits leads to disappointment.

## 1. AI does not know your product strategy

AI can infer behavior from pages, prompts, screenshots, and code. But it does not automatically know your business priorities.

It may not know which flows are revenue-critical. It may not know which customers matter most. It may not know which edge cases caused incidents in the past.

Humans still need to define priorities.

## 2. AI can generate weak assertions

A generated test may click through the right pages but assert very little.

For example, it may check that a page loaded, but not that the correct user data appears.

Weak assertions create false confidence.

The test passes, but the important behavior may still be broken.

## 3. AI can create too much

Because AI makes creation easier, teams may generate too many tests too quickly.

That sounds good until the suite becomes slow, noisy, and expensive to maintain.

Good test automation means having the right tests at the right layers, not the largest number of tests.

You still need a balanced strategy:

- Unit tests for small logic
- API tests for service behavior
- Integration tests for system boundaries
- End-to-end tests for critical user journeys
- Manual exploratory testing for unknown risks

AI does not remove the need for that balance.

## 4. AI-generated code still creates code ownership problems

If AI generates test code, someone still has to own that code.

The team needs to understand it, review it, debug it, refactor it, and maintain it.

If the team cannot do that confidently, the code becomes a liability.

## 5. AI cannot fix unstable environments

If your staging environment is unreliable, your tests will be unreliable.

If test data is inconsistent, your tests will fail.

If third-party services behave unpredictably, your tests need proper handling.

AI can help diagnose issues, but it cannot make unstable systems stable by itself.

## 6. AI cost can increase with scale

AI usage can become expensive when every test creation, debugging session, maintenance task, and failure analysis sends large prompts to a model.

This is especially important for teams using general-purpose AI coding tools with large repositories.

Token-based billing means cost can grow with prompt size, output size, and frequency of use.

That is another reason why AI test automation should be designed as a controlled product workflow rather than a collection of ad-hoc prompts.

## When to use AI test automation

AI test automation is a strong fit for many use cases.

## Use AI for critical user journeys

AI is useful for creating end-to-end tests around flows such as:

- Signup
- Login
- Password reset
- Checkout
- Subscription upgrade
- Booking
- Search
- Account settings
- User invitations
- Email confirmation
- SMS verification
- Report generation
- File upload
- PDF validation

These flows are usually important to the business and expensive to test manually every release.

## Use AI when the team lacks automation capacity

Many companies know they need more automated tests, but they do not have enough automation engineers.

AI can help reduce the gap.

Instead of waiting for a specialist to write every test, QA and product team members can create first drafts and review them with the rest of the team.

## Use AI when tests need to be created in the same sprint

If tests are always created after the feature is shipped, coverage will lag behind.

AI can help teams create tests while the feature is still fresh.

That improves feedback speed and makes quality part of the development process, not a separate activity at the end.

## Use AI for maintenance assistance

Maintenance is one of the best uses of AI.

When a UI changes, AI can help find new locators, explain failures, or suggest updates.

This does not mean every change should be applied blindly. But it can reduce the manual effort needed to keep the suite stable.

## Use AI to make testing more collaborative

AI is useful when it makes tests easier for more people to create and understand.

That is why platforms with editable, human-readable steps matter so much.

They allow AI to accelerate the work without hiding the work.

## When not to rely only on AI test automation

AI should not be the only testing method.

Do not rely only on AI-generated end-to-end tests for:

- Low-level business logic
- Security testing
- Performance testing
- Accessibility testing
- Complex data validation
- Exploratory testing
- Compliance-heavy workflows
- Risk analysis
- Requirements clarification

AI can assist in some of these areas, but it should not replace specialized methods and human judgment.

A mature testing strategy uses multiple layers.

End-to-end AI test automation is one layer. It is an important layer, but it is not the entire quality strategy.

## What a reliable AI test automation platform should include

If you are evaluating AI test automation tools, look beyond the demo.

Ask what happens after the first 20 tests.

A reliable platform should include:

## Human-readable tests

The generated output should be understandable by the whole team.

If only developers can read the result, adoption will remain limited.

## Editable steps

AI-generated tests should not be black boxes.

The team should be able to edit steps, assertions, variables, data, and flows without regenerating everything.

## Deterministic execution

AI can help create and maintain tests, but execution should be stable and repeatable.

A test should not behave unpredictably because the AI "decided" something different during every run.

## Real browser infrastructure

Testing should run on real browsers, ideally in the cloud, with support for different operating systems and browser versions.

For serious cross-browser testing, real Safari on macOS matters.

## Strong debugging artifacts

Every failure should include useful evidence:

- Screenshots
- Videos
- Console logs
- Network logs
- Error messages
- Step-level details
- Environment information

Without good failure artifacts, the team wastes time asking whether a failure is a bug, a flaky test, or an environment issue.

## Email and SMS testing

Modern user flows often involve email and SMS.

A testing platform should make it easy to test:

- Confirmation emails
- Password reset emails
- Magic links
- Invite emails
- Two-factor authentication
- SMS verification codes
- Notification workflows

Endtest includes email testing and SMS testing capabilities, which are essential for complete end-to-end flows.

## Built-in maintenance

A reliable AI testing platform should help reduce maintenance through features such as self-healing, AI-assisted updates, reusable components, and clear failure analysis.

## Team collaboration

The platform should support the way real teams work.

That means multiple users, shared suites, permissions, reporting, scheduling, and integrations.

This is another reason why "a folder of generated Playwright files" is often not enough.

## How Endtest approaches AI test automation

Endtest is built around a simple idea:

AI should make test automation faster without making it harder to understand.

That is why Endtest does not generate opaque code and leave the team to maintain it.

The [AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/product/create/ai-test-creation-agent) can create tests from plain-English instructions, but the result is a normal Endtest test made of clear, editable steps. The team can inspect the flow, change steps, add assertions, modify variables, and run the test in the Endtest cloud.

Endtest also applies AI across the lifecycle, not only during creation:

- [AI Test Creation Agent](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-test-creation-agent) for creating tests from natural language
- [AI Assertions](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-assertions) for validating complex page conditions
- [AI Variables](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/ai-variables) for extracting dynamic values
- Visual AI for detecting visual regressions
- Self-healing tests powered by AI for reducing maintenance
- AI Test Import for migrating existing Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, and other test assets
- Email testing for complete email-based flows
- SMS testing for verification and 2FA scenarios
- Cross-browser cloud execution with real browsers on Windows and macOS machines
- Real Safari support on macOS machines
- Video playback, screenshots, logs, and debugging artifacts
- Reliable support from a team that understands end-to-end testing

This matters because most teams do not only need help creating tests.

They need help keeping tests useful.

A majority of Endtest customers we speak with arrive after trying to scale Selenium or Playwright internally. Their initial frameworks often worked well in a POC, but became difficult to maintain as the suite grew. The common problems are familiar: too few people understood the code, maintenance slowed the team down, cross-browser infrastructure became expensive, and test failures became noisy.

With Endtest, those teams usually see better adoption because tests are easier to create, easier to understand, and easier to maintain.

The ROI comes from faster creation, broader team participation, lower maintenance, better reliability, and less infrastructure burden, not from AI as a buzzword.

You can explore Endtest plans on the [pricing page](https://endtest.io/pricing), or read more about building a scalable testing strategy in our guide to [scalable test automation](https://endtest.io/blog/scalable-test-automation-practical-guide).

## A practical evaluation checklist

When evaluating AI test automation, ask these questions:

## Can the whole team understand the test?

If the answer is no, adoption will be limited.

## Can the test be edited without regenerating it?

If the answer is no, maintenance may become frustrating.

## Does the tool run tests on real browsers?

If the answer is no, browser-specific bugs may escape.

## Does it support real Safari?

If your users are on Safari, this matters.

## Does it support email and SMS workflows?

If your product uses email confirmation, password reset, invite flows, or two-factor authentication, this is essential.

## Does it produce strong failure evidence?

Screenshots and logs are helpful. Video, console logs, network logs, and step-level details are better.

## Does AI help with maintenance?

AI should not only create tests. It should help keep them stable.

## Does the platform reduce dependency on one specialist?

If only one person can use the tool effectively, the strategy is fragile.

## Does the pricing model scale predictably?

AI usage, test executions, parallelization, and users can all affect cost.

Predictability matters.

## Is AI test automation reliable enough for production teams?

Yes, AI test automation can be reliable enough for production teams.

But not when it is treated as magic.

It is reliable when:

- The team knows what should be tested.
- AI-generated tests are reviewed.
- The output is human-readable.
- Tests are editable.
- Execution is deterministic.
- The platform runs on real browsers.
- Maintenance is built into the workflow.
- Failures are easy to investigate.
- The whole team can participate.

It is not reliable when:

- AI generates code nobody understands.
- The team blindly accepts generated tests.
- Assertions are weak.
- Test data is unstable.
- The suite runs only in one local browser.
- Failures are ignored.
- Maintenance depends on one person.
- AI is used to avoid strategy instead of supporting it.

The most reliable future is "AI helps the whole team test better," not "AI replaces testers."

## Final thoughts

AI test automation is one of the most important changes in software testing.

It makes test creation faster and automation more accessible. It helps teams create coverage that would have taken much longer with traditional approaches, and it can reduce maintenance and make end-to-end testing more practical for fast-moving teams.

But AI does not remove the need for a good strategy.

It amplifies the strategy you already have.

If your testing process is unclear, AI will create more unclear tests. If your team does not review coverage, AI will create false confidence. If your automation is hidden inside code that only one person understands, AI may make that pile of code grow faster.

The winning approach is different.

Use AI to accelerate the work, but keep the output understandable. Let AI create and maintain tests, but keep humans in control of intent and coverage. Use intelligent tools that help the whole team contribute, rather than tools that only generate more code.

That is where AI test automation becomes reliable. The AI itself is not perfect, but the system around it is built for reliability.
