# A Practical Guide for Finding Elements with Selenium

Learn the most stable and reliable locator strategies for finding elements using Selenium or Endtest.

Published April 1, 2024 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/a-practical-guide-for-finding-elements

---
This article is for anyone who is using [Selenium](https://www.seleniumhq.org/) or [Endtest](https://endtest.io/) and wants to know the best ways to find elements.

The key here is to find the most stable and reliable locator for each element.

Keep in mind that asking Selenium to locate an element is like telling someone from out of town how to find a certain coffee shop in your city.

We'll be using the GitHub Sign Up page as an example.

I'll also be making some comparisons between Selenium and Endtest.

Even if you are using our [Endtest Chrome Extension](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/endtest/jbdgfkeimppmnfemmgfafiomihlibdfa) to locate your elements, you might still encounter situations where you need to fetch a locator.

## Locator types

We're going to use different locator types to find the **Username** input:

1. Find element by ID
2. Find element by Name
3. Find element by Class Name
4. Find element by XPath
5. Find element by CSS Selector
6. Find element by Link Text
7. Find element by Partial Link Text
8. Find element by Tag Name

![Join GitHub](https://endtest.io/images/github-signup.png "Join GitHub")

## 1. Find element by ID

Always the first choice.

To get the ID of your element, right-click on your element and click on the **Inspect** option.

![Inspect Illustration](https://endtest.io/images/practical-guide-inspect.png "Inspect Illustration")

The structure of your element will be highlighted in the console:

![Structure Highlighted](https://endtest.io/images/structure-highlighted.png "Structure Highlighted")

It seems that our element has the following ID:

`user_login`

This means that your line of code will look like this:
```python
username = driver.find_element_by_id("user_login")
```

Since an ID should be unique on a page, it's the most reliable locator type that you can use.
It's like having only one Starbucks in your city and telling your friends to meet you there. They can't miss.

## 2. Find element by Name
Just as good as ID, but you won't encounter it as often as you'd expect.

Elements from forms usually have the Name attribute.
![Find Element by Name](https://endtest.io/images/element-by-name.png "Find Element by Name")
We can easily see that our element has the following Name:

`user[login]`

```python
username = driver.find_element_by_name("user[login]")
```

## 3. Find element by Class Name
Not so reliable, since a Class Name is usually shared by multiple elements.

We can easily see that our element has the following Class Name:

`form-control`

And if we take a closer look at the rest of the inputs from that form, we'll see that all of them have the **form-control** Class Name.

```python
username = driver.find_element_by_class_name("form-control")
```
This means that you won't be able to locate that Username input with the Class Name locator type, since Selenium will throw an error.

[Endtest](https://endtest.io/) has a more elegant approach here than Selenium. If you provide that Class Name, it will only give you a warning, telling you how many elements it found with that Class Name and that the first one will be used.

![Endtest elegant approach](https://endtest.io/images/endtest-elegant-github.png "Endtest elegant approach")

If Starbucks had a Class Name, it would probably be `coffee-shop`. If you tell your friend to meet you at that coffee shop, they might not know which one you're talking about.

The most common mistake done by beginners is extracting all the Class Names instead of just one.

Let's take a look at this element:

![Complicated Element](https://endtest.io/images/complicated-element.png "Complicated Element")
A novice user might say that the element has the following Class Name:

`HeaderMenu-link d-inline-block no-underline border border-gray-dark`

But it actually has **5 different Class Names**:
- `HeaderMenu-link`
- `d-inline-block`
- `no-underline`
- `border`
- `border-gray-dark`

That's right, Class Names are separated by spaces.

Selenium does not have a validation for that, but Endtest does:
![Endtest validation](https://endtest.io/images/endtest-validation.png "Endtest validation")

## 4. Find element by XPath
You simply can't avoid having to use XPath for at least some elements. It's not as bad as they say.

An XPath is like a route. There are a lot of routes that your friend can take to get to that Starbucks.

Usually, an XPath looks something like this:

```css
/html/body/div[4]/main/div/div/div[1]/p
```

The fastest way to get the XPath is from the Chrome console:
![XPath in Chrome](https://endtest.io/images/xpath-chrome-console.png "XPath in Chrome")

In this case, we got the following XPath:

```xpath
//*[@id="user_login"]
```

If you have a stable ID, you shouldn't bother to use XPath.

And if you don't have a stable ID, the XPath that we got is not reliable.

There are lots of web applications which are using dynamic IDs for some elements.

An element with a dynamic ID is like a coffee shop which is changing its name every day.

You know that the coffee shop was called iCoffee yesterday, but you have no idea what name it is going to have today.

Telling your friend to meet you at iCoffee will be confusing.

That's when we need to write our own XPath.

**Find out what are the stable attributes and characteristics of that element.**

Going back to the example with the coffee shop that has a different name.

What is something that doesn't change about it?

Perhaps the location and the fact that it's a coffee shop.

This means that you can tell your friend from out of town to meet you at the coffee shop from the West Shopping Mall.

Let's take a look at our element and get the XPath of its parent:
![XPath of parent](https://endtest.io/images/xpath-parent.png "XPath of parent")

We get:
```python
//*[@id="signup-form"]/auto-check[1]/dl/dd
```

This is practically the address of the West Shopping Mall in our example.

Now all we have to do is add some details at the end.

Our **Username** element is an **input** and it has the **form-control** Class Name.

This means that we need to append the following to the parent:

```xpath
/input[@class="form-control"]
```

And that part translates to: **Look in that parent for an input which has the form-control Class Name.**

And the final XPath for our Username element will look like this:

```xpath
//*[@id="signup-form"]/auto-check[1]/dl/dd/input[@class="form-control"]
```

Always verify your XPath in the Chrome console by hitting Ctrl + F and searching for it. You should see your element highlighted like this:
![Highlighted element](https://endtest.io/images/highlighted-element.png "Highlighted element")

Writing your own XPaths isn't so scary. You will encounter situations where your element might not have an ID, but it will have a certain reliable attribute which makes it unique.

In that case, your XPath will look like this:

```xpath
//*[@attribute="attribute_value"]
```

You can also write an XPath which locates the element by using only part of the value of the attribute:

```xpath
//*[contains(@attribute, "part_of_attribute_value")]
```

For example, our **Username** element has the following attributes:

```html
<input 
  aria-describedby="description_2822cb3d798c" 
  name="user[login]" 
  autocapitalize="off" 
  autofocus="autofocus" 
  required="required" 
  class="form-control" 
  type="text" 
  id="user_login" 
  autocomplete="off" 
  spellcheck="false" 
/>
```

If we want to use the `aria-describedby` attribute, this will be the XPath:

```xpath
//*[@aria-describedby="description_2822cb3d798c"]
```

If you're using [Endtest](https://endtest.io/) instead of Selenium, their recorder will know how to automatically extract these custom XPaths.

## 5. Find element by CSS Selector
The CSS Selector locator type is similar to XPath.

Some people actually claim that it's faster.

Usually, a CSS Selector looks like this:

```css
body > div.application-main > main > div > div
```

And we extract it in a similar way:

![CSS selector](https://endtest.io/images/css-selector.png "CSS selector")

In this case, we got the following CSS Selector:

```bash
#user_login
```

If you're familiar with CSS, you'll know that **#** stands for **ID**.

The similarities with XPath don't stop here.

If you have a stable ID, you shouldn't bother to use CSS Selector.

And if you don't have a stable ID, the CSS Selector that we got is not reliable.

The solution is to write our own custom CSS Selector.

Let's start by extracting the CSS Selector for the parent of the **Username** element:

![CSS Selector for parent](https://endtest.io/images/username-selector.png "CSS Selector for parent")

We get:
```css
#signup-form > auto-check:nth-child(4) > dl > dd
```

Now, just like we did for XPath, we need to add some details at the end.

In case you forgot, our **Username** element is an **input** and it has the **form-control** Class Name.

This means that we need to append the following to the parent:

```css
> input.form-control
```
And that part translates to: Look in that parent for an input which has the form-control Class Name.

If you're familiar with CSS, the dot stands for Class Name.

And the final CSS Selector for our Username element will look like this:

```css
#signup-form > auto-check:nth-child(4) > dl > dd > input.form-control
```

It's not mandatory to add both the element type and the Class Name.

You can just use one of them:

```css
#signup-form > auto-check:nth-child(4) > dl > dd > input
#signup-form > auto-check:nth-child(4) > dl > dd > .form-control
```

Again, if you're using [Endtest](https://endtest.io/) instead of Selenium, their recorder will know how to automatically extract these custom CSS Selectors.

## 6. Find element by Link Text
The **Link Text** locator type only works for links.

Your element is a Link if it has the following format:

![link text selector](https://endtest.io/images/link-text-locator.png "link text selector")

The a stands for Anchor.

Since our **Username** element is an input and not a link, we won't be able to locate it by using Link Text.

Remember that the Link Text is only the text between the tags.

In the case of the link from the screenshot, the Link Text is **Enterprise**.

![link text](https://endtest.io/images/enterprise-link-text.png "Link text")

Our Selenium code would look like this:

```python
enterprise_link = driver.find_element_by_link_text("Enterprise")
```

## 7. Find element by Partial Link Text
As the name suggests, it's exactly like **Link Text**, but with the difference that you only need to add part of the Link Text.

And this would be our Selenium code:

```python
enterprise_link = driver.find_element_by_partial_link_text("Enterp")
```

## 8. Find element by Tag Name
As we have seen from the previous examples, an element always has a tag.

You can use the **Tag Name** locator type if that's the only unique characteristic of the element that you can grab on to.

Realistically speaking, I don't think you'll ever use this one.

[Endtest](https://endtest.io/) has an extra locator type, **Text Inside**, similar to Partial Link Text, but it works for all types of elements.

## Maintaining reliable locators

Even if your locators are reliable, you will encounter situations where your web application undergoes a revamp and you'll spend time keeping your tests in sync with your web applications.

One option to avoid this situation is to use [Self-Healing Tests](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/self-healing-tests).

# Sauce Labs vs Endtest: Different Tools

Sauce Labs is a device cloud. Endtest is a test automation platform. Here's the difference and how to tell which one you actually need.

Published April 1, 2024 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/endtest-vs-sauce-labs

---
Whenever someone asks us how Endtest compares to Sauce Labs, the honest answer is that we're not really competitors. We solve adjacent problems, and the gap between them is the part that confuses buyers.

This post is meant to be the clear explainer.

## What Sauce Labs is

Sauce Labs is a *cloud device farm*. You give it your Selenium or Appium tests; it gives you back a fleet of browsers and mobile devices to run them on. The product handles:

- Real and virtual browsers across Windows and macOS
- Real and emulated iOS and Android devices
- Live debugging, video capture, network logs
- Tunneling so tests can hit private/staging environments

If you have a working Selenium or Appium test suite and your only constraint is "we need to run these somewhere with more machines than we own," Sauce Labs is exactly the right tool.

## What Sauce Labs is *not*

Sauce Labs does not author tests, maintain them, schedule end-to-end suites, or replace the framework code that drives the browsers. The customer brings the tests; Sauce Labs brings the runtime.

That distinction is critical, because most teams don't actually have a "where do we run tests" problem. They have a "we don't have enough tests, the ones we have keep breaking, and only one engineer can maintain them" problem.

## What Endtest is

Endtest is a *test automation platform*. The platform includes a device cloud, but its job is everything *around* the runtime:

- Codeless test authoring (record, describe in natural language, or import existing flows)
- Agentic AI that creates tests and self-heals locators when your app changes
- Scheduling, notifications, and CI integrations out of the box
- First-class email, SMS, PDF, and API testing alongside browser tests
- The same kinds of real Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android machines you'd get from a device cloud

## How to tell which one you actually need

Ask: *what is currently capping our test coverage?*

- "We have great tests, we just can't run them at scale" → device cloud (Sauce Labs, BrowserStack)
- "We can't write tests fast enough, and they break too often" → test platform (Endtest)
- "We need both, and we don't want to glue two products together" → test platform (the device cloud is included)

If you're using Sauce Labs today and your QA team is still buried in flaky Selenium maintenance, the missing piece is the layer above the device cloud, not a bigger one.

For a side-by-side capability view, see the [Endtest vs Sauce Labs](https://endtest.io/vs/sauce-labs) comparison.

# Selenium Alternatives for Web Test Automation

Selenium WebDriver has been around for a long time. Let's explore some alternatives to Selenium for web test automation.

Published April 1, 2024 by Liviu Lupei on the Endtest blog. Canonical URL: https://endtest.io/blog/top-5-alternatives-to-selenium

---
Selenium WebDriver has been around for a number of years.

Like it or not, it has been the default option for web test automation.

Let's see what the alternatives are.

## 1. Endtest

[Endtest](https://endtest.io/) is a cloud platform where you can create, manage, and execute automated tests.

It's using webdrivers to send commands to the browsers, and it's significantly faster than Selenium.

A major advantage is that it provides all the additional components required for managing test automation, such as a cross-browser cloud grid and features for [collaboration](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/adding-collaborators) and [orchestration](https://endtest.io/docs/advanced/how-to-use-the-endtest-api).

**Features:**
- ✅ Works with Chrome
- ✅ Works with Firefox
- ✅ Works with Safari
- ✅ Works with Edge
- ✅ Works with Internet Explorer 11
- ✅ Works with mobile browsers
- ✅ Supports testing in iframes
- ✅ Supports testing in multiple browser tabs
- ✅ Multiple domains can be tested in same test
- ✅ Supports testing in Shadow DOM
- ✅ Advanced actions such as Drag and Drop
- ✅ Functionality to test API requests

That's why Endtest is a great option for [automated e2e testing](https://codoid.com/automation-testing/what-makes-endtest-io-a-great-option-for-automated-e2e-testing/).

## 2. Playwright

[Playwright](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/) is a Node.js library developed by Microsoft.

It can be used to automate Chromium-based browsers and Firefox.

Currently, there is no clear advantage in using Playwright over Selenium.

**Features:**
- ✅ Works with Chrome
- ✅ Works with Firefox
- ⬜ Works with Safari
- ✅ Works with Edge
- ⬜ Works with Internet Explorer 11
- ⬜ Works with mobile browsers
- ✅ Supports testing in iframes
- ✅ Supports testing in multiple browser tabs
- ✅ Multiple domains can be tested in same test
- ✅ Supports testing in Shadow DOM
- ✅ Advanced actions such as Drag and Drop
- ✅ Functionality to test API requests

## 3. Puppeteer

[Puppeteer](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer/) is a Node.js library developed by Google.

It can be used to automate Chromium-based browsers and it also offers beta support for Firefox.

Incredibly similar to Playwright, even when comparing the speed of execution.

**Features:**
- ✅ Works with Chrome
- ✅ Works with Firefox
- ⬜ Works with Safari
- ✅ Works with Edge
- ⬜ Works with Internet Explorer 11
- ⬜ Works with mobile browsers
- ✅ Supports testing in iframes
- ✅ Supports testing in multiple browser tabs
- ✅ Multiple domains can be tested in same test
- ✅ Supports testing in Shadow DOM
- ✅ Advanced actions such as Drag and Drop
- ✅ Functionality to test API requests

## 4. Cypress

[Cypress](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/) is a wrapper around Mocha that allows you to interact with elements on a web page.

Due to the severe limitations of their technology, it has limited cross-browser support and limited functionalities.

For example, it cannot be used to test in multiple browser tabs.

And the support for iframes seems to be extremely flaky.

**Features:**
- ✅ Works with Chrome
- ✅ Works with Firefox
- ⬜ Works with Safari
- ✅ Works with Edge
- ⬜ Works with Internet Explorer 11
- ⬜ Works with mobile browsers
- ⬜ Supports testing in iframes
- ⬜ Supports testing in multiple browser tabs
- ⬜ Multiple domains can be tested in same test
- ⬜ Supports testing in Shadow DOM
- ✅ Advanced actions such as Drag and Drop
- ⬜ Functionality to test API requests

## 5. Watir

[Watir](http://watir.com/) is an open-source Ruby library.

It can be described as a BDD wrapper around Selenium.

The main advantage is the API is a bit easier to use, adding a layer of simplicity over the heavy Selenium API.

The main disadvantage of using Watir is that it's less popular than Selenium and that makes finding answers for your questions a bit more difficult.

**Features:**
- ✅ Works with Chrome
- ✅ Works with Firefox
- ✅ Works with Safari
- ✅ Works with Edge
- ⬜ Works with Internet Explorer 11
- ⬜ Works with mobile browsers
- ✅ Supports testing in iframes
- ✅ Supports testing in multiple browser tabs
- ✅ Multiple domains can be tested in same test
- ⬜ Supports testing in Shadow DOM
- ⬜ Advanced actions such as Drag and Drop
- ⬜ Functionality to test API requests
